wiki.cat.glossary.desc: Technical terms every bartender should know
wiki.art.techniques.shake.description: Shaking is the most dynamic bartending technique. It rapidly chills, dilutes, and aerates cocktails. Used when recipes include juices, cream, eggs or syrups that need thorough mixing.
wiki.art.techniques.shake.when_to_use: Use shaking when your cocktail contains citrus juice, dairy, eggs, or thick syrups. If the recipe has only spirits and liqueurs, stir instead.
wiki.art.techniques.shake.steps: Fill the shaker with ice (about 2/3 full)|Add all ingredients|Seal the shaker firmly|Shake vigorously for 10-15 seconds|The shaker should feel ice-cold to the touch|Strain into the serving glass
wiki.art.techniques.shake.tips: Use fresh, large ice cubes — small or wet ice dilutes too fast. Shake hard and with confidence. A proper shake creates a "crack" sound rhythm.
wiki.art.techniques.shake.errors: Not shaking long enough (under-diluted, not cold enough). Using crushed ice (over-dilutes). Shaking spirit-only drinks (bruises the spirit, makes it cloudy).
wiki.art.techniques.stir.description: Stirring is the elegant technique for spirit-forward cocktails. It chills and dilutes without aerating, preserving the silky texture and clarity of the drink.
wiki.art.techniques.stir.when_to_use: Use stirring when the cocktail contains only spirits, liqueurs and bitters. Martinis, Negronis, Manhattans and Old Fashioneds are all stirred.
wiki.art.techniques.stir.steps: Fill the mixing glass with ice|Add all ingredients|Insert the bar spoon along the inside of the glass|Stir smoothly in a circular motion for 20-30 seconds|Strain into the serving glass
wiki.art.techniques.stir.tips: Keep the spoon against the glass wall for a smooth motion. Stir, don't chop. The drink should become ice-cold and slightly diluted but crystal clear.
wiki.art.techniques.muddle.description: Muddling gently presses fresh ingredients like herbs, fruit and sugar to release their essential oils and juices. It's about extraction, not destruction.
wiki.art.techniques.muddle.steps: Place fresh ingredients in the bottom of the glass or shaker|Press gently with the muddler using a twisting motion|For herbs: press gently to release oils (don't shred)|For fruits: press more firmly to extract juice|Add remaining ingredients
wiki.art.techniques.muddle.tips: Be gentle with herbs — over-muddling releases bitter chlorophyll. With citrus, press the peel side to extract oils. With sugar, ensure it dissolves completely.
wiki.art.techniques.build.sub: Layer ingredients directly in the glass
wiki.art.techniques.build.description: Building is the simplest technique: ingredients are added directly to the serving glass in order, then gently stirred or left to self-mix. Used for highballs and simple serves.
wiki.art.techniques.build.steps: Fill the serving glass with ice|Pour ingredients in the specified order|For carbonated mixers, pour last and gently|Stir briefly (2-3 rotations) to integrate|Garnish and serve
wiki.art.techniques.layer.description: Layering creates visually stunning drinks by floating ingredients on top of each other based on their density (sugar content). The heaviest liquids go first.
wiki.art.techniques.layer.steps: Pour the heaviest ingredient first (most sugar)|Hold a bar spoon upside down over the glass|Slowly pour the next liquid over the back of the spoon|The liquid should slide gently on top|Repeat for each layer
wiki.art.techniques.layer.tips: Pouring speed is key — go very slowly. Syrups and cream liqueurs sink, spirits float. Temperature affects density, so chill your ingredients.
wiki.art.techniques.strain.sub: Separating liquid from ice and solids
wiki.art.techniques.strain.description: Straining separates the finished cocktail from ice, fruit pulp, herbs and other solids. Different strainers serve different purposes.
wiki.art.techniques.strain.steps: Place the Hawthorne strainer on the shaker or mixing glass|For extra-smooth drinks, also use a fine mesh strainer (double strain)|Pour steadily into the serving glass|For cocktails "on the rocks," strain over fresh ice
wiki.art.techniques.blend.description: Blending creates frozen, smooth cocktails with a slushy consistency. Essential for tropical drinks and frozen margaritas.
wiki.art.techniques.blend.steps: Add all liquid ingredients to the blender|Add 1-2 cups of ice|Blend on high until smooth and uniform|Pour directly into the serving glass|Garnish and serve immediately
wiki.art.spirits.whisky.description: Whisky is a distilled spirit made from fermented grain mash, aged in wooden casks. The spelling varies: "whisky" in Scotland and Canada, "whiskey" in Ireland and the US.
wiki.art.spirits.whisky.types: Single Malt (one distillery, malted barley), Blended (mix of malt and grain whiskies), Bourbon (51%+ corn, American oak, USA), Rye (51%+ rye grain), Irish (triple distilled, smooth), Japanese (Scottish methods, Japanese precision).
wiki.art.spirits.whisky.production: Malting → Mashing → Fermentation → Distillation (pot or column still) → Aging in oak casks → Blending → Bottling. Minimum aging varies: Scotch 3 years, Bourbon no minimum but typically 2-4+ years.
wiki.art.spirits.whisky.regions: Scotland (Speyside, Islay, Highland, Lowland, Campbeltown), Ireland, USA (Kentucky, Tennessee), Canada, Japan, Taiwan, India.
wiki.art.spirits.whisky.origin: Scotland and Ireland both claim the birthright of whisky, with records dating back to 1494 in Scotland (Exchequer Rolls) and the 12th century in Ireland. The word derives from the Gaelic 'uisce beatha' (water of life). Today it is produced in over 30 countries, but Scotland, Ireland, the United States, Canada, and Japan are the five great regions recognized worldwide.
wiki.art.spirits.whisky.history: 1494: First written record of whisky distillation in Scotland. 1608: Old Bushmills receives the first distilling license in Ireland. 1789: Bourbon is born in Kentucky with Scottish and Irish settlers. 1823: The Excise Act legalizes distillation in Scotland, boosting the industry. 1920-1933: Prohibition in the US devastates American distillers but benefits Canada. 1923: Shinjiro Torii founds Yamazaki, Japan's first whisky distillery. 2003: Japanese whisky gains worldwide recognition with international awards.
wiki.art.spirits.whisky.tasting: Scotch Speyside: honey, fruit, vanilla, malt. Islay: intense peat, iodine, smoke, seaweed, medicinal. Highland: heather, dried fruits, spices. Bourbon: caramel, vanilla, sweet corn, toasted oak, cinnamon. Rye: spicy rye grain, black pepper, forest berries, dry finish. Irish: smooth, triple-distilled, green apple, cereals, touch of honey. Japanese: delicate, white fruits, floral, balanced, elegant finish.
wiki.art.spirits.whisky.cocktails: Old Fashioned (bourbon or rye, sugar, Angostura, orange peel — the cocktail that defined the word 'cocktail'). Whisky Sour (bourbon, lemon, sugar, optional egg white). Manhattan (rye or bourbon, sweet vermouth, Angostura). Rob Roy (Scotch, sweet vermouth, Angostura). Penicillin (blended Scotch, lemon, honey-ginger, Islay float). Mint Julep (bourbon, mint, sugar — the Kentucky Derby classic).
wiki.art.spirits.whisky.tips: Serve single malt at room temperature with a few drops of water to open up the aromas. Bourbon works well both neat and in cocktails. Ice dilutes and cools: use a large sphere to slow dilution. For tasting: nose first without swirling, then with a gentle circular motion. Store bottles upright, away from direct light.
wiki.art.spirits.gin.description: Gin is a spirit flavored primarily with juniper berries and other botanicals. From London Dry to New Western, gin offers incredible diversity of flavors.
wiki.art.spirits.gin.botanicals: Juniper (mandatory), coriander, angelica root, citrus peel (lemon, orange), orris root, cassia bark, cardamom, cubeb, grains of paradise. Modern gins may include cucumber, rose, lavender and exotic spices.
wiki.art.spirits.gin.styles: London Dry (classic, juniper-forward), Plymouth (slightly sweeter, earthy), Old Tom (sweeter, historical), New Western (contemporary, less juniper), Navy Strength (57%+ ABV), Sloe Gin (infused with sloe berries).
wiki.art.spirits.gin.origin: Holland, 17th century. Genever (juniper in Dutch) was created as medicine by physician Franciscus Sylvius at the University of Leiden around 1650. English soldiers discovered it during the Thirty Years' War ('Dutch courage') and brought it to England, where it evolved into the dry gin we know today.
wiki.art.spirits.gin.history: 1650: Dutch genever becomes popular as a medicinal remedy. 1689: William of Orange takes the English throne and encourages gin distillation. 1720-1751: The 'Gin Craze' devastates London; more gin is consumed than beer. 1751: The Gin Act regulates production and sales. 1830: Aeneas Coffey invents the column still, enabling purer distillates that give rise to London Dry. 1870s: Gin & tonic becomes popular in British India as a way to consume quinine against malaria. 2010s: The artisanal gin renaissance transforms the category with hundreds of new brands.
wiki.art.spirits.gin.tasting: London Dry: dominant juniper, fresh citrus, white pepper, earthy angelica root, clean dry finish. Plymouth: softer, earthy, root notes, slightly sweet, less aggressive than London Dry. Old Tom: notable sweetness, moderate juniper, liquorice, gentle spices. Navy Strength: amplified intensity of all botanicals, alcoholic warmth, long robust finish. New Western: juniper takes a back seat to botanicals like cucumber, rose, citrus, lavender, or exotic spices.
wiki.art.spirits.gin.cocktails: Gin & Tonic (gin, tonic water, lime or citrus — the perfect serve). Martini (gin, dry vermouth, olive or lemon twist — the king of cocktails). Negroni (gin, Campari, sweet vermouth — perfect bitter balance). Tom Collins (gin, lemon, sugar, soda). Gimlet (gin, lime cordial). Aviation (gin, maraschino, crème de violette, lemon). Last Word (gin, green Chartreuse, maraschino, lime — equal parts).
wiki.art.spirits.gin.tips: For a perfect G&T, use a balloon glass with plenty of ice, pour gin first then tonic down the side of the glass to preserve bubbles. A Martini should be stirred or shaken according to preference: stirred is clearer, shaken is colder and more diluted. Store gin at room temperature or slightly chilled. Floral gins pair better with mild tonics; classic gins with more bitter tonics.
wiki.art.spirits.rum.description: Rum is distilled from sugarcane juice or molasses. It ranges from light and crisp white rums to rich, complex aged dark rums.
wiki.art.spirits.rum.types: White/Silver (unaged or lightly aged, light), Gold (medium-aged, caramel notes), Dark (long-aged, rich and complex), Spiced (infused with spices and caramel), Overproof (high ABV, 60%+), Agricole (from fresh sugarcane juice).
wiki.art.spirits.rum.regions: Caribbean (Cuba, Jamaica, Puerto Rico, Barbados, Trinidad), Central America (Guatemala, Nicaragua, Panama), South America (Venezuela, Guyana), Indian Ocean (Mauritius, Réunion).
wiki.art.spirits.rum.origin: Caribbean, 17th century. Slaves on sugar cane plantations discovered that molasses, a byproduct of sugar refining, could be fermented and distilled. Barbados was likely the birthplace of commercial rum, with the first written record in 1651. The word 'rum' may derive from 'rumbullion' (tumult) or the Latin 'saccharum' (sugar).
wiki.art.spirits.rum.history: 1651: First record of rum in Barbados ('rumbullion'). 1655: The Royal Navy conquers Jamaica and adopts a daily rum ration for sailors. 1740: Admiral Vernon orders rum diluted with water, creating 'grog'. 1862: Don Facundo Bacardí founds his distillery in Santiago de Cuba, revolutionizing light rum with charcoal filtration. 1944: The rum ration is abolished in the US Navy. 1950s-60s: Tiki culture popularizes rum cocktails worldwide. 2000s: The premium rum renaissance and sipping rum culture emerges.
wiki.art.spirits.rum.production: Two main methods: 1) Industrial rum (majority): distilled from fermented molasses, a byproduct of sugar refining. 2) Rhum agricole: distilled from fresh sugarcane juice, producing a more herbaceous, earthy spirit (Martinique, Guadeloupe). Fermentation can last from 24 hours to several weeks. Distillation in pot stills (heavy rums, Jamaica) or column stills (light rums, Cuba, Puerto Rico). Aging in American oak barrels, often ex-bourbon casks.
wiki.art.spirits.rum.tasting: White: clean, subtle sweetness, fresh cane, mineral notes, ideal for cocktails. Gold: caramel, vanilla, banana, gentle oak, balanced. Dark/Aged: molasses, ripe tropical fruits, chocolate, tobacco, leather, warm spices, long complex finish. Agricole: herbaceous, earthy, green cane, floral, volcanic minerals. Jamaican: intense esters, tropical fruits, varnish, characteristic funk. Overproof: all flavours amplified, alcoholic heat, extreme intensity.
wiki.art.spirits.rum.cocktails: Mojito (white rum, lime, sugar, mint, soda — the Cuban classic). Daiquiri (white rum, lime, sugar — perfection in three ingredients). Piña Colada (rum, pineapple, coconut cream). Mai Tai (aged rums, curaçao, orgeat, lime — the tiki king). Cuba Libre (rum, cola, lime). Dark 'n' Stormy (Goslings dark rum, ginger beer). Planter's Punch (Jamaican rum, citrus, grenadine). Ti' Punch (rhum agricole, lime, cane syrup — the Antillean ritual).
wiki.art.spirits.rum.tips: Use light Cuban-style rum for mojitos. Quality aged rums are best enjoyed neat or with a large ice cube. Jamaican rum adds exceptional complexity to tiki cocktails. Store at room temperature, away from light. Rhum agricole is best appreciated at room temperature to capture its herbaceous notes.
wiki.art.spirits.vodka.description: Vodka is a clear, neutral spirit traditionally made from grains or potatoes. Valued for its purity and versatility in cocktails.
wiki.art.spirits.vodka.production: Made from fermented grains (wheat, rye, corn), potatoes, or even grapes. Distilled multiple times for purity, then filtered through charcoal or other media. Typically bottled at 40% ABV.
wiki.art.spirits.vodka.origin: Poland and Russia dispute vodka's origin, with Polish records from the 8th century and Russian from the 14th century. The word comes from the Slavic 'voda' (water), as a diminutive: 'little water'. Historically a medicine and popular peasant drink. Today it is produced worldwide, with Poland, Russia, Sweden, Finland, and France as the most prestigious producers.
wiki.art.spirits.vodka.history: 8th century: First distillation records in Poland. 14th century: First mentions of vodka in Russia. 1405: First documented mention of the word 'vodka' in a Polish manuscript. 1894: Dmitri Mendeleev (creator of the periodic table) supposedly establishes the 40% ABV standard in Russia. 1934: Smirnoff arrives in the US after the Russian revolution. 1941: The Moscow Mule is born in Hollywood and popularizes vodka in America. 1962: James Bond orders his Vodka Martini 'shaken, not stirred', catapulting vodka into popular culture. 1980s-2000s: Premium and ultra-premium vodka boom.
wiki.art.spirits.vodka.types: Grain-based: wheat (smooth, slightly sweet), rye (spicier, full-bodied), corn (sweet, creamy). Potato (rich, creamy, oily texture). Grape (smooth, fruity, elegant). Flavoured: lemon, raspberry, pepper, vanilla. Filtration: activated charcoal, quartz, diamond, silver (each method contributes different textures).
wiki.art.spirits.vodka.tasting: Although defined by its neutrality, quality vodkas have their own character. Wheat: clean, fresh bread notes, smooth sweet finish. Rye: spicier, white pepper, medium body, peppery finish. Potato: creamy, earthy, unctuous texture, warm finish. Grape: delicate, fruity, subtle floral notes, silky finish. On the palate: texture (viscosity, warmth, smoothness) is what distinguishes great vodkas.
wiki.art.spirits.vodka.cocktails: Vodka Martini (vodka, dry vermouth, lemon twist or olive). Moscow Mule (vodka, ginger beer, lime, served in a copper mug). Cosmopolitan (citrus vodka, triple sec, cranberry juice, lime). Bloody Mary (vodka, tomato juice, spices, celery). Espresso Martini (vodka, coffee liqueur, espresso). White Russian (vodka, Kahlúa, cream). Vodka Tonic (vodka, tonic, lemon — perfect simplicity).
wiki.art.spirits.vodka.tips: Keep vodka in the freezer to serve ice-cold with a dense, viscous texture. For tasting, serve at room temperature to appreciate differences between bases (wheat, rye, potato). Vodka is the most versatile spirit in cocktails: it doesn't dominate but enhances other ingredients. Use quality vodka for Martinis and simple drinks where its character takes centre stage.
wiki.art.spirits.tequila.description: Tequila is made exclusively from blue Weber agave in designated regions of Mexico. From unaged Blanco to complex Añejo, it offers remarkable depth.
wiki.art.spirits.tequila.types: Blanco/Silver (unaged, pure agave flavor), Reposado (aged 2-12 months, mellow), Añejo (aged 1-3 years, complex), Extra Añejo (aged 3+ years, ultra-premium), Cristalino (aged then charcoal-filtered clear).
wiki.art.spirits.tequila.production: Harvest blue agave (7-10 years to mature) → Cook piñas in ovens → Crush and extract juice → Ferment → Double distill → Age in oak barrels (optional). Must be 51%+ agave; "100% agave" is the quality standard.
wiki.art.spirits.tequila.origin: Jalisco, Mexico. Tequila was born in the Tequila region of Jalisco, where indigenous peoples already fermented agave to produce pulque. Spanish conquistadors first distilled agave in the 16th century, creating 'vino de mezcal'. The Denomination of Origin protects its production in Jalisco and limited regions of Guanajuato, Michoacán, Nayarit, and Tamaulipas.
wiki.art.spirits.tequila.history: 16th century: The Spanish first distil agave in New Spain. 1758: The Cuervo family obtains the first concession to produce commercial tequila. 1795: José María Guadalupe de Cuervo receives the first official licence. 1873: Cenobio Sauza exports tequila to the US for the first time. 1974: Mexico declares tequila a Denomination of Origin. 2003: The Extra Añejo category is created. 2006: UNESCO declares the agave landscapes of Tequila a World Heritage Site. 2010s: Global boom of premium and ultra-premium tequila.
wiki.art.spirits.tequila.tasting: Blanco: pure agave, citrus, white pepper, herbaceous, mineral, clean peppery finish. Reposado: softened agave, vanilla, light caramel, subtle oak, sweet spices, medium finish. Añejo: pronounced oak, intense vanilla, dark caramel, chocolate, dried fruits, long complex finish. Extra Añejo: dominant wood, leather, tobacco, deep vanilla, dark honey, ultra-long finish. Cristalino: combines the complexity of añejo with the visual clarity of blanco.
wiki.art.spirits.tequila.cocktails: Margarita (tequila, triple sec, lime, salt — the world's most famous Mexican cocktail). Paloma (tequila, grapefruit soda, lime, salt — Mexico's real favourite). Tequila Sunrise (tequila, orange juice, grenadine). Tommy's Margarita (tequila, lime, agave syrup — the modern, pure version). Batanga (tequila, Coca-Cola, lime, salt). Tequila Neat/Shot (with sangrita as a traditional accompaniment).
wiki.art.spirits.tequila.tips: Always look for '100% agave' on the label; mixto tequilas contain up to 49% other sugars. For tasting, use a Riedel-style glass or an elongated caballito. Blanco is ideal for cocktails; Reposado and Añejo for slow sipping. Salt and lime are for low-quality tequila; good tequila is sipped neat. Cristalino is the current trend, combining añejo smoothness with visual freshness.
wiki.art.spirits.brandy.description: Brandy is a spirit produced by distilling wine or fermented fruit juice. Cognac and Armagnac are the most prestigious varieties.
wiki.art.spirits.brandy.types: Cognac (from Cognac, France, double distilled), Armagnac (from Gascony, single distilled), Pisco (South America, from grapes), Calvados (from apples, Normandy), Grappa (from grape pomace, Italy), Fruit brandies (cherry, plum, pear).
wiki.art.spirits.brandy.origin: France and the Mediterranean basin. Brandy originated from wine distillation, a practice dating back to the Arabs in the Iberian Peninsula (8th century) that was perfected in the Cognac region of France in the 17th century. The word 'brandy' comes from the Dutch 'brandewijn' (burnt wine), because Dutch merchants distilled wine to facilitate maritime transport.
wiki.art.spirits.brandy.history: 8th century: Arabs introduce distillation to Europe. 16th century: The Dutch distil French wines to preserve them during transport. 1622: First mention of 'brandewijn'. 17th century: Cognac and Armagnac establish themselves as regions of excellence. 1713: The first age classification system is created (VS, VSOP, XO). 1800s: Phylloxera devastates French vineyards, drastically reducing production. 1882: The Pisco denomination is born in Peru and Chile.
wiki.art.spirits.brandy.production: Distilled from grape wine (or fermented fruit). Cognac: double distillation in charentais pot stills, minimum 2 years ageing in French Limousin or Tronçais oak. Armagnac: single distillation in a continuous still, ageing in Gascon oak. Pisco: distillation of fresh must, no ageing (pisco puro) or brief resting. Calvados: distillation of Norman apple cider. Grappa: distillation of pomace (skins, seeds, stems).
wiki.art.spirits.brandy.tasting: Cognac VS: young fruits, gentle oak, notes of flowers and spices. VSOP: dried fruits, vanilla, caramel, balanced oak. XO: dark chocolate, leather, tobacco, candied fruits, complex spices, extremely long finish. Armagnac: more rustic, plums, tobacco, walnuts, earthy character. Pisco: floral, fresh fruits (grape, apple), citrus, herbaceous, clean. Calvados: intense apple, cider, butter, vanilla, cinnamon. Grappa: intense, pomace, herbal, concentrated grape notes.
wiki.art.spirits.brandy.cocktails: Sidecar (cognac, triple sec, lemon — Parisian elegance). Brandy Alexander (cognac, crème de cacao, cream — liquid dessert). Sazerac (with cognac in its original version, Peychaud's, absinthe). Pisco Sour (pisco, lemon, sugar, egg white, Angostura — Peruvian pride). Corpse Reviver No. 1 (cognac, Calvados, sweet vermouth). Vieux Carré (cognac, rye, sweet vermouth, Bénédictine, bitters).
wiki.art.spirits.brandy.tips: Cognac is served in a balloon or tulip glass at room temperature; the warmth of the hand releases the aromas. Never heat with a direct flame: it destroys delicate aromas. Armagnac offers excellent value compared to Cognac. Pisco should be served cold for Pisco Sours. Italian grappa is served cold in small glasses as a digestif.
wiki.art.spirits.distillation.descriptio: Distillation is the process of heating a fermented liquid to separate alcohol from water, then condensing the vapor back into liquid. It's the fundamental process behind all spirits.
wiki.art.spirits.distillation.process: Heat the fermented wash in the pot still (caldera)|Alcohol evaporates first (lower boiling point than water)|Vapors rise through the swan neck (cuello de cisne)|Vapors cool in the condenser, becoming liquid again|The distiller separates heads, hearts and tails|Hearts (the good stuff) are collected for aging or bottling
wiki.art.spirits.fermentation.descriptio: Alcoholic fermentation is the metabolic process where yeast converts sugars into ethanol and carbon dioxide. It's the foundation of all alcoholic beverages.
wiki.art.spirits.fermentation.process: Sugars are present in the base material (grapes, grain, sugarcane)|Yeast is added (or wild yeast naturally present)|Yeast consumes sugar and produces ethanol + CO₂|Temperature is controlled (15-35°C depending on product)|Fermentation takes days to weeks|The result is a low-alcohol "wash" or "wine" ready for distillation or consumption
wiki.art.history.timeline.sub: From ancient times to modern era
wiki.art.history.origins.description: The word "cocktail" first appeared in print in 1806 in The Balance and Columbian Repository, defined as "a stimulating liquor composed of any kind of sugar, water, and bitters." However, the practice of mixing drinks dates back centuries. Ancient civilizations mixed wines with herbs and spices for medicinal purposes. The modern cocktail evolved from colonial-era punches and toddies in the Americas.
wiki.art.history.prohibition.description: The 18th Amendment banned alcohol production and sale in the US from 1920-1933. Paradoxically, it boosted cocktail culture: speakeasies thrived, bartenders emigrated to Europe and Cuba spreading their craft, and mixers were used to mask the taste of poorly-made bootleg spirits. The cocktail was forever changed — many classic recipes were born from necessity during this era.
wiki.art.history.iba.description: The International Bartenders Association (IBA) was founded in 1951 at the Grand Hotel in Torquay, England. It maintains the official list of cocktail recipes used in World Cocktail Competitions. Currently there are about 90 official IBA cocktails divided into three categories: The Unforgettables, Contemporary Classics, and New Era Drinks.
wiki.art.history.tiki-culture.descriptio: Tiki culture began in the 1930s with Don the Beachcomber (Ernest Gantt) and Trader Vic (Victor Bergeron). They created elaborate tropical cocktails with multiple rums, exotic juices and secret syrups, served in carved tiki mugs. The movement peaked in the 1950s-60s, faded, and experienced a major revival in the 2000s. Tiki gave us the Mai Tai, Zombie, Piña Colada and the art of complex, multi-layered drinks.
wiki.art.tools.shaker.description: The cocktail shaker is the most iconic bar tool. It rapidly chills and mixes ingredients through vigorous agitation.
wiki.art.tools.shaker.types: Boston Shaker (two-piece: tin + glass or tin + tin, preferred by professionals), Cobbler Shaker (three-piece: base + strainer + cap, easiest for beginners), French/Parisian Shaker (two-piece: elegant, no built-in strainer).
wiki.art.tools.shaker.tips: Always seal firmly before shaking. Point the top away from guests. A good shake lasts 10-15 seconds. The outside should frost over when properly chilled.
wiki.art.tools.jigger.description: The jigger is a dual-sided measuring tool essential for consistent cocktails. Accuracy in measurement is what separates a good drink from a great one.
wiki.art.tools.jigger.sizes: Standard: 30ml / 60ml (1oz / 2oz). Japanese-style jiggers offer more precise measurements with internal markings at 15ml, 22.5ml, 30ml, 45ml, 60ml.
wiki.art.tools.strainer.description: Strainers prevent ice, fruit pulp and herb pieces from entering the finished cocktail. Essential for a clean presentation.
wiki.art.tools.strainer.types: Hawthorne Strainer (spring-loaded, fits on shaker tins, most common), Julep Strainer (perforated bowl, fits in mixing glasses), Fine Mesh Strainer (for double-straining, catches tiny particles).
wiki.art.tools.muddler.description: A muddler is a pestle-like tool used to press fresh ingredients in the glass to release their flavors, oils and juices.
wiki.art.tools.muddler.tips: Use the flat end for pressing, not pounding. Wood and stainless steel are common materials. For herbs, a gentle press is enough — you want oils, not bitter chlorophyll.
wiki.art.tools.bar-spoon.description: The bar spoon is a long, twisted-handle spoon used for stirring, layering and measuring. The twist helps create a smooth stirring motion. One bar spoon equals approximately 5ml.
wiki.art.tools.glassware.sub: The right glass for every drink
wiki.art.tools.glassware.description: Choosing the right glass enhances the drinking experience — it affects aroma, temperature and presentation. Each glass shape serves a specific purpose.
wiki.art.wines.red-wines.description: Red wines are made from dark-skinned grapes, with the skins left in contact during fermentation to extract color, tannins and flavor. They range from light (Pinot Noir) to full-bodied (Cabernet Sauvignon).
wiki.art.wines.red-wines.varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon (bold, tannic, dark fruit), Merlot (medium, plummy, soft), Pinot Noir (light, elegant, cherry), Malbec (rich, dark, Argentine specialty), Tempranillo (Spanish classic, earthy), Syrah/Shiraz (spicy, peppery, dark).
wiki.art.wines.red-wines.origin: Reds are produced in every wine region worldwide. The most iconic: Bordeaux and Burgundy (France), Tuscany and Piedmont (Italy), Rioja and Ribera del Duero (Spain), Mendoza (Argentina), Napa Valley (USA), Barossa Valley (Australia), Stellenbosch (South Africa), Central Valley (Chile).
wiki.art.wines.red-wines.tasting: Cabernet Sauvignon: blackcurrant, cedar, green bell pepper, firm tannins, long finish. Pinot Noir: cherry, raspberry, damp earth, silky tannins, elegant. Malbec: black plum, violet, chocolate, sweet spices, velvety. Tempranillo: ripe cherry, leather, vanilla, earthy. Syrah/Shiraz: black pepper, blackberry, violet, smoky, powerful. Merlot: plum, cherry, milk chocolate, soft tannins.
wiki.art.wines.red-wines.cocktails: Sangria (red wine, fruits, brandy, sugar, soda — the Spanish classic). Kalimotxo (red wine, Coca-Cola — a Basque Country icon). Mulled Wine/Glühwein (heated red wine, spices, citrus — a winter tradition). New York Sour (whiskey sour with a red wine float). Red wine is also used in reductions and sauces for molecular mixology.
wiki.art.wines.red-wines.tips: Serve between 16-18°C; lighter reds (Pinot Noir) cooler, full-bodied (Cabernet) warmer. Decant young, powerful wines for at least 30 minutes. Tannins pair perfectly with proteins and fats (meats, aged cheeses). Store horizontally at 12-15°C, without vibration or direct light.
wiki.art.wines.white-wines.description: White wines are typically made from green-skinned grapes or from dark grapes without skin contact. They range from bone-dry to lusciously sweet.
wiki.art.wines.white-wines.varieties: Chardonnay (versatile, can be oaked or unoaked), Sauvignon Blanc (crisp, citrus, herbaceous), Riesling (aromatic, can be dry or sweet), Pinot Grigio (light, crisp, Italian), Albariño (Spanish, citrus, mineral), Gewürztraminer (aromatic, lychee, spice).
wiki.art.wines.white-wines.origin: Great white wine regions: Burgundy, Loire, Alsace (France), Mosel and Rheingau (Germany), Rías Baixas (Spain), Trentino-Alto Adige and Friuli (Italy), Marlborough (New Zealand), Margaret River (Australia), Casablanca (Chile), Stellenbosch (South Africa).
wiki.art.wines.white-wines.tasting: Unoaked Chardonnay: green apple, citrus, mineral. Oaked: butter, vanilla, ripe fruit, toasty. Sauvignon Blanc: cut grass, grapefruit, passion fruit, mineral, vibrant acidity. Dry Riesling: lime, petrol, white flowers, electric acidity. Albariño: white peach, citrus, saline, mineral. Gewürztraminer: lychee, rose, ginger, spicy, exotic.
wiki.art.wines.white-wines.cocktails: White wine Spritz (white wine, soda, citrus twist). Kir (white wine, crème de cassis — the Burgundian aperitif). Hugo (white wine/prosecco, elderflower, mint, soda). White Wine Sangria (white wine, tropical fruits, orange liqueur). Sauvignon Blanc is excellent as a base for summer punches.
wiki.art.wines.white-wines.tips: Serve between 8-12°C; lighter whites colder, oaked whites warmer. Don't over-chill: it destroys the aromas. Whites with high acidity (Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling) are the best pairing for seafood and fish. An oaked Chardonnay substitutes well for red with poultry and creamy pastas.
wiki.art.wines.sparkling.description: Sparkling wines contain significant CO₂, creating effervescence. The finest are made using the traditional method (méthode champenoise) with secondary fermentation in the bottle.
wiki.art.wines.sparkling.types: Champagne (France, traditional method, the gold standard), Prosecco (Italy, Charmat/tank method, lighter and fruitier), Cava (Spain, traditional method, great value), Crémant (French regions outside Champagne), Sekt (Germany), Franciacorta (Italy, traditional method).
wiki.art.wines.sparkling.origin: Champagne, France, is the birthplace of quality sparkling wine. Dom Pérignon (Benedictine monk, 17th century) perfected the method of secondary fermentation in bottle. Key regions: Champagne (France), Veneto (Prosecco, Italy), Penedès (Cava, Spain), Franciacorta (Italy), German regions (Sekt).
wiki.art.wines.sparkling.history: 1668: Dom Pérignon arrives at the Abbey of Hautvillers and revolutionizes winemaking. 1729: Ruinart becomes the first Champagne house. 1772: Veuve Clicquot perfects 'riddling' (remuage, lees removal). 1874: The Charmat method is invented for tank-produced sparkling wines (basis for Prosecco). 20th century: Spanish Cava and Italian Franciacorta gain worldwide recognition.
wiki.art.wines.sparkling.tasting: Champagne Brut: apple, brioche, almond, fine persistent bubbles, elegant acidity. Blanc de Blancs (100% Chardonnay): citrus, mineral, elegant, delicate bubbles. Blanc de Noirs (Pinot Noir/Meunier): red fruits, body, structure. Prosecco: pear, green apple, floral, larger bubbles, fresh and light. Cava: citrus, toasty, dried fruits, excellent value.
wiki.art.wines.sparkling.cocktails: French 75 (gin, lemon, sugar, champagne — pure elegance). Bellini (prosecco, peach purée — born at Harry's Bar, Venice). Kir Royal (champagne, crème de cassis). Mimosa (champagne, orange juice). Aperol Spritz (Aperol, prosecco, soda). Champagne Cocktail (champagne, sugar, Angostura, lemon twist). Death in the Afternoon (absinthe, champagne — created by Hemingway).
wiki.art.wines.sparkling.tips: Serve at 6-10°C. Use a flute or tulip glass to preserve bubbles and concentrate aromas. Never shake the bottle. When opening, hold the cork and turn the bottle, not the cork. Vintage Champagne improves in bottle for 10-20 years. Prosecco should be consumed young and fresh.
wiki.art.wines.fortified.description: Fortified wines have a distilled spirit (usually brandy) added during or after fermentation, raising the alcohol level and adding complexity.
wiki.art.wines.fortified.types: Port (Portugal, sweet, rich), Sherry/Jerez (Spain, ranges from dry Fino to sweet Pedro Ximénez), Madeira (Portuguese island, heated aging process), Marsala (Sicily, used in cooking and sipping).
wiki.art.wines.fortified.origin: Fortified wines were born from the need to preserve wine during long sea voyages. Port: Douro Valley, Portugal. Sherry: Jerez Triangle (Sanlúcar, El Puerto, Jerez), Spain. Madeira: Madeira Island, Portugal. Marsala: Sicily, Italy. The addition of brandy halted fermentation, preserving natural sweetness and stabilizing the wine.
wiki.art.wines.fortified.history: 14th century: English merchants begin exporting Port and Sherry wines. 1587: Sir Francis Drake raids Cádiz and takes 2,900 barrels of sherry to England. 17th century: The addition of brandy to Douro wine is standardized to create modern Port. 1775: The world's first Denomination of Origin is established: the Marco de Jerez. 19th century: Phylloxera devastates vineyards, but sherry and madeira zones partially survive.
wiki.art.wines.fortified.tasting: Fino/Manzanilla: almond, yeast, saline, dry, light, ideal as an aperitif. Amontillado: hazelnut, caramel, amber, dry, complex. Oloroso: walnut, dark caramel, leather, powerful. Pedro Ximénez: raisins, figs, honey, chocolate, extremely sweet. Port Ruby: red fruit, cherry, sweet, vibrant. Port Tawny: caramel, walnut, dried fruits, silky. Madeira: caramel, dried fruits, vibrant acidity, virtually indestructible.
wiki.art.wines.fortified.cocktails: Sherry Cobbler (sherry, sugar, fresh fruit — one of the earliest cocktails in history). Adonis (fino sherry, sweet vermouth, orange bitters). Port Tonic (white port, tonic, mint — a Portuguese trend). Bamboo (dry sherry, dry vermouth, bitters). Fino sherry is a secret ingredient for adding depth to many classic cocktails. PX is used as a sweet modifier in modern mixology.
wiki.art.wines.fortified.tips: Fino and Manzanilla must be served very cold (6-8°C) and consumed quickly once opened (1-2 weeks refrigerated). Olorosos and PX last weeks after opening. Tawny Port is served slightly cool (12-14°C). Madeira is virtually eternal once bottled thanks to its heating process (estufagem).
wiki.art.wines.vermouth.description: Vermouth is an aromatized, fortified wine flavored with botanicals. It is essential for cocktails like the Martini, Manhattan and Negroni.
wiki.art.wines.vermouth.types: Dry/French (pale, herbal, used in Martinis), Sweet/Italian/Rosso (dark, sweet, caramel, used in Negronis and Manhattans), Bianco (white, sweet, vanilla notes), Rosé (pink, light, modern style).
wiki.art.wines.vermouth.origin: Turin, Italy (sweet/rosso vermouth, 18th century) and southern France (dry vermouth, 19th century). Antonio Benedetto Carpano created the first commercial vermouth in Turin in 1786. Joseph Noilly created the first French dry vermouth in 1813 in Marseillan. The word 'vermouth' comes from the German 'Wermut' (wormwood), one of its key botanicals.
wiki.art.wines.vermouth.history: 1786: Antonio Benedetto Carpano invents modern vermouth in his Turin shop, becoming the favourite drink of the King of Sardinia's court. 1838: The Cinzano brothers found their vermouth house. 1863: Martini & Rossi is established. 1813: Joseph Noilly creates dry vermouth in France. 20th century: Vermouth becomes a pillar of classic cocktails (Martini, Manhattan, Negroni). 2010s: Renaissance of artisanal vermouth in Spain, Italy, and worldwide.
wiki.art.wines.vermouth.tasting: Sweet/Rosso: caramel, bitter herbs, vanilla, liquorice, dark fruits, warm spices. Dry: fresh herbs, chamomile, citrus peel, floral, clean bitter finish. Bianco: vanilla, white flowers, soft citrus, moderate sweetness. Rosé: red fruits, floral, light, fresh. Extra Dry: very dry, mineral, herbaceous, barely sweet.
wiki.art.wines.vermouth.cocktails: Martini (gin, dry vermouth — the absolute king). Manhattan (whiskey, sweet vermouth, Angostura). Negroni (gin, Campari, sweet vermouth — perfect balance). Americano (Campari, sweet vermouth, soda). Rob Roy (Scotch, sweet vermouth). Reverse Manhattan (more vermouth than whiskey). Vermouth on ice with orange and olive is the Mediterranean aperitivo tradition.
wiki.art.wines.vermouth.tips: ALWAYS refrigerate after opening; vermouth is wine and it oxidizes. Consume within 1-2 months once opened. Vermouth quality hugely affects the cocktail: a good Martini requires good vermouth. For a perfect Negroni, the classic ratio is 1:1:1. Sweet vermouth is served over ice with an orange slice and olive as an aperitif.
wiki.timeline.natural_fermentation: Natural fermentation occurs as fruits ferment spontaneously. Early humans discover the effects of alcohol.
wiki.timeline.agriculture: The agricultural revolution begins. Humans cultivate cereals and fruits, enabling intentional production of fermented beverages.
wiki.timeline.wine_beer: Evidence of wine production in Georgia and beer brewing in Mesopotamia. Fermented beverages become central to civilization.
wiki.timeline.egypt_mesopotamia: Egypt and Mesopotamia develop brewing and winemaking as sophisticated crafts. Beer is a daily staple, wine is for the elite.
wiki.timeline.greece_rome: Greeks and Romans spread wine culture across the Mediterranean. Symposiums and banquets make wine central to social life.
wiki.timeline.china_alchemy: Chinese alchemists experiment with distillation. Early proto-distillation techniques appear across Asia.
wiki.timeline.arab_distillation: Arab alchemists perfect the alembic (pot still). The word "alcohol" comes from Arabic "al-kuhl." María la Judía is credited with early distillation apparatus.
wiki.timeline.european_spirits: Distillation knowledge reaches Europe via Moorish Spain. Monks produce "aqua vitae" (water of life) for medicinal use.
wiki.timeline.coffee_discovery: Coffee is discovered in Yemen/Ethiopia. Coffeehouses spread across the Ottoman Empire, eventually reaching Europe.
wiki.timeline.colonial_spirits: Colonial era: rum production booms in the Caribbean, genever evolves into gin in England, whisky production develops in Scotland and Ireland.
wiki.timeline.cocktail_birth: The cocktail is born. The word appears in print in 1806. Bartending becomes a craft profession.
wiki.timeline.jerry_thomas: Jerry Thomas publishes "The Bar-Tender's Guide," the first cocktail book. He elevates bartending to an art form.
wiki.timeline.prohibition: Prohibition in the US (1920-1933). Speakeasies flourish, bartenders flee to Europe and Cuba, cocktail culture goes underground but thrives.
wiki.timeline.iba_founded: The International Bartenders Association (IBA) is founded in Torquay, England, standardizing cocktail recipes worldwide.
wiki.timeline.tiki_era: Tiki culture peaks. Don the Beachcomber and Trader Vic create tropical cocktail paradises with elaborate rum-based drinks.
wiki.timeline.craft_revolution: The craft cocktail revolution begins. Bartenders rediscover classic recipes, fresh ingredients and artisanal spirits.
wiki.timeline.modern_era: Modern era: sustainability, low-ABV, no-alcohol cocktails, technology in bartending. The future of mixology embraces innovation and tradition.
wiki.gloss.aguardiente.def: General term for distilled spirits, literally "fire water." Refers to various unaged or lightly aged spirits across different cultures.
wiki.gloss.destilado.def: Any alcoholic beverage produced by distillation of a fermented base.
wiki.gloss.alcohol.def: Ethyl alcohol (ethanol, C₂H₅OH), the type of alcohol safe for consumption. Produced by yeast fermentation of sugars.
wiki.gloss.ethanol.def: The chemical compound C₂H₅OH, the specific type of alcohol found in beverages. Boiling point 78.37°C.
wiki.gloss.proof.def: A measure of alcohol content. US proof = 2× ABV (e.g., 80 proof = 40% ABV). UK proof differs historically.
wiki.gloss.abv.def: Alcohol By Volume — the standard measure of alcohol content as a percentage of total volume.
wiki.gloss.cask_strength.def: Spirits bottled directly from the barrel without dilution, typically 50-65% ABV.
wiki.gloss.single_malt.def: Whisky made from 100% malted barley at a single distillery.
wiki.gloss.blended.def: A mix of malt and grain whiskies from multiple distilleries.
wiki.gloss.aged.def: Matured in wooden casks (usually oak) for a specified period, developing complexity.
wiki.gloss.barrel.def: Wooden container (usually oak) used to age spirits. Imparts color, flavor and smoothness.
wiki.gloss.pot_still.def: Traditional batch distillation apparatus. Produces fuller, more flavorful spirits. Used for whisky, cognac, mezcal.
wiki.gloss.column_still.def: Continuous distillation apparatus that produces lighter, higher-proof spirits. Used for vodka, gin, grain whisky.
wiki.gloss.mash.def: Ground grain mixed with hot water to convert starches into fermentable sugars.
wiki.gloss.wash.def: The low-alcohol liquid (~7-10% ABV) produced after fermentation, before distillation.
wiki.gloss.congeners.def: Chemical compounds other than ethanol produced during fermentation and distillation. They contribute flavor and aroma.
wiki.gloss.heads.def: The first fraction of distillate. Contains methanol and harsh compounds. Discarded.
wiki.gloss.hearts.def: The middle fraction of distillate — the purest and best-tasting portion. This is what becomes the final spirit.
wiki.gloss.tails.def: The last fraction of distillate. Contains heavier, oily compounds. Discarded or redistilled.
wiki.gloss.angel_share.def: The portion of aging spirit that evaporates through the barrel (typically 2-4% per year). "The angels' tax."
wiki.gloss.dash.def: A small amount of liquid, approximately 0.5-1ml. Typically used for bitters.
wiki.gloss.jigger.def: A double-sided measuring tool (usually 30ml/60ml) for precise cocktail making.
wiki.gloss.neat.def: A spirit served alone, at room temperature, without ice, water or mixers.
wiki.gloss.straight_up.def: Chilled by shaking or stirring with ice, then strained and served without ice.
wiki.gloss.dirty.def: A cocktail with olive brine added (e.g., Dirty Martini).
wiki.gloss.dry.def: Less sweet. In a Martini context, less vermouth.
wiki.gloss.twist.def: A strip of citrus peel twisted to express oils over the drink as garnish.
wiki.gloss.float.def: A small amount of spirit or liqueur poured on top of a drink, sitting as a separate layer.
wiki.gloss.rim.def: Coating the edge of a glass with salt, sugar or other dry ingredients.
wiki.gloss.chaser.def: A mild drink consumed immediately after a shot of spirits.
wiki.gloss.back.def: A non-alcoholic drink served alongside a spirit or cocktail (e.g., "whisky with a water back").
wiki.gloss.call.def: When a customer specifies a particular brand of spirit (e.g., "Tanqueray and tonic").
wiki.gloss.well.def: The house or default spirits used when no specific brand is requested. Stored in the speed rail.
wiki.gloss.top_shelf.def: Premium spirits stored on the highest shelf. Higher quality and price.
wiki.gloss.speed_rail.def: The metal rack at the bartender's workstation holding frequently used well spirits.
wiki.gloss.mise_en_place.def: French for "everything in its place." Setting up all tools, garnishes and ingredients before service.
wiki.gloss.free_pour.def: Pouring without a jigger, using count method to estimate volume.
wiki.gloss.measured_pour.def: Using a jigger or measured pourer for exact portions. Preferred for consistency.
wiki.gloss.nose.def: The aroma of a spirit or wine when smelled.
wiki.gloss.palate.def: The flavors perceived when tasting. "On the palate" refers to the taste experience.
wiki.gloss.finish.def: The lingering taste and sensation after swallowing. Can be short, medium or long.
wiki.gloss.body.def: The weight and texture of a drink in the mouth. Light, medium or full-bodied.
wiki.gloss.mouthfeel.def: The physical sensation of a drink in the mouth — silky, oily, thin, creamy, effervescent.
wiki.gloss.aroma.def: The smell of a beverage, originating from the ingredients and production process.
wiki.gloss.bouquet.def: Complex aromas that develop through aging (typically used for wine and aged spirits).
wiki.gloss.crisp.def: Clean, refreshing acidity without excess sweetness.
wiki.gloss.sweet.def: Perceived sweetness from sugars, glycerol or sweet-tasting compounds.
wiki.gloss.bitter.def: One of the five basic tastes. Important in cocktails (bitters, Campari, tonic water).
wiki.gloss.sour.def: Acidic taste from citrus juice, vinegar or fermentation. Key to cocktail balance.
wiki.gloss.umami.def: The "fifth taste" — savory, brothy. Found in some cocktails using ingredients like tomato juice.
wiki.gloss.astringent.def: A drying, puckering sensation caused by tannins. Common in red wine and tea.
wiki.gloss.smooth.def: Easy to drink, without harsh flavors or rough edges. Well-balanced.
wiki.gloss.upsell.def: Suggesting a premium spirit or upgrade to a customer's order.
wiki.gloss.suggestive_sell.def: Recommending cocktails, food pairings or extras to enhance the guest experience and sales.
wiki.gloss.comp.def: Complimentary — a drink or item given free of charge, usually authorized by management.
wiki.gloss.tab.def: An open running bill that a customer pays at the end of their visit.
wiki.gloss.last_call.def: The final opportunity to order drinks before the bar closes.
wiki.gloss.happy_hour.def: A promotional period with discounted drinks, typically in the early evening.
wiki.gloss.service_bar.def: A bar area dedicated to preparing drinks for table service, not directly serving guests.
wiki.gloss.garnish_tray.def: A compartmented container holding prepared garnishes (citrus, olives, cherries, herbs) for efficient service.
wiki.gloss.ice_well.def: The insulated bin at the bar station holding ice for drink preparation.
wiki.gloss.pour_test.def: A test to verify a bartender's accuracy in free-pouring standard measures.
wiki.art.spirits.world-map.description: Explore the regions of the world where the main spirits and distilled beverages are produced. Each point on the map marks an area with tradition in the production of a specific spirit.
wiki.map.scotch.desc: Scotland is home to Scotch Whisky, with regions like Speyside, Islay, Highlands, Lowlands and Campbeltown, each with its own character.
wiki.map.irish-whiskey.desc: Ireland produces triple-distilled whiskey known for its smoothness. Brands like Jameson, Bushmills and Redbreast are world references.
wiki.map.bourbon.desc: Kentucky is the heart of Bourbon, made with at least 51% corn and aged in new charred American oak barrels.
wiki.map.japanese-whisky.desc: Japan produces world-class whiskies inspired by Scottish tradition but with Japanese precision. Yamazaki, Hakushu and Nikka are benchmarks.
wiki.map.london-gin.desc: London is the birthplace of modern gin. The London Dry style, dry and juniper-forward, is the most widespread in the world.
wiki.map.genever.desc: The Netherlands and Belgium are the origin of genever, the ancestor of modern gin. More malty and full-bodied than London Dry.
wiki.map.tequila.desc: Jalisco, Mexico, is the heart of tequila. Made exclusively from blue Weber agave, with protected designation of origin.
wiki.map.mezcal.desc: Oaxaca produces most of Mexico's mezcal. Unlike tequila, it can be made from over 30 agave varieties using ancestral artisanal methods.
wiki.map.ron-cuba.desc: Cuba is home to light and elegant rum. Havana Club and the Cuban white rum style are fundamental to world cocktail culture.
wiki.map.ron-jamaica.desc: Jamaica produces intense, full-bodied rums known for their characteristic esters and funk. Appleton Estate is its flagship brand.
wiki.map.ron-puerto-rico.desc: Puerto Rico is home to Bacardí and produces light, smooth rums ideal for cocktails. The Piña Colada was born here.
wiki.map.ron-barbados.desc: Barbados is considered the birthplace of rum, with production documented since 1703. Mount Gay is the oldest rum distillery in the world.
wiki.map.ron-guatemala.desc: Guatemala produces premium rums aged at high altitude. Ron Zacapa, with its solera system, is world-renowned.
wiki.map.rhum-agricole.desc: Martinique produces rhum agricole with designation of origin, distilled from fresh cane juice instead of molasses. Unique herbaceous and floral flavor.
wiki.map.vodka-poland.desc: Poland disputes with Russia the origin of vodka. Production since the 8th century with a tradition of rye and potato vodka. Belvedere and Żubrówka are benchmarks.
wiki.map.vodka-russia.desc: Russia has a centuries-old tradition in vodka production. Typically distilled from wheat, valued for its purity and neutrality.
wiki.map.vodka-sweden.desc: Sweden produces premium winter wheat vodka. Absolut, founded in 1879, revolutionized vodka marketing worldwide.
wiki.map.cognac.desc: Cognac, France, produces the most prestigious brandy in the world. Double distillation in copper pot stills and aging in French Limousin oak.
wiki.map.armagnac.desc: Gascony produces Armagnac, the oldest French brandy (14th century). Single distillation that preserves more character and rusticity than cognac.
wiki.map.brandy-jerez.desc: Jerez, Spain, produces brandy aged using the solera and criaderas system in sherry casks. Fundador, Carlos I and Lepanto are references.
wiki.map.calvados.desc: Normandy, France, produces Calvados, an apple (and sometimes pear) brandy with designation of origin. Aged in oak, from young and fruity to aged and complex.
wiki.map.grappa.desc: Italy produces grappa from grape pomace (skins, seeds and stems). From rustic and strong to refined and single-varietal.
wiki.map.pisco-peru.desc: Peru produces pisco from aromatic and non-aromatic grapes on the southern coast. Not aged in wood, preserving the purity of the distillate.
wiki.map.pisco-chile.desc: Chile produces pisco in the Atacama and Coquimbo regions. Can be aged in wood, yielding varieties from clear to aged.
wiki.map.orujo.desc: Galicia, Spain, produces orujo distilled from grape pomace. The queimada, a Galician ritual with flambéed orujo, is part of its culture.
wiki.map.cachaca.desc: Brazil produces cachaça, distilled from fresh sugarcane juice. Base of the Caipirinha and the most consumed spirit in Latin America.
wiki.map.sake.desc: Japan produces sake (nihonshu) from polished and fermented rice. Not distilled but fermented, with a millennial tradition.
wiki.map.soju.desc: South Korea produces soju, a clear spirit from rice, wheat or potato. It is the best-selling alcoholic beverage in the world by volume.
wiki.map.baijiu.desc: China produces baijiu, a spirit from solid-state fermented grains. It is the most consumed spirit in the world with thousands of years of history.
wiki.map.aquavit.desc: Norway and Scandinavia produce aquavit, a spirit from potato or grain flavored with caraway and dill. Viking tradition.
wiki.map.raki.desc: Turkey produces rakı, an anise-flavored grape spirit. Called "lion's milk" because it turns white when water is added. Turkey's national drink.
wiki.map.ouzo.desc: Greece produces ouzo, an anise-flavored spirit that turns cloudy with water (louche effect). Iconic drink of Greek Mediterranean culture.
wiki.map.ron-dominicana.desc: The Dominican Republic produces smooth, aged rums. Brugal and Barceló are benchmarks of the premium Caribbean style.
wiki.map.ron-venezuela.desc: Venezuela produces dark, complex rums. Diplomático and Santa Teresa are among the most awarded worldwide.
wiki.map.ron-colombia.desc: Colombia produces light, accessible rums. Ron Medellín is the emblem of the Colombian style.
wiki.map.ron-panama.desc: Panama produces premium tropically-aged rums. Ron Abuelo and its solera system are a benchmark.
wiki.map.ron-trinidad.desc: Trinidad produces highly complex rums. Angostura, famous for its bitters, also distills excellent rums.
wiki.map.ron-guyana.desc: Guyana produces the legendary Demerara rum. Lemon Hart and El Dorado come from the last operational distillery.
wiki.map.raicilla.desc: Agave distillate from the western sierra of Jalisco. Historically considered contraband, now has denomination of origin.
wiki.map.sotol.desc: Distillate of Dasylirion (not agave) from the Chihuahua desert. Wild plant with a process similar to mezcal.
wiki.map.bacanora.desc: Agave Pacifica distillate from Sonora. Was banned for 77 years until legalization in 1992.
wiki.map.kirsch.desc: Clear cherry brandy from Germany's Black Forest. Base of the Black Forest cake.
wiki.map.absinthe.desc: The Green Fairy. High-proof distillate with wormwood, fennel and anise. Banned for decades, reborn in the 2000s.
wiki.map.shochu.desc: Japanese distillate of rice, sweet potato or barley. Stronger than sake, with centuries-old tradition in Kyushu.
wiki.map.fino-jerez.desc: The driest sherry. Aged under flor veil (yeast). Very saline and pungent. Tío Pepe is the reference.
wiki.map.manzanilla.desc: Fino made exclusively in Sanlúcar de Barrameda. Sea air gives it a unique saline touch, lighter and fresher.
wiki.map.porto.desc: Fortified wine from the Douro Valley. Ruby (fruity, young) and Tawny (oxidized, complex). Brandy added to stop fermentation.
wiki.map.madeira.desc: Wines 'cooked' in estufas (estufagem) of near-eternal resistance. From Sercial (dry) to Malmsey (sweet).
wiki.map.vermut-rosso.desc: Created by Carpano in Turin in 1786. Wine base + wormwood and spices. Antica Formula and Martini Riserva are benchmarks.
wiki.map.vermut-dry.desc: French style created by Joseph Noilly in 1813. Less sugar, more herbal botanicals. Noilly Prat and Dolin stand out.
wiki.map.dubonnet.desc: French wine aperitif flavored with quinine. Created to combat malaria in French colonies.
wiki.map.lillet.desc: Bordeaux aperitif with wine, fruit liqueurs and quinine. Lillet Blanc is essential in the Vesper Martini.
wiki.map.chartreuse.desc: Liqueur of 130 herbs made by Carthusian monks since 1605. Only liqueur that ages in bottle. Gave its name to the color chartreuse green.
wiki.map.benedictine.desc: Recipe from monk Dom Bernardo Vincelli (1510). Lost in the French Revolution, rediscovered by Alexandre Le Grand. D.O.M. = Deo Optimo Maximo.
wiki.map.galliano.desc: Created in 1896 by Arturo Vaccari. Iconic tall bottle. Vanilla and anise profile. Named after war hero Giuseppe Galliano.
wiki.map.strega.desc: 70-herb liqueur from Benevento, legendary meeting point of witches. Saffron gives its electric yellow color.
wiki.map.drambuie.desc: Scotch whisky and heather honey liqueur. Recipe from Prince 'Bonnie' Charlie Stuart given to a clan after defeat at Culloden (1745).
wiki.map.cointreau.desc: The definitive Triple Sec. Édouard Cointreau sought a purer, less sweet orange liqueur. Sweet and bitter orange peels.
wiki.map.grand-marnier.desc: Unlike Cointreau, uses Cognac as base instead of neutral spirit. Belle Époque success since 1880.
wiki.map.curacao.desc: Liqueur from bitter oranges of Curaçao island (Dutch Antilles). Drier and more complex than industrial Triple Sec.
wiki.map.maraschino.desc: Luxardo liqueur from Marasca cherries including the pit, which gives an almond note. Straw-wrapped bottle for sea voyages since 1821.
wiki.map.st-germain.desc: The 'bartender's ketchup' — works well with almost everything. Fresh elderflowers hand-picked in the French Alps.
wiki.map.chambord.desc: Black raspberry, honey and vanilla liqueur. Legend: presented to Louis XIV at Chambord castle. Iconic spherical bottle.
wiki.map.creme-cassis.desc: Dense blackcurrant liqueur from Burgundy. Base of the Kir Royale. Burgundy is the world capital of blackcurrant.
wiki.map.amaretto.desc: Liqueur from apricot pits (not almonds). Legend: gifted to painter Luini, Da Vinci's disciple, as gratitude (1525).
wiki.map.frangelico.desc: Piedmont hazelnut liqueur. Bottle shaped like a monk with a cord tied at the waist.
wiki.map.kahlua.desc: Veracruz Arabica coffee liqueur. Essential for Espresso Martini and Black Russian since 1936.
wiki.map.baileys.desc: World's first successful cream liqueur (1974). Technical challenge: keeping cream and whiskey from separating.
wiki.map.fernet-branca.desc: Created in Milan in 1845. 27 herbs with myrrh, rhubarb and saffron. Argentina consumes 75% of world production.
wiki.map.amaro-averna.desc: Gift from monks of Santo Spirito Abbey to Salvatore Averna in 1868. Sweeter, with licorice and Mediterranean citrus.
wiki.map.amaro-montenegro.desc: Named after Princess Elena of Montenegro (1885). 40 botanicals. One of its blend bottles is 'empty' of flavor but full of aroma.
wiki.map.cynar.desc: Star ingredient: artichoke (Cynara scolymus). Doesn't taste like vegetables: earthy, sweet and bitter. Created in Padua in 1952.
wiki.map.ramazzotti.desc: Italy's oldest commercial amaro (1815). No wine in its base. Calabrian orange peel stands out.
wiki.map.nonino.desc: The only amaro with high-quality grappa base. Elegant, less dense, with a clean Alpine finish. Since 1933 in Friuli.
wiki.map.braulio.desc: Aged 2 years in Slavic oak since 1875 in Bormio. Tastes of pine forests and icy high-mountain herbs.
wiki.map.jagermeister.desc: 'Master Hunter' with 56 botanicals. From grandpa's liqueur to global party phenomenon thanks to 80s marketing.
wiki.map.underberg.desc: Only in 20ml bottles wrapped in straw paper. Herbs from 43 countries. One shot after a heavy meal since 1846.
wiki.map.campari.desc: Created by Gaspare Campari in Milan in 1860. Vibrant red, the standard of citrus bitterness. Essential in Negroni and Americano.
wiki.map.aperol.desc: Light aperitif at only 11% ABV. Sweeter, very orange. Global explosion in the 2000s with the Aperol Spritz.
wiki.map.suze.desc: Gentian root (bitter) aperitif with bright yellow color. Pablo Picasso's favorite drink. Very earthy.
wiki.map.angostura.desc: Created in 1824 by Dr. Siegert as a tonic for soldiers. Label bigger than the bottle: design error that became its identity.
wiki.map.peychauds.desc: Created by Antoine Peychaud, Creole apothecary of New Orleans (1830). Lighter and sweeter, anise notes. Soul of the Sazerac.
dashboard.academy_desc: Learn step by step through cocktail families
academy.title: Cocktail Academy
academy.l0.title: Foundations
academy.l0.desc: Tools, techniques, base spirits, and measurements
academy.l0.t1: Every bartender needs essential tools: a shaker, mixing glass, strainer, jigger, and bar spoon. The Boston shaker (two pieces) is preferred by professionals, while the cobbler shaker (three pieces) is ideal for beginners.
academy.l0.tip1: Invest in a good double-sided jigger (30/60ml). Precision in measurements is the difference between a good cocktail and an extraordinary one.
academy.l0.t2: Standard measurements: 1 oz = 30 ml, 1 dash = ~1 ml, 1 barspoon = 5 ml. Most recipes use ounces (oz) or milliliters (ml). A standard cocktail contains 60–90 ml of total alcohol.
academy.l0.note1: In professional bartending, consistency is more important than speed. A bartender who measures precisely will always outperform one who improvises.
academy.l0.t3: The three fundamental techniques: SHAKE for cocktails with citrus, egg, or dairy; STIR for cocktails made only with spirits and liqueurs; BUILD for highballs and long drinks directly in the glass.
academy.l0.tip2: When shaking, shake vigorously for 10–15 seconds. The ice should sound like maracas. When stirring, rotate the spoon gently for 30–40 revolutions to dilute without breaking the ice.
academy.l0.t4: The 6 base spirits of mixology: Gin (botanicals), Vodka (neutral), Rum (sugarcane), Tequila/Mezcal (agave), Whisky (grains), and Brandy/Cognac (grape). Each one defines entire families of cocktails.
academy.l0.t5: Ice is an ingredient, not an accessory. Types: large cubes (slow dilution, ideal for spirit-forward), standard cubes (shaker), crushed ice (fast dilution, tiki and cobblers). Never reuse ice from the shaker.
academy.l0.tip3: Always use fresh ice straight from the freezer. 'Wet' ice that has been sitting out will dilute your cocktail too quickly.
academy.l0.note2: The golden rule: if the cocktail contains citrus or opaque ingredients, shake it. If it only has spirits, liqueurs, and clear bitters, stir it. Exceptions exist, but this rule covers 90% of cases.
academy.l0.q1: What is the correct technique for a cocktail that contains lemon juice?
academy.l0.q1exp: Cocktails with citrus are shaken to integrate and emulsify the ingredients.
academy.l0.q2: How many milliliters are in one ounce (oz)?
academy.l0.q2exp: One ounce equals 30 ml. It is the standard measurement in mixology.
academy.l0.q3exp: Tequila is distilled from blue agave (Agave tequilana Weber), exclusive to certain regions of Mexico.
academy.l0.q4: For what type of cocktails is the stirring technique used?
academy.l0.q4exp: Stirring is used for spirit-forward cocktails without opaque ingredients, such as the Manhattan or the Negroni.
academy.l0.q5exp: A dash is approximately 1 ml, the amount that comes out of a bitters bottle with a single shake.
academy.l0.q6: Which shaker is preferred by professionals?
academy.l0.q6exp: The two-piece Boston shaker (tin + glass or tin + tin) is the professional standard due to its speed and ease of cleaning.
academy.l0.q7: What type of ice is ideal for spirit-forward cocktails like the Old Fashioned?
academy.l0.q7exp: Large cubes dilute slowly, keeping the cocktail cold without watering it down quickly. Perfect for spirit-forward drinks.
academy.l0.q8exp: Rum is distilled from sugarcane or its byproducts (molasses, cane juice).
academy.l0.q9: How many revolutions are recommended when stirring a cocktail?
academy.l0.q9exp: 30–40 gentle revolutions with the bar spoon is the standard to achieve the correct dilution and temperature.
academy.l0.q10: How much total alcohol does a standard cocktail contain?
academy.l0.q10exp: A standard cocktail contains 60–90 ml of total alcohol, equivalent to about 2–3 oz of spirit.
academy.l0.les0.q1: How many pieces does a Boston shaker have?
academy.l0.les0.q1exp: The Boston shaker has 2 pieces (tin + glass or tin + tin) and is the professional standard for its speed and ease of cleaning.
academy.l0.les0.q2: What type of shaker is recommended for beginners?
academy.l0.les0.q2exp: The cobbler shaker has 3 pieces (tin, strainer, cap) and is ideal for beginners because of its built-in strainer.
academy.l0.les0.q3: What are the standard measures of a jigger?
academy.l0.les0.q3exp: A standard jigger has two sides: 30 ml (1 oz) and 60 ml (2 oz), providing precise measurements for cocktail recipes.
academy.l0.les1.q1: Which technique should be used for cocktails containing citrus juice?
academy.l0.les1.q1exp: Cocktails with citrus, egg, or dairy ingredients must be shaken to integrate and emulsify the components properly.
academy.l0.les1.q2: How long should a cocktail typically be shaken?
academy.l0.les1.q2exp: The standard shaking time is 10-15 seconds, enough to chill and dilute the cocktail properly.
academy.l0.les1.q3: How many base spirits are considered fundamental in mixology?
academy.l0.les1.q3exp: The 6 base spirits are gin, vodka, rum, tequila, whisky, and brandy — the foundation of virtually all classic cocktails.
academy.l0.les2.q1: What type of ice is best for spirit-forward cocktails?
academy.l0.les2.q1exp: Large cubes dilute slowly, keeping spirit-forward cocktails cold without watering them down too quickly.
academy.l0.les2.q2: Why should you never reuse shaker ice in a cocktail?
academy.l0.les2.q2a1: It is already diluted and will over-dilute the drink
academy.l0.les2.q2a2: It changes color from the ingredients
academy.l0.les2.q2a4: It is too large to fit in the glass
academy.l0.les2.q2exp: Shaker ice has already melted and absorbed flavors during shaking. Using fresh ice in the glass ensures proper dilution control.
academy.l0.les2.q3: What is the golden rule of cocktail technique selection?
academy.l0.les2.q3a1: Citrus means shake; spirits-only means stir
academy.l0.les2.q3a4: Use the build technique for all cocktails
academy.l0.les2.q3exp: The golden rule: if a cocktail has citrus or opaque ingredients, shake it; if it is spirits and liqueurs only, stir it.
academy.l1.title: Highballs & Collins
academy.l1.desc: Simple long drinks using the build technique
academy.l1.t1: A highball is the simplest form of cocktail: a spirit + a long mixer (soda, tonic, ginger ale) served in a tall glass with ice. The technique is 'build': pour directly into the glass. The classic ratio is 1:2 or 1:3 (spirit:mixer).
academy.l1.tip1: Always pour the mixer down the side of the glass to preserve carbonation. Never shake a highball — you would destroy the bubbles.
academy.l1.note1: In Japan, the Highball is an art form. Hand-carved ice is used, the glass is pre-chilled, and exactly one stir of the spoon is given. Perfection lies in simplicity.
academy.l1.t2: The highball family includes: Buck (spirit + ginger beer + citrus), Rickey (spirit + lime + soda, no sugar), Mule (spirit + ginger beer + lime), and Collins (spirit + lemon + sugar + soda). Each is a variation on the same concept.
academy.l1.tip2: The Collins glass is narrower and taller than the Highball glass. Use a Collins glass for higher-volume drinks and a Highball glass for shorter ones.
academy.l1.t3: The rules for the perfect highball: 1) Pre-chilled glass, 2) Ice to the top, 3) Spirit first, 4) Mixer down the side, 5) A single stir, 6) Minimal garnish. Carbonation is your friend — treat it with respect.
academy.l1.note2: The Dark 'n' Stormy is a registered trademark of Gosling's: it can officially only be made with Gosling's Black Seal rum. It is one of the few cocktails with a protected designation.
academy.l1.q1: What is the technique for preparing a highball?
academy.l1.q1exp: Highballs are built directly in the glass, without a shaker or mixing glass.
academy.l1.q2: What defines a 'Buck' within the highball family?
academy.l1.q2exp: A Buck combines a spirit with ginger beer and a citrus element (lime or lemon).
academy.l1.q3: What is the classic spirit:mixer ratio in a highball?
academy.l1.q3exp: The classic ratio is 1:2 or 1:3 (one part spirit to two or three parts mixer).
academy.l1.q4: Why is the mixer poured down the side of the glass?
academy.l1.q4exp: Pouring down the side preserves the CO2 bubbles, keeping the drink effervescent longer.
academy.l1.q5: What spirit does a Moscow Mule contain?
academy.l1.q5exp: The Moscow Mule is made with vodka, ginger beer, and lime juice, traditionally served in a copper mug.
academy.l1.q6: What sets a Rickey apart from other highballs?
academy.l1.q6exp: The Rickey is a dry highball: spirit + lime + soda, with no sugar or sweetener of any kind.
academy.l1.q7: Which of these is a Collins?
academy.l1.q7exp: The Tom Collins (gin + lemon + sugar + soda) is the quintessential Collins.
academy.l1.q8: Which brand holds the Dark 'n' Stormy as a registered trademark?
academy.l1.q8exp: The Dark 'n' Stormy is a registered trademark of Gosling's and can officially only be made with Gosling's Black Seal rum.
academy.l1.q9: How many stirs of the spoon are given in a Japanese highball?
academy.l1.q9exp: In the Japanese highball technique, exactly one stir is given to integrate without losing carbonation.
academy.l1.q10: What tequila cocktail is more popular than the Margarita in Mexico?
academy.l1.q10exp: The Paloma (tequila + grapefruit + soda) is the most consumed tequila cocktail in Mexico.
academy.l1.les0.q1: What technique is used to prepare a highball?
academy.l1.les0.q1a1: Build — pour directly into the glass
academy.l1.les0.q1exp: Highballs use the build technique: ingredients are poured directly into the serving glass over ice.
academy.l1.les0.q2: What is the classic spirit-to-mixer ratio in a highball?
academy.l1.les0.q2exp: The standard highball ratio is 1 part spirit to 2 or 3 parts mixer, keeping the drink refreshing and light.
academy.l1.les0.q3: Why should you never shake a highball?
academy.l1.les0.q3a2: It would make the drink too cold
academy.l1.les0.q3a3: It would cause the glass to crack
academy.l1.les0.q3exp: Shaking a highball destroys the carbonation of the mixer. The mixer is poured down the side of the glass to preserve bubbles.
academy.l1.les1.q1: What defines a Buck within the highball family?
academy.l1.les1.q1exp: A Buck is a highball variation combining a spirit with ginger beer and a citrus element (usually lime or lemon).
academy.l1.les1.q2: What distinguishes a Rickey from other highballs?
academy.l1.les1.q2exp: The Rickey is a dry highball: spirit + lime + soda, with no sugar or sweetener. It is austere and refreshing.
academy.l1.les1.q3: What spirit does the Moscow Mule use?
academy.l1.les1.q3exp: The Moscow Mule is made with vodka, ginger beer, and lime, traditionally served in a copper mug.
academy.l1.les2.q1: What is the rule for the number of stirs in a perfect highball?
academy.l1.les2.q1exp: The perfect highball requires only a single stir to integrate without losing carbonation — especially prized in Japanese technique.
academy.l1.les2.q2: Why is the Dark 'n' Stormy a unique cocktail legally?
academy.l1.les2.q2a1: It is a registered trademark of Gosling's
academy.l1.les2.q2a2: It is banned in several countries
academy.l1.les2.q2a3: It can only be served in copper mugs
academy.l1.les2.q2a4: It requires a special bartender license
academy.l1.les2.q2exp: The Dark 'n' Stormy is a registered trademark of Gosling's — it can officially only be made with Gosling's Black Seal rum.
academy.l1.les2.q3: What is the most popular tequila cocktail in Mexico?
academy.l1.les2.q3exp: The Paloma (tequila + grapefruit + soda) is the most consumed tequila cocktail in Mexico, surpassing even the Margarita.
academy.l2.title: Sours & Daisies
academy.l2.desc: Shaken cocktails, citrus balance, and egg white
academy.l2.t1: The Sour is one of the oldest cocktail families: spirit + citrus + sweet. The classic ratio is 2:1:1 (60ml spirit, 30ml citrus, 30ml sweet) or the 'Golden Ratio' 2:¾:¾. The acid-sweet balance is the key.
academy.l2.tip1: Always use freshly squeezed juice. Bottled juice contains preservatives that alter the flavor. Lemon juice lasts 4 hours max; lime juice, 8 hours.
academy.l2.note1: Egg white transforms a sour: it adds silky texture and foam. Use the 'dry shake' technique (shake without ice first), then 'wet shake' (with ice). The result is a creamy, stable foam.
academy.l2.t2: The sour template allows infinite variations by swapping each component: Whiskey Sour (bourbon), Daiquiri (rum + lime), Margarita (tequila + lime + triple sec), Gimlet (gin + lime). Same concept, different spirits.
academy.l2.tip2: For a perfect Daiquiri: 60ml white rum, 22ml lime, 15ml syrup. Shake vigorously for 12 seconds. Double-strain into a chilled coupe. Do not add fruit or serve it frozen — that is a different drink.
academy.l2.t3: A Daisy is a sour that uses a liqueur as the sweetener instead of simple syrup. The Margarita is a tequila Daisy (in fact, 'margarita' means 'daisy' in Spanish). The Sidecar is a cognac Daisy with Cointreau.
academy.l2.note2: The Pisco Sour includes egg white and Angostura as decoration on the foam. The bitters are not mixed in: they are dropped onto the foam and a pattern is drawn with a toothpick.
academy.l2.t4: Modern sours explore alternative sweeteners: honey (Gold Rush, Bee's Knees), honey-ginger syrup (Penicillin), agave (Tommy's Margarita). Each sweetener brings its own character to the cocktail's balance.
academy.l2.tip3: The Penicillin uses a float of smoky Islay whisky at the end. This 'float' is poured gently over a spoon so it sits on the surface, creating a smoky aroma before each sip.
academy.l2.q1: What is the classic ratio of a Sour?
academy.l2.q1exp: The classic sour ratio is 2:1:1 — 2 parts spirit, 1 part citrus, and 1 part sweet.
academy.l2.q2: What technique is used to create foam with egg white?
academy.l2.q2a1: Dry shake (no ice) + wet shake (with ice)
academy.l2.q2exp: The dry shake (without ice first) emulsifies the egg white; then the wet shake (with ice) chills and dilutes.
academy.l2.q3a1: A sour with a liqueur as the sweetener
academy.l2.q3exp: A Daisy is a sour that uses a liqueur (Cointreau, maraschino, etc.) as the sweetener instead of simple syrup.
academy.l2.q4: Which cocktail is essentially a 'tequila Daisy'?
academy.l2.q4exp: 'Margarita' means 'daisy' in Spanish. It is a tequila sour with triple sec as the sweetener.
academy.l2.q5: How long does fresh lemon juice last for mixology?
academy.l2.q5exp: Fresh lemon juice loses its properties after 4 hours. Lime juice lasts a bit longer, up to 8 hours.
academy.l2.q6: What sweetener does the Gold Rush use instead of simple syrup?
academy.l2.q6exp: The Gold Rush substitutes the Whiskey Sour's simple syrup with honey syrup, adding depth.
academy.l2.q7: What spirit does the classic Daiquiri contain?
academy.l2.q7exp: The classic Daiquiri contains white rum, fresh lime juice, and simple syrup. No fruit, no frozen.
academy.l2.q8: How is Angostura applied in a Pisco Sour?
academy.l2.q8a1: Dropped onto the foam as decoration
academy.l2.q8a3: At the bottom of the glass
academy.l2.q8exp: The Angostura is dropped onto the egg white foam and a pattern is drawn with a toothpick. It is not mixed in.
academy.l2.q9: What whisky does the Penicillin use as a 'float'?
academy.l2.q9exp: The Penicillin features a float of smoky Islay whisky (such as Lagavulin) on the surface of the cocktail.
academy.l2.q10: Which cocktail family includes the Sidecar, Margarita, and Cosmopolitan?
academy.l2.q10exp: They are all Daisies: sours that use a liqueur as the sweetener (Cointreau, triple sec).
academy.l2.les0.q1: What is the Golden Ratio for a Sour?
academy.l2.les0.q1exp: The Golden Ratio for sours is 2:¾:¾, producing a slightly drier and more spirit-forward result than the classic 2:1:1.
academy.l2.les0.q2: Why must you always use fresh juice in sours?
academy.l2.les0.q2a1: Bottled juice has preservatives that alter the flavor
academy.l2.les0.q2a4: Fresh juice has a nicer color
academy.l2.les0.q2exp: Bottled juice contains preservatives that alter the flavor profile. Fresh lemon juice lasts only 4 hours max for optimal taste.
academy.l2.les0.q3: How long does fresh lemon juice remain viable for cocktails?
academy.l2.les0.q3exp: Fresh lemon juice loses its balanced flavor after 4 hours. Lime juice lasts slightly longer, up to 8 hours.
academy.l2.les1.q1: What base spirit does a classic Daiquiri use?
academy.l2.les1.q1exp: The classic Daiquiri uses white rum with fresh lime juice and simple syrup — no fruit, no frozen.
academy.l2.les1.q2: What citrus does a Gimlet use?
academy.l2.les1.q2exp: The Gimlet combines gin with lime juice (and traditionally lime cordial), making it a gin-based sour.
academy.l2.les1.q3: What technique creates the foam in an egg white sour?
academy.l2.les1.q3a1: Dry shake first, then wet shake with ice
academy.l2.les1.q3a2: Blend with ice in a blender
academy.l2.les1.q3a3: Stir vigorously in a mixing glass
academy.l2.les1.q3exp: A dry shake (without ice) first emulsifies the egg white to create foam, then a wet shake (with ice) chills and dilutes.
academy.l2.les2.q1: What makes a Daisy different from a standard Sour?
academy.l2.les2.q1a1: It uses a liqueur as the sweetener instead of simple syrup
academy.l2.les2.q1a4: It is stirred instead of shaken
academy.l2.les2.q1exp: A Daisy is a sour that replaces simple syrup with a liqueur (like Cointreau or triple sec) as the sweetener.
academy.l2.les2.q2: The Sidecar is a Daisy made with which base spirit?
academy.l2.les2.q2exp: The Sidecar is a cognac Daisy with Cointreau as the sweetening liqueur.
academy.l2.les2.q3: How is Angostura bitters applied in a Pisco Sour?
academy.l2.les2.q3a1: Dropped onto the egg white foam as decoration
academy.l2.les2.q3a3: Muddled at the bottom of the glass
academy.l2.les2.q3a4: It is not used in a Pisco Sour
academy.l2.les2.q3exp: In a Pisco Sour, Angostura bitters are dropped onto the egg white foam and a pattern is drawn with a toothpick.
academy.l2.les3.q1: What sweetener does Tommy's Margarita use instead of triple sec?
academy.l2.les3.q1exp: Tommy's Margarita replaces triple sec with agave syrup, letting the tequila shine with a cleaner agave-forward sweetness.
academy.l2.les3.q2: What unique syrup does the Penicillin cocktail use?
academy.l2.les3.q2exp: The Penicillin uses honey-ginger syrup combined with blended Scotch, finished with an Islay whisky float for smokiness.
academy.l2.les3.q3: What do the Gold Rush and Bee's Knees have in common?
academy.l2.les3.q3a1: Both use honey as the sweetener
academy.l2.les3.q3exp: Both the Gold Rush and the Bee's Knees use honey syrup as their sweetener instead of simple syrup, adding depth and floral notes.
academy.l3.title: Spirit-Forward
academy.l3.desc: Martini, Manhattan, Negroni, Old Fashioned, and stirred cocktails
academy.l3.les0: The Old Fashioned and its variations
academy.l3.t1: Spirit-forward cocktails let the spirit shine. They use little or no citrus and are prepared stirred in a mixing glass. Controlled dilution and temperature are crucial. Large ice is essential when serving.
academy.l3.tip1: When stirring, the spoon should glide gently along the wall of the mixing glass. The motion comes from the fingers, not the wrist. Goal: chill and dilute without aerating.
academy.l3.note1: The Old Fashioned is the oldest cocktail in existence — it IS the original 'cocktail.' Its recipe (spirit + sugar + bitters + water) defines the entire category. Everything else came after.
academy.l3.t2: The Manhattan (whiskey + sweet vermouth + bitters) established the pattern for dozens of variations: Rob Roy (Scotch), Boulevardier (with Campari), Black Manhattan (with Amaro Averna). Changing one ingredient creates a new cocktail.
academy.l3.tip2: Vermouth is a fortified wine. Once opened, it oxidizes like any wine. Store it in the refrigerator and use it within 4–6 weeks. Stale vermouth ruins any cocktail.
academy.l3.t3: The Dry Martini is the most debated cocktail: the gin/vermouth ratio has varied from 1:1 to nearly straight gin. 'Dry' means less vermouth. A 'wet' Martini has more vermouth. 'Dirty' adds olive brine.
