academy.l3.note2: The Sazerac is the official cocktail of New Orleans. It is prepared with an absinthe 'rinse': the glass is rinsed with absinthe and the excess is discarded. Only a whisper of anise remains.
academy.l3.t4: The Negroni (gin + Campari + sweet vermouth) in equal parts is the gateway to bitter cocktails. The Boulevardier replaces the gin with bourbon. The Vieux Carré adds Bénédictine to the Manhattan, creating extra complexity.
academy.l3.tip3: For spirit-forward garnish: the citrus twist is expressed over the cocktail to release essential oils, then rubbed along the rim of the glass. The oils from the twist are an ingredient, not just decoration.
academy.l3.q1: What is the technique for preparing spirit-forward cocktails?
academy.l3.q1exp: Spirit-forward cocktails are stirred in a mixing glass to chill without aerating, preserving the silky texture.
academy.l3.q2: What are the 3 ingredients of a Negroni?
academy.l3.q2exp: The Negroni is made with equal parts gin, Campari, and sweet red vermouth.
academy.l3.q3: What does 'Dry' mean in a Dry Martini?
academy.l3.q3exp: 'Dry' in a Martini means using less vermouth. The drier it is, the more the gin dominates.
academy.l3.q4: How should vermouth be stored once opened?
academy.l3.q4a4: It doesn't matter how it's stored
academy.l3.q4exp: Vermouth is a fortified wine and oxidizes once opened. It must be refrigerated and used within 4–6 weeks.
academy.l3.q5: Which cocktail is essentially a Negroni with bourbon instead of gin?
academy.l3.q5exp: The Boulevardier replaces the Negroni's gin with bourbon or rye whiskey.
academy.l3.q6: What special technique does the Sazerac use?
academy.l3.q6exp: The Sazerac uses an absinthe 'rinse': the glass is rinsed and the excess is discarded, leaving only a whisper of anise.
academy.l3.q7: What is the Old Fashioned in the history of mixology?
academy.l3.q7a1: The original cocktail that defined the category
academy.l3.q7exp: The Old Fashioned (spirit + sugar + bitters + water) is literally the original recipe of the 'cocktail.'
academy.l3.q8: Why is the citrus twist expressed over a spirit-forward cocktail?
academy.l3.q8a2: To add acidity to the cocktail
academy.l3.q8a4: To change the color of the cocktail
academy.l3.q8exp: The twist releases essential oils from the citrus peel, which add aroma to the cocktail. They are an ingredient, not just decoration.
academy.l3.q9: What spirit does the Rob Roy contain?
academy.l3.q9exp: The Rob Roy is a Manhattan made with Scotch Whisky instead of bourbon or rye. It is the 'Scottish Manhattan.'
academy.l3.q10: What herbal liqueur does the Vieux Carré add to the Manhattan pattern?
academy.l3.q10exp: The Vieux Carré adds Bénédictine to the Manhattan framework, creating a more complex cocktail with honey notes.
academy.l3.les0.q1: Why are spirit-forward cocktails stirred instead of shaken?
academy.l3.les0.q1a1: To chill and dilute without aerating
academy.l3.les0.q1exp: Spirit-forward cocktails are stirred to achieve controlled dilution and temperature while preserving a silky, clear texture without aeration.
academy.l3.les0.q2: What are the four components of an Old Fashioned?
academy.l3.les0.q2exp: The Old Fashioned (spirit + sugar + bitters + water) is the original cocktail recipe that defined the entire category.
academy.l3.les0.q3: Where should the stirring motion come from when making a spirit-forward cocktail?
academy.l3.les0.q3exp: The stirring motion should come from the fingers, not the wrist, allowing the spoon to glide gently along the wall of the mixing glass.
academy.l3.les1.q1: What are the three ingredients of a Manhattan?
academy.l3.les1.q1a3: Bourbon, dry vermouth, and orange liqueur
academy.l3.les1.q1exp: The Manhattan combines whiskey with sweet vermouth and bitters, establishing a pattern for dozens of variations.
academy.l3.les1.q2: How long does vermouth last once opened, if properly refrigerated?
academy.l3.les1.q2exp: Vermouth is a fortified wine that oxidizes once opened. It must be refrigerated and used within 4-6 weeks.
academy.l3.les1.q3: What is the ratio of ingredients in a Negroni?
academy.l3.les1.q3a1: Equal parts gin, Campari, and sweet vermouth
academy.l3.les1.q3a2: 2 parts gin, 1 part Campari, 1 part vermouth
academy.l3.les1.q3a3: 3 parts gin, 1 part Campari, 1 part vermouth
academy.l3.les1.q3a4: 1 part gin, 2 parts Campari, 1 part vermouth
academy.l3.les1.q3exp: The Negroni uses equal parts of gin, Campari, and sweet vermouth — a perfectly balanced three-way split.
academy.l3.les2.q1: What does 'dirty' mean in a Dirty Martini?
academy.l3.les2.q1a3: It is served at room temperature
academy.l3.les2.q1exp: A 'dirty' Martini includes olive brine, which adds a savory, briny character to the drink.
academy.l3.les2.q2: What is an absinthe rinse in a Sazerac?
academy.l3.les2.q2a1: The glass is coated with absinthe and the excess is discarded
academy.l3.les2.q2a2: Absinthe is mixed into the cocktail as a main ingredient
academy.l3.les2.q2a3: The ice cubes are soaked in absinthe
academy.l3.les2.q2a4: Absinthe is floated on top of the cocktail
academy.l3.les2.q2exp: In a Sazerac, the glass is rinsed with absinthe and the excess is discarded, leaving only a whisper of anise flavor.
academy.l3.les2.q3: What are the two main ingredients of a Dry Martini?
academy.l3.les2.q3exp: The classic Dry Martini combines gin with dry vermouth, stirred and strained. 'Dry' indicates less vermouth.
academy.l3.les3.q1a1: A Negroni with bourbon instead of gin
academy.l3.les3.q1a2: A Manhattan with Campari instead of bitters
academy.l3.les3.q1a3: A Martini with Scotch instead of gin
academy.l3.les3.q1exp: The Boulevardier replaces the Negroni's gin with bourbon, creating a richer, warmer variation of the classic.
academy.l3.les3.q2: What does the Vieux Carré add to the Manhattan formula?
academy.l3.les3.q2exp: The Vieux Carré adds Bénédictine to the Manhattan framework, creating a more complex cocktail with honey and herbal notes.
academy.l3.les3.q3: Why is a citrus twist expressed over a spirit-forward cocktail?
academy.l3.les3.q3a1: To release essential oils that add aroma — it is an ingredient, not just decoration
academy.l3.les3.q3a2: To add citrus juice to the cocktail
academy.l3.les3.q3a4: To change the color of the drink
academy.l3.les3.q3exp: The citrus twist is expressed to release essential oils over the cocktail. These oils are a functional ingredient adding aroma, not merely decoration.
academy.l4.title: Tropical & Tiki
academy.l4.desc: Multi-spirit, exotic ingredients, blending, and tiki
academy.l4.t1: Tiki culture was born in the 1930s with Don the Beachcomber and Trader Vic in California. Their philosophy: use multiple rums, tropical juices, and exotic syrups to create complex, impossible-to-guess flavors. Recipes were secret, with coded ingredients.
academy.l4.note1: Trader Vic and Don the Beachcomber disputed the invention of the Mai Tai for decades. Trader Vic won the debate, but both profoundly influenced tiki culture.
academy.l4.tip1: Tiki cocktails typically use 2–3 different rums (white, gold, dark/Demerara). Each rum contributes different notes: white brings cleanliness, gold brings depth, and Demerara brings caramelized richness.
academy.l4.t2: Essential tiki ingredients: Falernum (lime, clove, almond), Orgeat (almond), Allspice Dram (allspice), Coconut cream, Tropical juices (pineapple, passion fruit, grapefruit). Many tiki recipes are secret and use the bar's own proprietary 'mixes.'
academy.l4.tip2: The tiki 'flash blend' uses a blender with crushed ice for only 5 seconds — it is not a frozen daiquiri. The goal is to integrate and chill, not make a smoothie. The result should have a granita-like texture.
academy.l4.t3: The Planter's Punch follows the mnemonic rule: 'One of Sour, Two of Sweet, Three of Strong, Four of Weak' (1 part citrus, 2 sweet, 3 rum, 4 ice/water). The Singapore Sling started the trend of long, fruity tropical cocktails.
academy.l4.note2: Tiki garnishes are part of the experience: tiny umbrellas, carved fruit, edible orchids, and literal fire (with overproof rum). Tiki is liquid theater.
academy.l4.q1: Who are the two founding fathers of tiki culture?
academy.l4.q1a1: Don the Beachcomber and Trader Vic
academy.l4.q1exp: Don the Beachcomber (Ernest Gantt) and Trader Vic (Victor Bergeron) founded tiki culture in California in the 1930s.
academy.l4.q2: How many rums do tiki cocktails typically use?
academy.l4.q2exp: Tiki cocktails typically blend 2–3 rums of different styles to create flavor complexity.
academy.l4.q3a1: A syrup/liqueur of lime, clove, and almond
academy.l4.q3exp: Falernum is a Caribbean syrup or liqueur made with lime, clove, almond, and spices. It is essential in tiki cocktails.
academy.l4.q4: What is the mnemonic rule for Planter's Punch?
academy.l4.q4exp: 'One of Sour, Two of Sweet, Three of Strong, Four of Weak' is the classic Planter's Punch rule.
academy.l4.q5: Which tiki cocktail introduced Campari to the tropical world?
academy.l4.q5exp: The Jungle Bird, created in 1978 at the Kuala Lumpur Hilton, broke the mold by combining Campari with rum and tropical juices.
academy.l4.q6: What is the 'flash blend' in tiki?
academy.l4.q6a1: Blending with ice for only 5 seconds
academy.l4.q6exp: The flash blend means blending with crushed ice for only 5 seconds, creating a granita-like texture without making a smoothie.
academy.l4.q7: What does the name 'Three Dots and a Dash' mean in Morse code?
academy.l4.q7exp: Three Dots and a Dash (· · · —) is Morse code for V, for Victory. It was created by Don the Beachcomber during WWII.
academy.l4.q8: What ingredient contributes almond notes in tiki cocktails?
academy.l4.q8exp: Orgeat is an almond syrup with orange flower water that contributes almond and marzipan notes to cocktails.
academy.l4.q9exp: The Painkiller was created at the Soggy Dollar Bar in the Virgin Islands, where patrons would swim to the bar.
academy.l4.q10: What rum does the Barbadian Corn 'n' Oil use?
academy.l4.q10exp: Corn 'n' Oil uses blackstrap rum (dark, dense rum) with falernum. Its name describes its dark, oily appearance.
academy.l4.les0.q1: In what decade did tiki culture originate?
academy.l4.les0.q1exp: Tiki culture was born in the 1930s in California, founded by Don the Beachcomber and Trader Vic.
academy.l4.les0.q2: Why were tiki recipes originally kept secret?
academy.l4.les0.q2a1: They used coded ingredients to prevent copying
academy.l4.les0.q2a4: They were too simple to patent
academy.l4.les0.q2exp: Don the Beachcomber and Trader Vic used coded ingredient names in their recipes to prevent competitors from copying their drinks.
academy.l4.les0.q3: Who is generally credited with inventing the Mai Tai after a long dispute?
academy.l4.les0.q3exp: Trader Vic and Don the Beachcomber disputed the Mai Tai's authorship for decades; Trader Vic generally won the debate.
academy.l4.les1.q1: Why do tiki cocktails use multiple rums?
academy.l4.les1.q1a1: Each rum contributes different flavor notes for complexity
academy.l4.les1.q1a3: Because a single rum would be too sweet
academy.l4.les1.q1a4: It is required by tiki tradition but has no practical purpose
academy.l4.les1.q1exp: Tiki cocktails blend 2-3 rums (white, gold, Demerara) because each brings different notes: cleanliness, depth, and caramelized richness.
academy.l4.les1.q2exp: Orgeat is an almond syrup (often with orange flower water) used in tiki cocktails like the Mai Tai for almond and marzipan notes.
academy.l4.les1.q3: How long does a tiki 'flash blend' last?
academy.l4.les1.q3exp: The flash blend uses a blender with crushed ice for only 5 seconds — just enough to integrate and chill without making a smoothie.
academy.l4.les2.q1: What is the mnemonic formula for Planter's Punch?
academy.l4.les2.q1exp: The classic Planter's Punch follows 'One of Sour, Two of Sweet, Three of Strong, Four of Weak' as its ratio formula.
academy.l4.les2.q2: What role do garnishes play in tiki cocktails?
academy.l4.les2.q2a1: They are part of the full tiki experience
academy.l4.les2.q2a2: They are purely optional and decorative
academy.l4.les2.q2a3: They are only used in competitions
academy.l4.les2.q2a4: They replace the need for bitters
academy.l4.les2.q2exp: Tiki garnishes (umbrellas, carved fruit, fire) are part of the experience — tiki is 'liquid theater' where presentation matters.
academy.l4.les2.q3: What cocktail started the trend of long, fruity tropical drinks?
academy.l4.les2.q3exp: The Singapore Sling started the trend of long, fruity tropical cocktails and influenced the tiki movement.
academy.l5.title: Advanced Techniques
academy.l5.desc: Flips, Punches, Cobblers, Fizzes, and modern techniques
academy.l5.t1: The Fizz is a sour served with soda. The Ramos Gin Fizz is its masterpiece: gin + citrus + egg white + cream + orange flower water, shaken for 12+ minutes (historically) to create an impossibly silky foam. Today a dry shake + extended wet shake is used.
academy.l5.tip1: For a modern Ramos Gin Fizz: dry shake 30 seconds without ice, then wet shake 2 minutes with ice. Pour into a glass with no ice and slowly add the soda — you'll see the foam rise above the rim like a soufflé.
academy.l5.note1: Henry C. Ramos employed teams of 'shaker boys' at his New Orleans bar. Each bartender would shake for minutes and pass the shaker to the next. It was said the sound could be heard a block away.
academy.l5.t2: A Flip contains a whole egg (yolk + white), spirit, and sugar, with no citrus. The result is creamy and rich. A Cobbler is spirit + fresh fruit + sugar over crushed ice. Punches are the mothers of all cocktails: batch versions meant for sharing.
academy.l5.tip2: For a perfect Flip: use a fresh whole egg, vigorous dry shake, then wet shake. Freshly grated nutmeg at the end is essential — it adds a spiced aroma that complements the creaminess.
academy.l5.t3: The Brandy Crusta (1850s, New Orleans) is considered the grandmother of sours. Its sugar 'crusta' and the complete lemon peel inside the glass were revolutionary. The Last Word resurfaced in 2004 after decades of obscurity — a perfect equal-parts cocktail.
academy.l5.note2: The cocktail renaissance of the 2000s rediscovered dozens of forgotten recipes. Bartenders like Murray Stenson (Last Word), Sam Ross (Penicillin), and Audrey Saunders (Gin-Gin Mule) created modern classics worthy of the originals.
academy.l5.t4: Champagne cocktails: the French 75 (gin + lemon + sugar + champagne) is the star. The base is shaken and topped with cold champagne. The Gin Fizz marked the transition between classic and modern mixology with its refined foam and carbonation technique.
academy.l5.tip3: When making champagne cocktails, never shake the champagne — it loses its bubbles. Only shake the base (spirit + citrus + sweet) and top with cold champagne directly in the glass.
academy.l5.q1: How long was the Ramos Gin Fizz historically shaken?
academy.l5.q1exp: The Ramos Gin Fizz was historically shaken for 12+ minutes to achieve its iconic foam. Today a dry shake + extended wet shake is used.
academy.l5.q2: What distinguishes a Flip from a Sour?
academy.l5.q2a1: It contains a whole egg and no citrus
academy.l5.q2exp: A Flip uses a whole egg (yolk + white), spirit, and sugar, but no citrus. It is creamy and rich, not acidic.
academy.l5.q3: Which cocktail from the 1850s is considered the 'grandmother of sours'?
academy.l5.q3exp: The Brandy Crusta (1850s, New Orleans) introduced the sugar crusta and the lemon peel, being the precursor to all sours.
academy.l5.q4: What special ingredient does the Ramos Gin Fizz contain besides egg white?
academy.l5.q4exp: The Ramos Gin Fizz contains cream and orange flower water, in addition to the egg white.
academy.l5.q5a1: Spirit + fresh fruit + sugar over crushed ice
academy.l5.q5exp: A Cobbler is served over crushed ice with fresh fruit and sugar. It was the cocktail that popularized the use of the straw.
academy.l5.q6: Who rediscovered the Last Word in 2004?
academy.l5.q6exp: Murray Stenson, a Seattle bartender, rediscovered the Last Word from a forgotten 1916 recipe and brought it back to fame.
academy.l5.q7: How is champagne added in a French 75?
academy.l5.q7a1: Topped at the end, without shaking
academy.l5.q7exp: The base is shaken separately (gin + lemon + sugar) and topped with cold champagne directly in the glass to preserve the bubbles.
academy.l5.q8: What spice is grated as a final garnish on a Flip?
academy.l5.q8exp: Freshly grated nutmeg is the classic garnish for a Flip, complementing the creaminess of the egg.
academy.l5.q9: What are Punches in the history of mixology?
academy.l5.q9a1: The mothers of all cocktails, prepared in batches
academy.l5.q9exp: Punches are the ancestors of mixology: batch drinks meant for sharing, predating the individual cocktail.
academy.l5.q10: What modern technique is used today for the Ramos Gin Fizz?
academy.l5.q10exp: Today a dry shake of 30 seconds (without ice) is done to emulsify, followed by a wet shake of 2 minutes with ice to chill and dilute.
academy.l5.les0.q1exp: A Fizz is a sour (spirit + citrus + sweet) topped with soda water for effervescence.
academy.l5.les0.q2: What ingredients make the Ramos Gin Fizz unique compared to a regular Gin Fizz?
academy.l5.les0.q2exp: The Ramos Gin Fizz adds cream and orange flower water to the standard fizz formula, creating its legendary silky foam.
academy.l5.les0.q3: In the modern technique for a Ramos Gin Fizz, how long is the dry shake?
academy.l5.les0.q3exp: The modern technique calls for a 30-second dry shake (without ice) to emulsify, followed by a 2-minute wet shake with ice.
academy.l5.les1.q1a1: Whole egg + spirit + sugar, no citrus
academy.l5.les1.q1exp: A Flip uses a whole egg (yolk and white) with spirit and sugar but never contains citrus, resulting in a creamy, rich drink.
academy.l5.les1.q2: What is the classic garnish for a Flip?
academy.l5.les1.q2exp: Freshly grated nutmeg is the traditional Flip garnish, adding a spiced aroma that complements the egg's creaminess.
academy.l5.les1.q3: What are Punches in the context of cocktail history?
academy.l5.les1.q3exp: Punches are batch drinks made for sharing and predate the individual cocktail — they are the ancestors of modern mixology.
academy.l5.les2.q1: When was the Brandy Crusta created?
academy.l5.les2.q1exp: The Brandy Crusta was created in the 1850s in New Orleans and is considered the grandmother of sours.
academy.l5.les2.q2: What makes the Brandy Crusta distinctive in its presentation?
academy.l5.les2.q2a1: A sugar crusta on the rim and a full lemon peel inside the glass
academy.l5.les2.q2exp: The Brandy Crusta features a sugar-crusted rim and an entire lemon peel lining the inside of the glass — revolutionary for its time.
academy.l5.les2.q3: In what year was the Last Word rediscovered by Murray Stenson?
academy.l5.les2.q3exp: Murray Stenson, a Seattle bartender, rediscovered the Last Word from a forgotten recipe and brought it back to fame in 2004.
academy.l5.les3.q1: What is the base spirit of a French 75?
academy.l5.les3.q1exp: The French 75 combines gin with lemon juice, sugar, and champagne. The name refers to a French 75mm field gun.
academy.l5.les3.q2: Why should you never shake champagne when making a champagne cocktail?
academy.l5.les3.q2a2: It makes the drink too cold
academy.l5.les3.q2a3: It causes the bottle to explode
academy.l5.les3.q2a4: It changes the flavor of the champagne
academy.l5.les3.q2exp: Shaking champagne destroys its carbonation. Only the base (spirit + citrus + sweet) is shaken, then topped with cold champagne.
academy.l5.les3.q3: What is the correct method for preparing a French 75?
academy.l5.les3.q3a1: Shake the base, then top with cold champagne in the glass
academy.l5.les3.q3a2: Stir everything together in a mixing glass
academy.l5.les3.q3a3: Shake all ingredients including the champagne
academy.l5.les3.q3a4: Build directly in the glass without shaking
academy.l5.les3.q3exp: The base (gin + lemon + sugar) is shaken with ice and strained, then topped with cold champagne directly in the glass.

wiki.art.techniques.double-strain.sub: Crystal-clear cocktails with no pulp or particles
wiki.art.techniques.double-strain.descri: Double straining is an essential technique for crystal-clear cocktails with a clean mouthfeel, removing ice shards, pulp, herbs, seeds, and other solids. You strain the cocktail TWICE simultaneously: first through a hawthorne strainer (on the shaker), then through a fine mesh strainer held over the serving glass. The result is a silky texture and flawless presentation.
wiki.art.techniques.double-strain.how: 1) Shake the cocktail normally with ice. 2) Place the hawthorne strainer on top of the shaker. 3) Hold the fine mesh strainer with your left hand OVER the serving glass. 4) With your right hand, pour the cocktail through both strainers at once in one fluid motion. 5) Tilt slightly to speed up the flow. The drink passes hawthorne → fine mesh → glass, removing every solid before it hits the glass.
wiki.art.techniques.double-strain.tips: Always use a FINE mesh strainer (not a regular one) — coarse mesh lets small particles through. The best ones are stainless steel with very tight mesh. Clean the fine strainer immediately after use — it clogs easily with pulp. Never press a spoon through the mesh (it pushes solids through). The correct technique is to let gravity do the work. A small investment ($15-30) for a huge difference in the cocktail's visual quality.
wiki.art.techniques.double-strain.when: Mandatory for shaken cocktails with muddled herbs (mint, basil, jalapeño), fresh fruit, egg white, or when using crushed ice in the shaker. Essential for: Margarita (lime pulp), Gin Basil Smash (basil leaves), Whiskey Sour (egg white foam), Daiquiri (lime pulp), any cocktail with fresh berries, tiki drinks with spices. Unnecessary in stirred drinks (Manhattan, Martini — no solids to strain).
wiki.art.techniques.dry-shake.descriptio: The dry shake is the technique of shaking a cocktail WITHOUT ice before the regular shake, to fully emulsify egg whites or aquafaba and create the dense, silky foam that defines Sours. Ice would chill the proteins prematurely and prevent proper emulsification. Two shakes: first dry (no ice) to emulsify, then with ice to chill and dilute.
wiki.art.techniques.dry-shake.how: STANDARD METHOD: 1) Add all ingredients (including the egg white) to the shaker WITHOUT ice. 2) Shake vigorously for 10-15 seconds (no ice, a muted sound). 3) Open, add ice. 4) Shake again 10-15 seconds with ice (bright metallic sound). 5) Double-strain into the glass. REVERSE DRY SHAKE: shake FIRST with ice, strain the ice out, then dry shake the already chilled liquid — produces even denser foam.
wiki.art.techniques.dry-shake.tips: For perfect foam: use FRESH egg white (ideally unpasteurized). Aquafaba (canned chickpea liquid) is an identical vegan substitute. Adding a small hawthorne spring inside the shaker during the dry shake speeds up emulsification — 5-7 seconds is enough. For the iconic Angostura "painting": dry shake → ice → shake → double-strain → dashes of Angostura on the foam → use a toothpick to draw. Without a dry shake, the modern Whiskey Sour is impossible.
wiki.art.techniques.dry-shake.when: Mandatory in any cocktail with egg white or aquafaba: Whiskey Sour, Pisco Sour, Gin Sour, Ramos Gin Fizz, Clover Club, Pink Lady, Aviation with egg, Whiskey Fix. Without a dry shake, the foam is thin and short-lived. Also useful for cocktails with whipped cream or pasteurized whites. Unnecessary for cocktails without proteins (most modern sours use the technique).
wiki.art.techniques.fat-wash.sub: Infusing fats to add texture and flavor
wiki.art.techniques.fat-wash.description: Fat-washing is a modern technique that infuses a spirit with animal or vegetable fats to add flavor and a silky texture. The fat is mixed with the alcohol at room temperature, frozen (the fat solidifies), and removed — leaving the fat-soluble aromatics in the spirit while eliminating the fat itself. The result: a spirit with unique character and silky mouthfeel. It is the most revolutionary technique of 2000s modern bartending.
wiki.art.techniques.fat-wash.how: METHOD: 1) Render the fat (cook bacon to get liquid fat, or melt butter). 2) Mix 60ml of rendered fat with 750ml of spirit at room temperature in a container. 3) Shake to emulsify. 4) Let stand 4 hours at room temperature — aromatic molecules transfer to the alcohol. 5) Freeze for 12-24h — the fat solidifies on the surface. 6) Strain through a coffee filter (or mesh + cheesecloth) to remove all fat. The resulting spirit is clear and clean but with transformed flavor and texture.
wiki.art.techniques.fat-wash.tips: Standard ratio: 60ml fat per 750ml spirit (adjust to desired intensity). Liquid fats at room temperature (oils) only need refrigeration (4h), not freezing. Solid fats (bacon, butter) require deep freezing. Filter TWICE with a coffee filter for crystal-clear results. Fat-washed spirits keep for months refrigerated. Bacon + bourbon + maple syrup = Benton's Old Fashioned, the cocktail that launched the technique. Experiment with olive oil + gin, coconut oil + rum, duck fat + cognac.
wiki.art.techniques.fat-wash.when: Use it to create unique spirits with flavors unattainable any other way: Bacon-washed bourbon (Benton's Old Fashioned, Don Lee 2007), coconut fat-washed rum, duck fat bourbon, butter-washed rum, sesame oil gin, olive oil gin (for textured Martinis). Best in stirred/refined cocktails where the silky mouthfeel shines (Old Fashioned, Manhattan). Invented by bartender Eben Freeman (Tailor NYC, 2006) and popularized by Don Lee.
wiki.art.techniques.infusion.sub: Macerating ingredients in spirits to create unique flavors
wiki.art.techniques.infusion.description: Infusion is the technique of macerating ingredients (fruits, herbs, spices, chilies, tea, coffee) in a spirit for hours or days to transfer their flavors and aromas to the alcohol. It is one of the most versatile cocktail techniques — it allows you to create custom spirits you cannot buy. From classic jalapeño-infused tequila for spicy Margaritas to exotic herbal infusions, it expands the bartender's repertoire infinitely.
wiki.art.techniques.infusion.how: APPROXIMATE TIMES by ingredient: Fresh chilies (jalapeño, habanero): 2-4 hours. Fresh herbs (basil, rosemary): 1-2 hours (longer turns bitter). Tea: 10-30 minutes (longer becomes tannic). Soft fruits (strawberry, peach): 24-48 hours. Whole spices (cinnamon, clove): 2-7 days. Coffee: 12-24 hours. Vanilla: 1-2 weeks. METHOD: cut ingredient into pieces, add to spirit in a sealed jar, store cool and dark, taste daily, strain once you hit desired intensity. Label with date and ingredient.
wiki.art.techniques.infusion.tips: TASTE every 2-4 hours (chilies/herbs) or every 12-24h (fruits/spices) — over-infusion is irreversible. Chilies: remove seeds and white ribs to avoid extreme heat. Tea and tender herbs: do NOT exceed times — they go bitter quickly. Fruits: cut small for more contact area. For clear infusions, use neutral spirits (vodka, unaged); for complex infusions, spirits with character (bourbon, tequila, dark rum). ALWAYS label with date and content. They keep 2-4 weeks refrigerated.
wiki.art.techniques.infusion.when: Whenever you want a specific flavor in a spirit that doesn't exist commercially, or when quality/freshness beats any industrial product. Classic examples: Tequila + jalapeño (4h), Vodka + cucumber (24h), Gin + Earl Grey tea (2h), Bourbon + apple + cinnamon (48h), Rum + vanilla + coffee (1 week), Vodka + habanero (12h). Essential technique for creative bars and original cocktail menus. Also used for syrups, vinegars, and sauces.
wiki.art.techniques.swizzle.sub: The tiki technique with the Caribbean stick
wiki.art.techniques.swizzle.description: The swizzle is a traditional Caribbean technique that uses a swizzle stick (bois lelé) to mix and chill cocktails directly in the serving glass full of crushed ice. By rotating the stick between the palms of your hands, you create turbulent motion that chills the cocktail without over-diluting, while the crushed ice builds the signature frost on the outside of the glass. It is the technique that defines the tiki style and classic tropical cocktails.
wiki.art.techniques.swizzle.how: 1) Build the cocktail directly in a highball/Collins glass. 2) Fill the glass COMPLETELY with crushed ice (not cubes). 3) Insert the swizzle stick to the bottom of the glass. 4) Rotate the stick rapidly between the palms of your hands in a friction motion — up and down, side to side, for 15-20 seconds. 5) The glass should frost over on the outside — the sign that it's cold enough. 6) Top up with more crushed ice. 7) Add bitters and garnish.
wiki.art.techniques.swizzle.tips: The traditional swizzle stick is the bois lelé (Quararibea turbinata tree) — its three split prongs at the base act as a natural whisk. Substitutes: long bar spoon (less effective), long-handled whisk. For perfect frost on the glass: press against the ice with a vertical motion, not circular. The Queen's Park Swizzle is the canonical example: gently muddled mint, lime, demerara sugar, dark rum, crushed ice, swizzle, Angostura on top. A technique that sets serious tiki bartenders apart.
wiki.art.techniques.swizzle.when: Essential for traditional tiki cocktails and Caribbean drinks with crushed ice: Queen's Park Swizzle (rum, mint, lime, sugar, bitters — Trinidad, 1915), Bermuda Rum Swizzle (various rums, juices, bitters), Gin-Gin Mule, tiki-style drinks from Don the Beachcomber and Trader Vic. Also for any cocktail where you want the iconic exterior frost. Do not use for classic stirred cocktails (Martini, Manhattan) or for cocktails with egg white.
wiki.art.families.sours-family.descripti: The Sour family is THE MOST IMPORTANT STRUCTURE in classic and modern bartending. It rests on three pillars: spirit (base), acid (citrus), and sweet (syrup/liqueur). This simple trinity generates infinite variations: from the Whiskey Sour to the Margarita, Daiquiri, and Sidecar. Mastering the Sour is mastering bartending — any professional can build a cocktail on its template. The traditional Sour also includes egg white for silky texture.
wiki.art.families.sours-family.examples: WHISKEY SOUR (bourbon, lemon, syrup, egg white) — the prototype. MARGARITA (tequila, lime, Cointreau — Cointreau replaces the syrup). DAIQUIRI (white rum, lime, syrup). SIDECAR (cognac, Cointreau, lemon). PISCO SOUR (pisco, lime, syrup, egg white, Angostura). GIMLET (gin, lime cordial). SOUTHSIDE (gin, lime, syrup, mint). CLOVER CLUB (gin, raspberry, lemon, egg white). PAPER PLANE (bourbon, Aperol, Amaro Nonino, lemon — modern). PENICILLIN (scotch, lemon, honey-ginger, Islay float).
wiki.art.families.sours-family.origin: USA, 19th century. The term "sour" first appears in Jerry Thomas's "The Bon Vivant's Companion" (1862) as a cocktail category. Derived from British naval grog (rum + lime + sugar + water, to prevent scurvy), which Royal Navy sailors drank from 1740. The Whiskey Sour became the American standard by the 1870s-1880s and spread worldwide.
wiki.art.families.sours-family.structure: CLASSIC FORMULA: 60ml spirit + 22ml citrus juice (lemon/lime) + 15ml simple syrup. RATIO 2:¾:½, or David Embury's "Gold Standard" 8:3:2. Optional: egg white (20ml) or aquafaba for silky texture. To modify: citrus and syrup can be replaced by liqueurs that provide both (Cointreau is acid+sweet, Aperol is bitter+sweet). The Sour test: it should have a gentle acid kick on the first sip and a sweetness that accompanies, not dominates.
wiki.art.families.sours-family.tips: BALANCE: the 60/22/15 formula is a starting point — adjust for the spirit's intensity (overproof bourbon needs more acid/sweet; neutral vodka less). ALWAYS shake with ice to chill and aerate. Egg white transforms a sour into the modern silky-foam version (see dry-shake). SYRUP: simple (1:1) for clarity, demerara (2:1) for richness, diluted honey for depth. A perfect Whiskey Sour should be the first thing any new bartender masters — everything else derives from it.
wiki.art.families.fizz-family.sub: Sours with bubbles — long and refreshing
wiki.art.families.fizz-family.descriptio: The Fizz is a variant of the Sour where soda water is added at the end, turning the short cocktail into a long, refreshing one. Typically served in a highball glass WITHOUT ice (maximum effervescence) or over ice. The name "fizz" is onomatopoeia for the sound of bubbling soda. The Gin Fizz is the prototype; the Ramos Gin Fizz is the category's masterpiece — a technical cocktail that requires 12 minutes of shaking.
wiki.art.families.fizz-family.examples: GIN FIZZ (gin, lemon, syrup, soda). SILVER FIZZ (Gin Fizz + egg white — with foam). RAMOS GIN FIZZ (gin, lemon, lime, cream, egg white, orange flower water, sugar, soda — 12-minute shake). SLOE GIN FIZZ (sloe gin, lemon, syrup, soda). DIAMOND FIZZ (gin, lemon, sugar, champagne — instead of soda). MORNING GLORY FIZZ (scotch, lemon, syrup, egg white, absinthe, soda). ROYAL GIN FIZZ (Gin Fizz with a whole egg). NEW ORLEANS FIZZ = Ramos Gin Fizz.
wiki.art.families.fizz-family.origin: New Orleans and San Francisco, second half of the 19th century. The Gin Fizz appears in Jerry Thomas's 1887 book. Henry Ramos creates the Ramos Gin Fizz at the Imperial Cabinet Saloon in New Orleans in 1888 — it becomes so popular the bar hired teams of shakers to shake cocktails in assembly-line fashion during Mardi Gras. In 1915, 35 "shaker boys" shook Ramos Gin Fizzes non-stop throughout Carnival.
wiki.art.families.fizz-family.structure: FORMULA: Sour + soda at the end. Standard: 60ml spirit + 22ml citrus + 15ml syrup + egg white (optional) + 60-90ml soda. Shake vigorously WITHOUT the soda, strain into a highball glass (cold, traditionally without ice), and top with soda. Silver Fizz = with egg white. Golden Fizz = with yolk. Royal Fizz = with whole egg. Ramos Fizz = Silver Fizz + cream + orange flower water + lime (the only one using two citrus juices). The effervescence should last several minutes of sipping.
wiki.art.families.fizz-family.tips: RAMOS GIN FIZZ: dry shake 1 min, ice and shake 3 min (or 12 min traditional), strain into a chilled highball with no ice, top with soda VERY SLOWLY — the foam should rise above the rim forming a "head". Orange flower water (1-2 dashes) is essential — without it, it's not a Ramos. Serve without ice for maximum effervescence. If using ice, add it after pouring. Drink with a straw to enjoy the layers: creamy foam on top, icy liquid below.
wiki.art.families.flip-family.descriptio: The Flip is a family of sumptuous cocktails that combine spirit, sugar, and a WHOLE egg (yolk and white), shaken vigorously to create a creamy, custard-like drinkable texture. Finished with a grating of nutmeg, it is a classic dessert cocktail that nearly disappeared after Prohibition but was revived by the cocktail renaissance. Originally served hot with a red-hot iron (hence "flipped"), today Flips are prepared cold with a dry-shake technique.
wiki.art.families.flip-family.examples: PORTO FLIP (tawny port, cognac, whole egg, nutmeg — the standard). BRANDY FLIP (brandy, sugar, egg — Jerry Thomas original). SHERRY FLIP (oloroso sherry, sugar, egg). COFFEE FLIP (coffee, egg, sugar, rum — hot). RUM FLIP (dark rum, sugar, egg — traditional Caribbean). WHISKEY FLIP (rye or bourbon, sugar, egg). CHOCOLATE FLIP (crème de cacao, egg, rum). MODERN FLIP (any spirit, honey, whole egg, creative variants).
wiki.art.families.flip-family.origin: England, late 17th century. The first Flips appear in the 1690s in dockside taverns — a mix of beer, rum, and sugar heated with a red-hot iron (loggerhead) that bartenders plunged into the drink, "flipping" the brew as it warmed. 19th century: the form evolves with a whole egg and is served cold. 1862: Jerry Thomas documents several Flips in "The Bon Vivant's Companion". 1920s-1970s: they nearly vanish. 2000s-present: revival with the cocktail renaissance.
wiki.art.families.flip-family.structure: CLASSIC FORMULA: 60ml spirit + 15ml syrup + 1 whole egg. Dry shake (without ice) 10-15 seconds to emulsify, then shake with ice another 10-15 seconds. Double-strain into a small coupe or Nick & Nora glass. Garnish: freshly grated nutmeg on top. Variations: swap syrup for honey, add a splash of cream for extra richness, change the spirit. Can be HOT (served in mugs, toddy-style) or COLD (modern style, more common).
wiki.art.families.flip-family.tips: The modern Flip IS a dessert cocktail — serve after dinner, not as an aperitif. Use a FRESH whole egg (the yolk gives body, the white the foam). Dry shake is MANDATORY to emulsify properly. ALWAYS freshly grated nutmeg on top — the aroma defines the Flip. 10-year tawny port is the quintessential Flip. Guest worried about raw egg: use pasteurized egg (the result is virtually identical). Aquafaba does NOT work for Flips — the yolk is irreplaceable for the creamy body.
wiki.art.families.julep-family.sub: Mint + crushed ice — American Southern elegance
wiki.art.families.julep-family.descripti: The Julep is a traditional cocktail of the American South, built on four elements: spirit, fresh mint, sugar, and abundant crushed ice. It is traditionally served in a silver julep cup that frosts over on the outside — the silver conducts the cold from the crushed ice and creates an iconic tactile and visual experience. The Mint Julep is the official cocktail of the Kentucky Derby (over 120,000 are served every year) and the emblem of Southern hospitality.
wiki.art.families.julep-family.examples: MINT JULEP (bourbon, mint, sugar, crushed ice — the Kentucky prototype). COGNAC JULEP (cognac, mint, sugar — the original version before bourbon replaced it in the 1830s). PEACH JULEP (bourbon, mint, sugar, peach purée). CHAMPAGNE JULEP (mint, sugar, champagne — Jerry Thomas). PINEAPPLE JULEP (rum, mint, pineapple, sugar). GIN JULEP (gin, mint, sugar — modern twist). SMOKY JULEP (mezcal, mint, agave).
wiki.art.families.julep-family.origin: Eighteenth century, American South (Kentucky, Virginia, Maryland). The word "julep" derives from Arabic "julab" (rose water) via Persian and Latin. The first written references appear in 1785 in Philadelphia newspapers. 1830s: the Mint Julep is established as the signature cocktail of the South, associated with the planter aristocracy. 1938: Churchill Downs (home of the Kentucky Derby) names it the race's official cocktail. Today it is an untouchable cultural symbol of the Derby.
wiki.art.families.julep-family.structure: CLASSIC FORMULA: 60-75ml spirit + 8-10 fresh mint leaves + 15ml simple syrup (or 2 sugar cubes + splash of water) + abundant crushed ice. LIGHTLY muddle the mint with the syrup in the bottom of the julep cup. Add the spirit. Fill completely with crushed ice. Stir with a julep spoon until the cup frosts on the outside. Add MORE crushed ice to form a dome above the rim. Garnish: fresh mint bouquet, short straw.
wiki.art.families.julep-family.tips: SILVER CUP: traditional and functional — conducts the cold from the ice. If you don't have one, use a highball with plenty of crushed ice. CRUSHED ICE: essential (not cubes) — creates the surface that frosts. Buy an ice crusher or pound with a Lewis bag. MINT: do NOT muddle aggressively — just press gently to release the oils, never tear the leaves (they release bitter chlorophyll). The mint bouquet garnish goes near the straw — so you smell the mint with every sip. Use bourbon at 45-50% ABV minimum (the crushed ice dilutes a lot).
wiki.art.families.punch-family.sub: Bowl cocktails — the oldest social tradition
wiki.art.families.punch-family.descripti: Punch is the MOTHER OF ALL COCKTAILS — the oldest family in bartending, originating in the 17th century before the term "cocktail" even existed. It is prepared in a large bowl for sharing, with five classic components: spirit (strong), citrus (sour), sugar (sweet), water (weak), and spices (tea/bitters). The traditional rhyming rule: "One of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak." It is the father of the modern cocktail — all Sours and Highballs derive from Punch structure.
wiki.art.families.punch-family.examples: PLANTER'S PUNCH (dark rum, lime, syrup, bitters, water — the Jamaican classic). PHILADELPHIA FISH HOUSE PUNCH (rum, cognac, peach, lemon, tea — since 1732). REGENT'S PUNCH (champagne, rum, green tea, citrus, pineapple — 1820s, favorite of King George IV). CHATHAM ARTILLERY PUNCH (bourbon, cognac, rum, champagne, tea, lemon — brutal, "the most deadly drink ever devised"). CHRISTMAS BOWL (mulled wine, brandy, orange, spices). BAJAN RUM PUNCH (Mount Gay rum, lime, syrup, Angostura, nutmeg — traditional Barbados recipe).
wiki.art.families.punch-family.origin: British colonial India, 1600s. The word "punch" derives from Hindi "pāñc" or Sanskrit "pañca" (five) — for its five ingredients. British sailors of the East India Company took it back to England and from there to the world. 1632: first written mention in an English document. 17th-19th centuries: the golden age of Punch — it was THE way to drink socially, served from bowls in taverns and homes. The modern individual cocktail emerges as a "mini-punch" in the mid-19th century.
wiki.art.families.punch-family.structure: CLASSIC FORMULA (the rhymed recipe): "1 sour, 2 sweet, 3 strong, 4 weak" — 1 part citrus, 2 parts sweet, 3 parts spirit, 4 parts "weak" (tea, water, champagne). Spices at the end (cinnamon, clove, nutmeg, bitters). For a 10-person bowl: 250ml citrus + 500ml sugar/syrup + 750ml spirit + 1000ml tea/water. Large ice block in the center (chills without fast dilution). Abundant garnish: citrus slices, berries, whole spices floating.
wiki.art.families.punch-family.tips: LARGE ICE BLOCK: freeze water in a big container (Tupperware, bundt pan) 24h ahead — melts 5x slower than small cubes. Add to the bowl just before serving. MAKE SPICED SYRUPS: strong black tea, spice infusions, super juice for higher yield. Punch is EXCELLENT for events — prepare a batch and guests serve themselves (less work for the bartender). Always taste before serving — adjust acid/sweet. A well-made Punch bowl is more impressive than 10 individual cocktails.
wiki.art.families.tiki-family.sub: Complex tropical cocktails — the Polynesian fantasy
wiki.art.families.tiki-family.descriptio: Tiki is an aesthetic and cultural cocktail category created in California in the 1930s that imagined an exotic Polynesian fantasy. Tiki cocktails are complex — often with 5-10 ingredients — blending multiple rums, citrus, spiced syrups (falernum, orgeat), fruit liqueurs, and bitters. Served in dramatic vessels (tiki mugs, coconuts, hollowed pineapples) with excessive tropical garnishes. It was the most popular bar style of the 1940s-1960s, disappeared, and returned with force in the 2000s.
wiki.art.families.tiki-family.examples: MAI TAI (aged rum, dark rum, lime, orgeat, curaçao — Trader Vic 1944). ZOMBIE (3 rums, falernum, lime, grapefruit, grenadine, absinthe, Angostura, allspice dram — Don 1934). SCORPION (rum, brandy, lime, orange, orgeat). NAVY GROG (3 rums, lime, grapefruit, honey, soda). PAINKILLER (rum, coconut, pineapple, orange, nutmeg). JUNGLE BIRD (dark rum, Campari, pineapple, lime). THREE DOTS AND A DASH (rhum agricole, falernum, lime, orange, honey, Angostura, allspice dram). SATURN (gin, falernum, orgeat, lime, passion fruit). BLUE HAWAII, MISSIONARY'S DOWNFALL, HURRICANE, SUFFERING BASTARD.
wiki.art.families.tiki-family.origin: California, USA. 1933: Ernest Raymond Beaumont-Gantt opens "Don the Beachcomber" in Hollywood after the end of Prohibition — the first tiki bar. 1937: Victor Bergeron opens "Trader Vic's" in Oakland. These two men created most of the classic tiki cocktails — and fiercely rivaled each other, guarding recipes as trade secrets. 1944: Trader Vic creates the Mai Tai. 1960s: tiki cultural explosion driven by Polynesian films, the Pacific War, and Californian leisure culture. 1970s: decline. 2000s: revival led by bartenders like Jeff Berry (Beachbum).
wiki.art.families.tiki-family.structure: There is NO simple formula — each tiki cocktail is unique. Common principles: MULTIPLE RUMS (white + dark + overproof + agricole), 2-3 CITRUS JUICES (lime, grapefruit, orange), SPICED SYRUP (falernum, orgeat, honey, cinnamon), FRUIT LIQUEUR (maraschino, curaçao, crème de menthe), BITTERS (Angostura, pimento dram), SOMETIMES ABSINTHE. Technique: vigorous shake with crushed ice, serve over more crushed ice in a tiki mug or exotic glass. Abundant garnish: mint, lime, cherries, parasols, flamed cinnamon spray. Each cocktail tells a story.
wiki.art.families.tiki-family.tips: MULTIPLE RUMS: the key to tiki. Minimum stock: white rum (Bacardí/Plantation 3 Stars), Jamaican dark (Smith & Cross, Appleton), Demerara (El Dorado 5yo), overproof (Wray & Nephew 63%). Homemade FALERNUM AND ORGEAT are notably better than commercial. TIKI MUGS: not a gimmick — they insulate cold better and create the theatrical experience. GENEROUS GARNISH: mint, tropical fruits, parasols, edible flowers. Jeff "Beachbum" Berry's books are the modern tiki bible. A good tiki bar is a full experience — aromas, visuals, rituals.
wiki.art.beer.cerveza.sub: The most-consumed fermented drink in the world
wiki.art.beer.cerveza.description: Beer is the oldest and most-consumed alcoholic drink in the world — 190 billion liters a year. Made from cereals (mainly malted barley), water, hops, and yeast, it ranges from light lagers to dense, opaque stouts. For a professional bartender, knowing beer styles is essential: beer cocktails (Michelada, Shandy, Snakebite), pairings, and beer as the highest-grossing category in any bar.
wiki.art.beer.cerveza.history: 4000 BC: first evidence of beer in Sumer. 3000 BC: Egypt produces beer on an industrial scale. 6th century: European monks master the craft. 1516: Reinheitsgebot in Bavaria. 1842: Josef Groll creates the first Pilsner in Plzeň (Czechia) — the golden lager that would conquer the world is born. 1876: Pasteur discovers yeast — a revolution in quality control. 20th century: macro-breweries dominate. 1980s-present: the craft beer revolution restores diversity.
wiki.art.beer.cerveza.origin: Mesopotamia and Egypt, c. 4000-3000 BC. The first beers were fermented bread porridges. Sumer had Ninkasi, the goddess dedicated to beer. Egypt paid the pyramid workers in beer. Medieval Europe: monasteries (Belgian Trappists, German Benedictines) perfected brewing. 1516: the Reinheitsgebot (Bavarian Purity Law) rules that beer may contain only water, barley, and hops.
wiki.art.beer.cerveza.production: Malting: barley is soaked, germinated, and kiln-dried (gives color and flavor). Mashing: ground malt + hot water extract sugars (wort). Boiling: hops are added (bitterness, aroma, preservative). Fermentation: yeast turns sugars into alcohol + CO₂. Ale = top fermentation (Saccharomyces cerevisiae, 15-24°C, 5-7 days — fruity, complex). Lager = bottom fermentation (S. pastorianus, 7-13°C, weeks — clean, crisp). Conditioning, filtering, and packaging.
wiki.art.beer.cerveza.tasting: Pilsner: golden, crisp, floral hops, dry, clean finish. IPA: amber-gold, intense hops (citrus, tropical, pine), pronounced bitterness. Wheat: hazy, banana, clove, soft and refreshing. Stout: opaque black, roasted coffee, chocolate, creamy. Porter: dark brown, caramel, nut, soft coffee. Belgian Tripel: strong gold, fruit, spice, honey, effervescent. Sour/Lambic: acidic, complex, funk, fruit. The diversity of styles is infinite — each one is a world.
wiki.art.beer.cerveza.tips: Serve each style at its temperature: lagers 3-5°C, pale ales 7-10°C, stouts 10-13°C, Belgians 8-12°C. The glass matters: pilsner in a tall glass, IPA in a tulip, stout in a pint, wheat in a weizen glass, Belgians in a chalice. Always pour at a 45° tilt, straightening to form two fingers of foam. Guinness: pour in two stages (fill ¾, wait, top up). Michelada: use a light beer (Corona, Modelo Especial). A strong beer list is as important as the cocktail menu.
wiki.art.beer.cerveza.types: LAGERS: Pilsner (Pilsner Urquell, Heineken — golden, hoppy, crisp). Helles (Munich — soft malt, low hops). Vienna Lager (amber, caramel — Negra Modelo). Bock/Doppelbock (strong, malty — Paulaner Salvator). ALES: Pale Ale/IPA (hoppy, citrus, tropical — Sierra Nevada, Punk IPA). Wheat Beer/Weizen (wheat, banana, clove — Paulaner, Hoegaarden). Stout (dark, coffee, chocolate — Guinness). Porter (dark, lighter than stout). Belgian (Dubbel, Tripel, Quad — Chimay, Westmalle). Sour/Lambic (acidic, spontaneous fermentation — Cantillon).
wiki.art.beer.cerveza.cocktails: Michelada (beer, lime, salt, hot sauce, Worcestershire, Clamato — the Mexican Bloody Mary with beer). Shandy (beer + lemonade 1:1 — universal and refreshing). Radler (beer + lemon soda — German tradition). Snakebite (lager + cider 1:1 — British). Black Velvet (stout + champagne — elegant and surprising). Boilermaker (whiskey shot + beer — working-class tradition). Beer Margarita (beer, tequila, lime, lemonade concentrate).
wiki.art.beer.sidra.description: Cider is an alcoholic drink (4-8% ABV) made by fermenting apple juice (and sometimes pear — then called perry/perada). It is the most important fermented beverage after beer and wine, with a thousand-year tradition in Asturias, the Basque Country, Normandy, Brittany, and the British Isles. In bartending, cider is the base of Snakebite, Kir Normand, and many autumn spritzers.
wiki.art.beer.sidra.history: 1st century BC: Celts in northern Hispania and Gaul ferment apples. 1066: the Normans bring the cider tradition to England. 13th century: cider becomes the main drink in Asturias, Normandy, and western England. 1760s: the Bulmer family founds the first commercial cider house in Herefordshire. 20th century: Strongbow and Magners popularize commercial cider. 2010s: the craft cider boom restores diversity — natural, dry, quality ciders.
wiki.art.beer.sidra.origin: Atlantic Europe: Asturias and Basque Country (Spain), Normandy and Brittany (France), England (Somerset, Herefordshire), Ireland. Cider apples are specific varieties — bitter, acidic, and tannic, different from table apples. Asturias has more than 200 native varieties. Normandy distills Calvados from its cider. In England the tradition traces back to the Norman conquest (1066).
wiki.art.beer.sidra.production: Cider apples are washed, crushed, and pressed to obtain the must. Natural fermentation (wild yeasts) or controlled (added yeasts) for weeks or months. Asturian/natural cider: spontaneous fermentation with no additions, no added carbonation. Commercial cider: added carbonation, filtered, pasteurized. Pear cider (perry): same process with specific pears. ABV usually 4-8%. The best ciders are dry, complex, and have no added sugar.
wiki.art.beer.sidra.tasting: Asturian natural cider: acidic apple, yeast, earthy, tannic, dry, subtle natural fizz. Normandy cidre: sweet-tart apple, floral, lightly sparkling, elegant. English dry: crisp apple, tannins, dry and refreshing. Commercial sweet cider: candied apple, pronounced sweetness, carbonated. Perry: fresh pear, floral, light. Ice cider: concentrated apple, honey, raisins — a liquid dessert. The diversity between ciders is as wide as between wines.
wiki.art.beer.sidra.tips: Asturian cider is "escanciada": pour from a height with an extended arm into a wide glass to oxygenate and release aromas — drink immediately in one gulp (culín). Always serve dry cider well chilled (5-7°C). For cocktails, use dry cider (never sweet) — Strongbow Dry or Aspall are solid options. The Snakebite is built by pouring the cider first, then slowly layering the lager on top. An opened natural cider should be consumed the same day. El Gaitero and Trabanco are Asturian benchmarks.
wiki.art.beer.sidra.types: Asturian natural cider (dry, acidic, hazy, still — escanciada). Basque cider (sagardoa — similar to Asturian). Normandy/Breton cidre (slightly sweet, sparkling, low ABV — Pays d'Auge is the premium). English cider (dry or sweet, carbonated — Strongbow, Aspall). Irish cider (Bulmers/Magners — sweeter). Swedish cider (Kopparberg — fruity, sweet). Perry/Perada (pear — Babycham, Oliver's). Ice cider (Canada — frozen apples, sweet and concentrated like an eiswein).
wiki.art.beer.sidra.cocktails: Snakebite (lager + cider 1:1 — British, controversial; some pubs ban it). Kir Normand (crème de cassis + cider — the Norman version of the Kir). Calvados & Cider (Calvados in hot cider — warming in winter). Cider Spritz (dry cider + Aperol + soda — autumn aperitif). Stone Fence (bourbon + cider — a colonial American cocktail). Apple Mojito (rum, mint, lime, cider instead of soda). Wassail (hot cider + spices + roasted apple — English Christmas punch).
wiki.art.wines.sherry.sub: The most versatile fortified wine in the world
wiki.art.wines.sherry.description: Sherry (jerez in Spanish) is a fortified wine with protected designation of origin, produced exclusively in the "sherry triangle" (Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María, and Sanlúcar de Barrameda) in Andalusia. From dry, mineral fino to honey-sweet PX, sherry offers the broadest range of any wine. In modern bartending, fino and manzanilla are the new stars — Sherry Cobbler, Adonis, Bamboo, and Rebujito.
wiki.art.wines.sherry.history: 8th century: the Moors plant vines in Sherish (Jerez). 1587: Sir Francis Drake sacks Cádiz and takes 2,900 barrels — England discovers sherry. 17th-19th centuries: sherry becomes the favorite wine of the English aristocracy (Shakespeare mentions it repeatedly). 1860s: phylloxera destroys the vineyards; they are replanted with Palomino. 20th century: decline due to overproduction and poor quality. 2010s: the sherry renaissance — bartenders and sommeliers rediscover fino and manzanilla as gastronomic and cocktail wines.
wiki.art.wines.sherry.origin: Marco de Jerez, Cádiz, Andalusia, Spain. The triangle between Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María, and Sanlúcar de Barrameda, with albariza (white chalk) soils that retain moisture. The Palomino Fino grape is dominant (95%); Pedro Ximénez and Moscatel are used for sweet wines. The warm climate with the easterly levante wind and the Atlantic westerly (poniente) breeze creates unique conditions for the solera system and biological ageing under flor.
wiki.art.wines.sherry.production: Palomino grapes are pressed and fermented to a dry base wine (11-12% ABV). It is fortified with wine spirit: to 15-15.5% for biological ageing (fino, manzanilla — the flor yeast protects the wine) or to 17%+ for oxidative ageing (oloroso, palo cortado — no flor). Solera and criaderas system: barrels are stacked by age; wine is drawn from the oldest and topped up from the next — ensuring consistency year after year. PX: Pedro Ximénez grapes sun-dried (pasificadas) before pressing.
wiki.art.wines.sherry.tasting: Fino: fresh almond, bread yeast, mineral, saline, dry, clean finish. Manzanilla: lighter than fino, sea breeze, chamomile (the flor), subtle iodine. Amontillado: toasted hazelnut, caramel, spice, complex balance between biological and oxidative. Oloroso: walnut, dried fruit, tobacco, leather, cocoa — powerful and long. PX: raisins, figs, honey, chocolate, molasses — thick as syrup. Palo Cortado: the most complex — elegant nose, powerful palate.
wiki.art.wines.sherry.tips: Fino and manzanilla must be served VERY cold (5-7°C) and consumed within 1-2 days after opening — they are the most fragile wines in the world. Always keep them refrigerated. Amontillado and oloroso last weeks once opened. PX over vanilla ice cream is an instant, spectacular dessert. The Rebujito is perfect for summer events and fiestas. Tio Pepe (fino) and La Guita (manzanilla) are the accessible references. Lustau and Equipo Navazos for exceptional quality.
wiki.art.wines.sherry.types: Fino (15% ABV, under flor, dry, pale, almondy — Tio Pepe, La Ina). Manzanilla (fino from Sanlúcar, saltier and fresher thanks to the sea breeze — La Guita, Papirusa). Amontillado (starts as fino, loses its flor, turns oxidative — dry, hazelnut, amber). Oloroso (oxidative ageing from the start — dark, walnut, dried fruit, dry). Palo Cortado (rare — combines amontillado's nose with oloroso's body). Cream (oloroso + PX, sweet). Pedro Ximénez/PX (ultra-sweet, raisins, honey, chocolate — poured over ice cream).
wiki.art.wines.sherry.cocktails: Sherry Cobbler (amontillado, orange, sugar, berries — the cocktail that popularized the drinking straw in 1840). Adonis (fino, sweet vermouth, orange bitters — low-ABV, elegant). Bamboo (fino, dry vermouth, orange bitters — the low-ABV Martini). Rebujito (fino, 7Up/Sprite, mint, ice — the Andalusian Feria spritz). Sherry Flip (oloroso, egg, sugar, nutmeg). East India (oloroso, sweet vermouth, bitters, maraschino).
wiki.art.wines.port.description: Port wine is a sweet fortified wine produced exclusively in the Douro region of Portugal and aged in the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia, across the river from the city of Porto. Fermentation is stopped by adding grape spirit, preserving the grape's natural sugar. From young, fruity Ruby to 40+ year-old Vintage Port, it is one of the world's great wines.
wiki.art.wines.port.history: 1386: the Treaty of Windsor binds Portugal and England commercially. 1678: English merchants discover Douro wine — they add brandy so it survives the sea journey. 1756: the Marquis of Pombal creates the world's first appellation of origin for the Douro. 1800s: the great English houses (Graham's, Taylor's, Dow's, Cockburn's) dominate the trade. 1994: the Douro is declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Today: port's rebirth as a cocktail and pairing ingredient.
wiki.art.wines.port.origin: Douro Valley, northern Portugal — one of the oldest and most spectacular vineyards in the world (UNESCO Heritage). Grapes grow on terraces carved into the schist slopes of the Douro. More than 80 native varieties are permitted, with Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz, Tinto Cão, and Tinta Barroca being the main ones. The ageing cellars are in Vila Nova de Gaia, across the Douro from Porto.
wiki.art.wines.port.production: Hand harvest in September on the Douro terraces. Fermentation is stopped ("mutage") by adding grape spirit (77% ABV) when the must has fermented to 6-9% — the residual sugar is preserved. The resulting wine is 19-22% ABV and naturally sweet. Ruby ports age in large vats (little oxidation, preserving fruit). Tawny ports age in 550L barrels (slow oxidation, developing dried fruit and caramel notes).
wiki.art.wines.port.tasting: Ruby: intense dark fruit (cherry, blackberry, plum), chocolate, spice, juicy tannins. LBV: like ruby but more concentrated and structured. Vintage: extraordinarily complex — dark fruit, violets, chocolate, minerals, silky tannins, decades of evolution. Tawny 10-year: walnut, caramel, candied orange, toffee, dried fruit. Tawny 20+: sublime complexity — honey, hazelnut, noble rancio, Eastern spices. White: citrus, almond, honey.
wiki.art.wines.port.tips: Port & Tonic with white port is the Portuguese aperitif of the moment — serve in a large wine glass with plenty of ice, mint, and orange slice. 10-year tawny is the best introduction to port — perfect balance between fruit and cask. Ruby is too young to sip neat; better in cocktails or with chocolate. A Vintage Port is decanted 2-4 hours before serving. Open tawny keeps for weeks refrigerated. Taylor's, Graham's, Niepoort, and Quinta do Noval are benchmarks.
wiki.art.wines.port.types: Ruby (young, fruity, intense — "Reserva" is the superior selection). Late Bottled Vintage/LBV (4-6 years in vat, more structure). Vintage/Vintage Port (from a single exceptional year, ages 20-40+ years in bottle — the great cellar wine). Tawny (aged in cask — 10, 20, 30, 40-year indications, with walnut and caramel notes). Colheita (single-vintage tawny). White Port (white grapes, dry or sweet — for Port & Tonic). Rosé Port (recent, for spritzers).
wiki.art.wines.port.cocktails: Porto Flip (tawny port, cognac, whole egg, nutmeg — a 19th-century classic, liquid dessert). Port & Tonic (white port, tonic, mint, orange — the trendy aperitif in Portugal). Porto Cobbler (ruby port, orange, sugar, berries). Chicago Fizz (port, rum, lemon, egg white, soda). Bishop (port, orange, spices, hot — winter punch). Port Negus (hot port, sugar, lemon, nutmeg — the classic British hot drink).
wiki.art.wines.madeira.sub: The indestructible wine from the Atlantic island
wiki.art.wines.madeira.description: Madeira is a fortified wine produced on the Portuguese island of Madeira, in the Atlantic. It is the most resilient wine in the world — 100+ year-old bottles are still drinkable thanks to its unique heating process (estufagem). From dry Sercial to sweet Malmsey, it was the favorite wine of the American Founding Fathers.
wiki.art.wines.madeira.history: 1419: the Portuguese plant vines on Madeira. 16th-18th centuries: the heat in ship holds improves the wine — they discover estufagem. 1776: the Founding Fathers toasted with Madeira when signing the Declaration of Independence. 1800s: phylloxera and oidium devastate the vineyards. 21st century: revival as a cult wine.
wiki.art.wines.madeira.origin: Madeira Island, Portugal (Atlantic archipelago, 600 km west of Morocco). Discovered in 1419. Terraced vineyards (poios). The four noble varieties: Sercial (dry), Verdelho (off-dry), Bual (semi-sweet), Malmsey/Malvasia (sweet). Tinta Negra is the most planted grape (85%).
wiki.art.wines.madeira.production: Fermentation is partially stopped with grape spirit. Estufagem: the wine is heated to 45-50°C for 3+ months. Canteiro: the premium method, ageing under the roof with natural heating. The heat caramelizes sugars and oxidizes the wine in a controlled way — making it practically indestructible. An opened bottle lasts years.
wiki.art.wines.madeira.tasting: Sercial: citrus, green walnut, almond, vibrant acidity, dry. Verdelho: orange, caramel, smoke. Bual: toffee, chocolate, dried fruit. Malmsey: figs, raisins, molasses, dark chocolate, dense. All share high acidity, toasted notes from estufagem, and extraordinary longevity.
wiki.art.wines.madeira.tips: An open bottle lasts months or years without degrading — perfect for bars with low turnover. Chilled Sercial as an aperitif; Malmsey at room temperature as a digestif. Frasqueiras from the early 1900s are among the oldest drinkable wines in the world. Blandy's and Henriques & Henriques are the references. Madeira Punch is a historical talking point — Washington and Jefferson drank it.
wiki.art.wines.madeira.types: Sercial (dry, acidic, almondy — aperitif). Verdelho (off-dry, citrus, honey). Bual (semi-sweet, caramel, chocolate). Malmsey (sweet, molasses, figs — dessert). Rainwater (light, off-dry). Colheita (single vintage, 5+ years). Frasqueira/Vintage (single vintage, 20+ years — bottles of 50-100+ years are possible).
wiki.art.wines.madeira.cocktails: Madeira Punch (Madeira, lemon, sugar, spices, hot water — George Washington's punch). Baltimore Eggnog (Madeira, cognac, rum, eggs, milk). Prince of Wales (Madeira, champagne, curaçao, Angostura). Madeira is more gastronomic than cocktail-focused, but its place in historical punches is essential.
wiki.art.wines.lillet.description: Lillet is a French aperitif made from Bordeaux wine flavored with fruit liqueurs and citrus peels. Created in 1872, it is lighter and fruitier than vermouth, with an elegant profile that made it James Bond's secret ingredient (Vesper Martini). Its delicacy makes it perfect both on the rocks and in sophisticated cocktails.
wiki.art.wines.lillet.history: 1872: the Lillet brothers create the aperitif in Podensac. 1895: it is exported to the French colonies as a tonic against malaria (thanks to the quinine). 1953: Ian Fleming specifies "Kina Lillet" in the Vesper Martini recipe in Casino Royale. 1986: reformulated — less quinine, fruitier — and renamed simply "Lillet". 2011: Lillet Rosé is launched and becomes an instant hit. Today it is an essential ingredient in modern bartending, especially in the White Negroni.
wiki.art.wines.lillet.origin: Podensac, Bordeaux, France. Brothers Paul and Raymond Lillet created the recipe in 1872, blending Bordeaux wines with liqueurs made from sweet and bitter oranges from Spain and Morocco and Peruvian quinine. The original formula (Kina Lillet) contained more quinine; today's version (reformulated in 1986) is softer and fruitier.
wiki.art.wines.lillet.production: Base of Sémillon and Sauvignon white wines from Bordeaux (85%). Sweet oranges from Spain, bitter oranges from Haiti, and Peruvian quinine are separately macerated in grape spirit. The wine is then blended with the macerated fruit liqueurs. Ageing in oak tanks for months. Bottled at 17% ABV. Each expression (Blanc, Rosé, Rouge) uses a different wine base.
wiki.art.wines.lillet.tasting: Blanc: nose of orange-blossom honey, sweet citrus, white peach. On the palate: smooth, fruity entry, light bitterness from orange peel, clean refreshing finish. Rosé: fresh strawberry, pink grapefruit, spring flowers, lively finish. Rouge: ripe red fruit (cherry, currant), soft spice, silky tannins, a longer more complex finish. All three share a characteristic Bordeaux elegance.
wiki.art.wines.lillet.tips: Always serve very cold (6-8°C) — straight from the fridge. Lillet Blanc on the rocks with an orange or cucumber slice is the simplest, most elegant aperitif. Refrigerate after opening; consume within 3-4 weeks. It is not interchangeable with dry vermouth — Lillet is sweeter and fruitier. In the Vesper, the original recipe calls for "Kina Lillet" which no longer exists; Lillet Blanc + a dash of quinine bitters comes closer. Some bartenders use Lillet Rouge in Negronis for a Bordeaux twist.
wiki.art.wines.lillet.types: Lillet Blanc (the original — white wine, citrus, honey, floral, the most versatile in bartending). Lillet Rosé (2011 — strawberry, raspberry, pink grapefruit, perfect for summer). Lillet Rouge (red wine, red fruit, spice, more complex and less known). All three serve at 6-8°C. Lillet Blanc is the most used in cocktails (Vesper, White Negroni, Corpse Reviver).
wiki.art.wines.lillet.cocktails: Vesper Martini (gin, vodka, Lillet Blanc — "shaken, not stirred," James Bond). Corpse Reviver No. 2 (gin, Lillet Blanc, Cointreau, lemon, absinthe — a revived classic). White Negroni (gin, Suze, Lillet Blanc — the modern reinvention). Lillet Spritz (Lillet, tonic or soda, orange slice — the perfect French aperitif). Lillet Vive (Lillet Blanc, tonic, cucumber, strawberry, mint — the brand's official serve).
wiki.art.wines.dubonnet.description: Dubonnet is a French wine-based aperitif flavored with quinine, herbs, and spices. Created as a malaria tonic for French colonial troops, it became the favorite aperitif of Queen Elizabeth II of England (always paired with gin). It is sweeter and spicier than vermouth, with a subtle quinine bitterness that makes it unique among aperitif wines.
wiki.art.wines.dubonnet.history: 1846: Joseph Dubonnet creates the quinine-laced aperitif for the colonial troops in Algeria. 1860s: it becomes popular in Parisian cafés as an elegant aperitif. 1900s: it is exported to London and becomes a favorite of British high society. 1940s-2022: Queen Elizabeth II drinks her daily "Dubonnet & Gin" before lunch — a royal ritual spanning decades. 2000s: the cocktail revival movement rediscovers Dubonnet as an ingredient in classic cocktails.
wiki.art.wines.dubonnet.origin: Paris, France. Parisian chemist Joseph Dubonnet created the formula in 1846, commissioned by the French government, which was looking for a way to make quinine palatable for soldiers in North Africa. Quinine prevented malaria but was extremely bitter — Dubonnet masked it with sweet wine, herbs, and spices.
wiki.art.wines.dubonnet.production: Base of red wine (Dubonnet Rouge) or white wine (Dubonnet Blanc) from the Languedoc-Roussillon region. Quinine (cinchona bark), green coffee, cacao, cinnamon, chamomile, and other herbs are added. Extended maceration in fortified wine. Lightly sweetened and bottled at 14.8% ABV. The American version (made under license) has a slightly different profile from the original French.
wiki.art.wines.dubonnet.tasting: Rouge: aroma of ripe red fruit, chocolate, coffee, warm spices (cinnamon, clove). On the palate: balanced sweet-bitter, candied cherry, subtle quinine, Mediterranean herbs, spicy lingering finish. Blanc: lighter, white flowers, citrus, honey, delicate bitterness. The profile is richer and sweeter than red vermouth, with extra complexity from the quinine and cacao.
wiki.art.wines.dubonnet.tips: Serve cold (6-8°C), on the rocks with a slice of lemon. The classic Dubonnet & Gin ratio is 1:1, but Queen Elizabeth took it 2:1 (more Dubonnet). Refrigerate after opening; lasts 2-3 weeks. Dubonnet can replace sweet vermouth in any cocktail for a spicier, quinine-forward profile. The French version is superior to the American — look for the import. Cocchi Americano is the closest alternative if Dubonnet is unavailable.
wiki.art.wines.dubonnet.types: Dubonnet Rouge (the original — red wine, quinine, spices, sweet-bitter, deep ruby color). Dubonnet Blanc (white version — lighter, floral, less known). Dubonnet Gold (limited edition, aged). Belongs to the "quinquinas" family of quinine-laced wines, along with Lillet (Kina Lillet), Bonal, Cocchi Americano, and Byrrh. Dubonnet Rouge is the standard for the classic recipe.
wiki.art.wines.dubonnet.cocktails: Dubonnet & Gin (Dubonnet Rouge, gin 1:1, lemon slice — Queen Elizabeth II's cocktail). Dubonnet Manhattan (Dubonnet replaces sweet vermouth — more complex). Zaza Cocktail (Dubonnet, gin, orange bitters — pre-Prohibition classic). Opera Cocktail (gin, Dubonnet, maraschino — elegant and forgotten). BLT Cocktail (bourbon, Lillet, tonic, Dubonnet float). Napoleon Cocktail (gin, Dubonnet, Fernet — potent).
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-italiano.descripti: Italian amaro is a broad category of bitter herbal liqueurs, traditionally consumed as a digestif after meals. Every Italian region has its own distinctive amaros, from sweet Sicilian Averna to elegant Friulian Nonino. They are the soul of Italy's after-dinner ritual.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-italiano.history: 13th century: Italian monks craft medicinal herbal elixirs. 1815: Gaspare Campari creates his bitter (see separate article). 1868: Salvatore Averna receives the recipe from Benedictine monks in Sicily. 1885: Stanislao Cobianchi creates Amaro Montenegro in Bologna. 1897: Ausano Ramazzotti launches his amaro in Milan. 1973: the Nonino family creates the first amaro based on single-varietal grappa. 2010s: amaros take over craft bartending worldwide.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-italiano.origin: All of Italy. Amaros were born as herbal medicines in medieval monasteries and pharmacies. Every region developed its own style: Sicily (Averna), Bologna (Montenegro), Friuli (Nonino), Milan (Ramazzotti), Calabria (Vecchio Amaro del Capo), Lombardy (Braulio), Basilicata (Lucano).
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-italiano.productio: Base of neutral alcohol or wine in which herbs, roots, barks, flowers, and spices (gentian, rhubarb, quinine, angelica, thistle, mint, citrus) are macerated. Filtered, sweetened with syrup or caramel, and briefly aged. Each amaro has its secret recipe. Typical ABV: 16-40%.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-italiano.tasting: Averna: candied orange, caramel, sweet herbs, smooth finish. Montenegro: perfect sweet-bitter balance, orange, vanilla, rose, spice. Nonino: elegant grappa, alpine herbs, honey, long refined finish. Ramazzotti: bitter orange, gentian, licorice. Braulio: mint, gentian, alpine pine, intense bitterness. Each one is its own universe.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-italiano.tips: Montenegro is the most versatile amaro in cocktails: it works as a sweet-vermouth substitute in almost anything. Nonino is the premium sipper. Averna is perfect for amaro newcomers (sweeter). Serve at room temperature or with a large ice cube. Exploring regional amaros is exploring the geography of Italy.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-italiano.types: Averna (Sicily, sweet, orange, herbs, 29% ABV). Montenegro (Bologna, balanced, 40 botanicals, 23% ABV — "the perfect amaro"). Nonino Quintessentia (Friuli, grappa base, elegant, 35% ABV). Ramazzotti (Milan, bitter orange, 30% ABV). Braulio (Alpine Valtellina, mountain herbs, 21% ABV). Lucano (Basilicata, minty). Vecchio Amaro del Capo (Calabria, fresh herbal).
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-italiano.cocktails: Paper Plane (bourbon, Amaro Nonino, Aperol, lemon — equal parts, the cocktail that put Nonino on the map). Black Manhattan (rye, Averna, Angostura — Amaro replacing sweet vermouth). Montenegro Sour (Montenegro, lemon, syrup, egg white). Bicicletta (Campari or amaro, white wine, soda — rural Italian aperitif). Amaro on the rocks with an orange peel — the classic Italian after-dinner sip.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-nonino.sub: The Friulian amaro of the Paper Plane
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-nonino.description: Amaro Nonino Quintessentia is a premium Italian amaro (35% ABV) from Friuli-Venezia Giulia, made on an aged grappa base and infused with alpine herbs, roots, and barks. It is the amaro that conquered modern bartending thanks to the Paper Plane — Sam Ross's cocktail that became an instant modern classic. Its profile is more elegant and fruity than other Italian amari, with exceptional balance.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-nonino.history: 1897: Orazio Nonino founds the distillery in Percoto. 1973: Giannola Nonino creates the first single-varietal grappa (Picolit) — a revolution in the grappa world. 1990s: she creates Amaro Nonino Quintessentia on an aged grappa base. 2007: Sam Ross creates the Paper Plane (bourbon, Nonino, Aperol, lemon) at Milk & Honey in NYC — the cocktail that made Nonino globally famous. 2010s-present: it becomes the most in-demand amaro for bartenders worldwide.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-nonino.origin: Percoto, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, northeastern Italy. The Nonino family is one of the most respected dynasties in Italian distillation — famous for their single-varietal grappas that revolutionized the industry. Giannola Nonino created Amaro Quintessentia in the 1990s, using native-variety grappa as a base instead of the usual neutral alcohol, giving the amaro unique depth and elegance.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-nonino.production: Base of aged grape grappa (not neutral alcohol like most amari). Infused with alpine herbs from Friuli, roots (gentian, rhubarb), citrus peels, and spices. Rested in oak barrels to soften and integrate. Bottled at 35% ABV. The grappa base is what sets Nonino apart from every other amaro — it adds a vinous fruit depth that neutral alcohol cannot deliver.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-nonino.tasting: Aroma: candied orange, caramel, alpine herbs, honey, a touch of grappa. Palate: sweet-fruity entry (orange, caramel), evolves into elegant bitter herbs (gentian, rhubarb), warm spices, a vinous grappa base. Finish: long, balanced bitter-sweet, with lasting orange and herbs. It is notably more elegant and less aggressively bitter than Fernet or Campari — the sophisticated bartender's amaro.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-nonino.tips: The Paper Plane is a must on any serious bar menu — equal parts of everything, shaken, strained, served up. Nonino is the amaro that converts skeptics — its fruity elegance is approachable without losing complexity. Do not substitute another amaro in the Paper Plane — Montenegro is similar but not the same. Store at room temperature. More expensive than other amari, but justified by the grappa base. It is professional bartenders' favorite amaro for a reason.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-nonino.types: Amaro Nonino Quintessentia (35% ABV — the flagship product and the only one that matters in cocktails). The Nonino family also makes: Grappa Nonino (single-varietal from Moscato, Prosecco, Picolit — among the best in Italy). ÙE (honey-and-herb liqueur). Gioiello (light amaro). But Quintessentia is the star and the one every bartender needs.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-nonino.cocktails: Paper Plane (bourbon, Amaro Nonino, Aperol, lemon — equal parts, the quintessential modern classic, created by Sam Ross). Naked & Famous (mezcal, Nonino, yellow Chartreuse, lime — the mezcal version of the Paper Plane). Black Manhattan (rye, Nonino replaces sweet vermouth, bitters — more bitter and complex). Nonino Spritz (Nonino, prosecco, soda — Friulian aperitif). Nonino Old Fashioned (Nonino as the base, sugar, bitters).
wiki.art.amaros.angostura-bitters.descri: Angostura Aromatic Bitters are the most important and iconic bitters in the cocktail world. Their oversized label (a famous design error that stuck) and secret herb-and-spice content make them unmistakable. They are essential in the Old Fashioned, Manhattan, Whiskey Sour, and dozens of classic cocktails.
wiki.art.amaros.angostura-bitters.histor: 1824: Dr. Siegert creates the bitters in Angostura, Venezuela, as a tonic for Bolívar's troops. 1830: commercial sales begin. 1875: the Siegert family emigrates to Trinidad after Venezuelan political turmoil. 1900: the oversized label (a design-contest mistake) is kept as brand identity. 20th century: they become the global standard for aromatic bitters.
wiki.art.amaros.angostura-bitters.origin: Ciudad Bolívar (formerly Angostura), Venezuela. Dr. Johann Gottlieb Benjamin Siegert, a German military surgeon in Simón Bolívar's army, created the formula in 1824 as a medicinal tonic. Production moved to Trinidad and Tobago in 1875 and continues there to this day.
wiki.art.amaros.angostura-bitters.produc: The exact recipe is secret, known only to 5 people. It is known to include gentian, cinnamon, clove, cardamom, bitter orange peel, and other herbs and spices, macerated in high-proof alcohol (44.7% ABV). Despite the high ABV, it is used in dashes, not sipped neat.
wiki.art.amaros.angostura-bitters.tastin: Aromatic: intense warm spice (cinnamon, clove, cardamom), bitter gentian, herbs, orange peel, long spicy finish. Orange: concentrated bitter orange, cardamom, soft spices. Cocoa: bitter cacao, vanilla, warm spices. All three are ultra-concentrated — a dash transforms a cocktail.
wiki.art.amaros.angostura-bitters.tips: 2-3 dashes are enough in most cocktails — bitters are concentrated. A dash ≈ 1ml. No Angostura, no Old Fashioned and no Manhattan. Orange Bitters are perfect in dry Martinis. Store at room temperature; they keep indefinitely. The Trinidad Sour (1oz Angostura as the base) is the ultimate test for bitter lovers.
wiki.art.amaros.angostura-bitters.types: Angostura Aromatic Bitters (the original, oversized white label, 44.7% ABV), Angostura Orange Bitters (orange, launched in 2007, 28% ABV), Angostura Cocoa Bitters (cacao, launched in 2019). All three are essentials in a professional bar. There are hundreds of bitters brands, but Angostura is king.
wiki.art.amaros.angostura-bitters.cockta: Old Fashioned (whiskey, sugar, 2-3 dashes Angostura — the oldest cocktail). Manhattan (rye, sweet vermouth, 2 dashes Angostura). Whiskey Sour (with Angostura on the foam as a decoration). Pink Gin (gin, Angostura — a Royal Navy classic). Champagne Cocktail (champagne, sugar, Angostura). Trinidad Sour (30ml of Angostura bitters as the base — the most extreme cocktail).
wiki.art.amaros.aperol.description: Aperol is a bright-orange Italian bitter liqueur, softer and sweeter than Campari (11% ABV). Created in 1919 in Padua, it became a global phenomenon thanks to the Aperol Spritz, the most popular cocktail of the 2010s.
