wiki.art.amaros.aperol.history: 1919: the Barbieri brothers launch Aperol at the Padua Fair. 1950s: Aperol becomes a popular aperitif in northeastern Italy. 2003: Campari Group acquires the brand. 2000s-2010s: the Aperol Spritz conquers Europe and then the world, becoming synonymous with the summer aperitif. 2019: Aperol's centenary; global sales have multiplied by 10 in a decade.
wiki.art.amaros.aperol.origin: Padua, Veneto, Italy. Created by brothers Luigi and Silvio Barbieri in 1919 and presented at the Padua Fair. The orange color comes from an infusion of bitter oranges, gentian, rhubarb, and herbs. Today owned by Campari Group.
wiki.art.amaros.aperol.production: Infusion of bitter and sweet oranges, gentian, rhubarb, quinine, and a secret herb blend in alcohol. The exact recipe is secret. Lower in ABV (11%) and less bitter than Campari, which makes it more approachable for the mainstream drinker.
wiki.art.amaros.aperol.tasting: Bitter orange, grapefruit, soft herbs, gentian, rhubarb, moderate sweetness, a light and approachable bitterness. Vibrant orange color. Short, refreshing finish. Far less bitter than Campari — the "gateway" to the world of bitter liqueurs.
wiki.art.amaros.aperol.tips: Perfect Spritz: large wine glass with lots of ice, 90ml prosecco, 60ml Aperol, splash of soda, orange slice. Order matters: ice, prosecco, Aperol, soda. Do not shake. Select is the authentic Venetian alternative for a more bitter, complex Spritz. Aperol fades in the light: store in a dark place.
wiki.art.amaros.aperol.types: Aperol (the single product, 11% ABV). No official variants. Aperol Spritz pre-mixed (ready to drink, in bottle and can). Segment competitors: Select (another Venetian aperitif, more complex), Cappelletti (Trentino aperitif).
wiki.art.amaros.aperol.cocktails: Aperol Spritz (Aperol, prosecco, soda — 3:2:1, in a wine glass with ice and an orange slice — THE cocktail of summer). Naked & Famous (mezcal, yellow Chartreuse, Aperol, lime). Paper Plane (bourbon, Aperol, Amaro Nonino, lemon — equal parts). Division Bell (mezcal, Aperol, maraschino, lime).
wiki.art.amaros.becherovka.sub: The Czech herbal liqueur from Karlovy Vary
wiki.art.amaros.becherovka.description: Becherovka is a Czech herbal liqueur (38% ABV) produced exclusively in Karlovy Vary (Carlsbad) since 1807. With a profile dominated by cinnamon, clove, and more than 20 herbs, it is the Czech national digestif and the most famous Central European amaro. The Beton (Becherovka + tonic) is the quintessential Czech highball — refreshing, herbal, and surprisingly versatile.
wiki.art.amaros.becherovka.history: 1807: Josef Becher creates "English Bitter" in his Karlovy Vary pharmacy. 1841: His son Johann Becher industrializes production. 1890s: it becomes the standard digestif of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. 1945: nationalized by the communist government. 1997: privatized; acquired by Pernod Ricard in 2001. Today: sold in 35+ countries. The Beton (Becherovka + tonic) became popular in the 2000s as an alternative to the G&T.
wiki.art.amaros.becherovka.origin: Karlovy Vary (Carlsbad), Bohemia, Czech Republic. Josef Vitus Becher, a pharmacist, created the recipe in 1807 with the help of English doctor Christian Frobrig, who visited the thermal spas of Karlovy Vary. The formula uses the local thermal waters as an ingredient. The original distillery is still in Karlovy Vary and can be visited.
wiki.art.amaros.becherovka.production: More than 20 herbs and spices (the full recipe is known by only 2 people): dominant Ceylon cinnamon, clove, anise, cardamom, allspice, ginger, and aromatic herbs. They are macerated in alcohol and thermal water from Karlovy Vary. Blended with sugar. Rested in Slovak oak barrels for 2 months. Bottled at 38% ABV. The local thermal water is considered an essential part of the recipe.
wiki.art.amaros.becherovka.tasting: Aroma: intense cinnamon, clove, Christmas spices, herbs, a balsamic medicinal touch. Palate: dominant cinnamon and clove, balanced sweetness, underlying bitter herbs, warm spices. Finish: long, warm, lingering cinnamon over an herbal base. It is like liquid Christmas — spiced, warm, and comforting. Sweeter than Jägermeister, spicier than Fernet.
wiki.art.amaros.becherovka.tips: The Beton (Becherovka + tonic 1:3) is mandatory for any bartender — refreshing and unique. Serve the Original cold (from the freezer) as a digestif after dinner. Becherovka with hot apple cider is the perfect winter grog. The tour of the Becherovka museum in Karlovy Vary includes a tasting. Keep in the freezer for shots. It naturally pairs with apple, cinnamon, honey, and citrus. It is the most popular souvenir in the Czech Republic.
wiki.art.amaros.becherovka.types: Becherovka Original (38% ABV — the classic, dominant cinnamon). Becherovka Lemond (20% ABV — with lemon, lighter, for summer). Becherovka KV 14 (14% ABV — a soft version, aperitif). Becherovka Ice & Fire (30% ABV — with menthol, for cold shots). The Original is the only one that matters for serious bartending. The variants are more for casual drinking.
wiki.art.amaros.becherovka.cocktails: Beton (Becherovka + tonic + lemon slice — "concrete" in Czech, the national highball). Becherovka Mule (Becherovka, ginger beer, lime — a spiced Moscow Mule). Becherovka Old Fashioned (Becherovka, bourbon, bitters — warm and spiced). Hot Becherovka (Becherovka, hot water, honey, lemon — perfect in winter). Czech Christmas (Becherovka, apple, cinnamon, champagne). Becherovka Sour (Becherovka, lemon, syrup, egg white).
wiki.art.amaros.campari.sub: The iconic red bitter from Milan
wiki.art.amaros.campari.description: Campari is an intensely red Italian bitter liqueur, the world's most famous aperitif and a cornerstone of classic bartending. Its bitter-sweet flavor and unmistakable color make it essential in the Negroni, Americano, and Spritz. The secret recipe includes an infusion of herbs, spices, and fruits.
wiki.art.amaros.campari.history: 1860: Gaspare Campari creates the "Bitter all'Uso d'Olanda" in Novara. 1867: he opens Caffè Campari in Milan's Galleria. 1904: Davide Campari (his son) founds the company and begins exporting. 1932: the Americano (Campari, vermouth, soda) becomes the cocktail of the moment. 1947: Count Negroni adds gin to the Americano in Florence, and the Negroni is born. 2000s: the Aperol Spritz and the Negroni revival send global sales soaring.
wiki.art.amaros.campari.origin: Milan, Italy. Gaspare Campari created the recipe in Novara in 1860 and perfected it at his Caffè Campari in the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II in Milan, which became the epicenter of Milanese aperitif culture.
wiki.art.amaros.campari.production: The recipe contains more than 60 ingredients — herbs, spices, barks, and fruits — macerated and infused in alcohol. The exact list is secret and known only to the master blender. The original red color came from cochineal carmine; today an artificial colorant is used. 25% ABV.
wiki.art.amaros.campari.tasting: Intense, defined bitterness, bitter orange, chinotto peel, medicinal herbs, licorice, tart cherry. Sweetness that balances the bitterness without dominating it. Bright red color. Long, bitter, dry finish with an aftertaste of bitter citrus and herbs.
wiki.art.amaros.campari.tips: The classic Negroni is 1:1:1 (30ml of each) with a large ice cube and an orange peel. The Garibaldi needs "fluffy" orange juice (whipped with air) for the perfect texture. Campari is an acquired taste: the first sip can surprise you, but the palate adapts and it becomes addictive. Store at room temperature.
wiki.art.amaros.campari.types: Campari (the flagship product, 25% ABV), Campari Soda (pre-mixed in its iconic conical 10cl bottle, designed by Fortunato Depero in 1932), Campari Cask Tales (barrel-aged, limited edition). There are no variants — Campari is Campari. The flavor varies slightly across markets.
wiki.art.amaros.campari.cocktails: Negroni (gin, Campari, sweet vermouth — equal parts, the king of bitterness). Americano (Campari, sweet vermouth, soda — the forerunner of the Negroni). Boulevardier (bourbon, Campari, sweet vermouth — Negroni with whiskey). Campari Spritz (Campari, prosecco, soda). Jungle Bird (dark rum, Campari, pineapple, lime — bitter tiki). Garibaldi (Campari, fresh orange juice — "fluffy orange juice").
wiki.art.amaros.cynar.description: Cynar is an Italian amaro made with artichoke (carciofo) and 12 more herbs and plants. Despite its main ingredient, it does not taste of artichoke: it is herbal, bitter-sweet, and earthy. A bartender favorite for its versatility and complexity.
wiki.art.amaros.cynar.history: 1952: Angelo Dalle Molle creates Cynar in Padua. 1960s-70s: advertising campaigns starring actor Ernesto Calindri drinking Cynar in the middle of traffic make the brand iconic in Italy. 1995: Campari Group acquires the brand. 2010s: bartenders rediscover Cynar as a cocktail ingredient — the Trident and other drinks bring it back into fashion.
wiki.art.amaros.cynar.origin: Padua, Italy. Created by Venetian entrepreneur Angelo Dalle Molle in 1952. The name comes from "Cynara scolymus", the botanical name for artichoke. The artichoke logo on the bottle is unmistakable. Today owned by Campari Group.
wiki.art.amaros.cynar.production: Artichoke (Cynara scolymus) and 12 herbs and plants are macerated in alcohol. The blend is filtered and sweetened. The artichoke gives a unique vegetal-earthy character but not a literal artichoke flavor. 16.5% ABV (standard) or 35% ABV (Cynar 70 Proof).
wiki.art.amaros.cynar.tasting: Herbal, earthy, dark caramel, gentian, subtle vegetal notes (not artichoke-tasting), a moderate and elegant bitterness, hints of dark chocolate. The 70 Proof: everything amplified, drier, more bitter, more complex. Medium-long finish with a herbal aftertaste.
wiki.art.amaros.cynar.tips: Cynar 70 Proof is the version to use in cocktails: more body and bitterness, stands up better to dilution. On the rocks with an orange slice it makes an excellent aperitif. Swap it for Campari in Negronis for a more herbal, less bitter version. Pairs especially well with agave (tequila, mezcal).
wiki.art.amaros.cynar.types: Cynar Original (16.5% ABV, sweeter and lighter), Cynar 70 Proof (35% ABV, more bitter and intense, preferred by bartenders). No other variants. The 70 Proof is significantly better for cocktails.
wiki.art.amaros.cynar.cocktails: Cynar Spritz (Cynar, prosecco, soda — a more bitter alternative to the Aperol Spritz). Trident (aquavit, Cynar, dry sherry, peach bitters — the cocktail that revived Cynar). Rabo de Galo (cachaça, Cynar — the Brazilian Negroni). Cynar Julep (Cynar, bourbon, mint). Cynar on the rocks with orange as an aperitif.
wiki.art.amaros.fernet.sub: The world's most intense digestive bitter
wiki.art.amaros.fernet.description: Fernet-Branca is an Italian amaro of intense bitterness, nearly black color, and a mentholated-herbal profile that makes it unmistakable. It is the most popular digestif in Argentina (where it's consumed more than in Italy) and a cult ingredient in bartending worldwide.
wiki.art.amaros.fernet.history: 1845: Bernardino Branca creates Fernet-Branca in Milan as a "medicinal remedy". 1862: it is presented at the Great Exhibition in London. 1900s: it is exported to Argentina with Italian immigrants. 1980s: Fernet con Coca becomes a cultural phenomenon in Argentina, especially in Córdoba. 2000s: American bartenders adopt Fernet as the industry "handshake" — ordering Fernet shows you know bars.
wiki.art.amaros.fernet.origin: Milan, Italy. Created by Bernardino Branca in 1845. The Branca family has kept the secret recipe ever since. Argentina is the world's largest consumer of Fernet-Branca, where it is mixed with Coca-Cola as the unofficial national drink.
wiki.art.amaros.fernet.production: 27 herbs and spices from 4 continents, including myrrh, rhubarb, chamomile, cardamom, aloe, saffron, and mint. They are macerated in grape alcohol, distilled, and aged in oak barrels for at least a year. 39% ABV. The exact recipe is known only by the president of Branca and the master distiller.
wiki.art.amaros.fernet.tasting: Intense mint, eucalyptus, myrrh, medicinal herbs, licorice, extreme bitterness, notes of camphor and mushroom. Dense, almost viscous texture. Ultra-long finish, mentholated and bitter, with a "medicinal" effect that divides opinion. An acquired taste — you either love it or hate it.
wiki.art.amaros.fernet.tips: Argentine Fernet con Coca: 30% Fernet, 70% Coke, lots of ice, in a tall glass. The Hanky Panky only needs 2 bar spoons of Fernet — it is very potent. As a neat digestif, a cold shot after a heavy meal is unbeatable. If the bitterness is too much, start with Branca Menta.
wiki.art.amaros.fernet.types: Fernet-Branca (the original, 39% ABV, ultra-bitter), Branca Menta (with mint, sweeter and more approachable, 28% ABV), Argentine Fernet-Branca (slightly different formulation, locally produced). Other fernets: Fernet Stock (Czech), Fernet 1882 (Argentine), Luxardo Fernet. Branca is the benchmark.
wiki.art.amaros.fernet.cocktails: Fernet con Coca (Fernet-Branca, Coca-Cola, ice — the Argentine national cocktail). Hanky Panky (gin, sweet vermouth, two dashes of Fernet — created by Ada Coleman at the Savoy in 1903). Toronto (Canadian whisky, Fernet, sugar, Angostura). Industry Sour (Fernet, green Chartreuse, lime, syrup). As a shot: the bartenders' "handshake".
wiki.map.advocaat.desc: Dutch liqueur made from egg yolks, sugar, and brandy. Custard-like texture.
wiki.map.airag.desc: Fermented mare's milk of the Mongolian nomads. 2-3% alcohol, national drink for millennia.
wiki.map.alentejo.desc: Warm plains of southern Portugal. Ripe reds and traditional vinification in talha clay amphorae.
wiki.map.allspice-dram.desc: Jamaican liqueur of allspice berries and rum. Tiki cocktail staple (Pimento Dram).
wiki.map.alsace.desc: Aromatic Riesling, Gewürztraminer, and Pinot Gris on the Franco-German border.
wiki.map.amarula.desc: South African cream with marula fruit. Elephants also enjoy it wild.
wiki.map.ancho-reyes.desc: Artisanal Mexican liqueur of ancho chili. 1927 Puebla recipe revived in 2013.
wiki.map.applejack.desc: American apple brandy (jack freezing). Laird's Distillery (New Jersey, 1698), the oldest operating distillery in the USA.
wiki.map.appletiser.desc: Carbonated apple juice from South Africa (Elgin, 1966). Popular non-alcoholic brunch alternative.
wiki.map.asti.desc: Sweet Piedmontese sparkling wine from Moscato. Low-alcohol, fruity, and floral.
wiki.map.australian-whisky.desc: Tasmania leads the craft scene with Sullivans Cove and Lark. Oceanic air and local barley.
wiki.map.bandol.desc: Mourvèdre-dominant wines on Provence coastal terraces. Characterful reds and saline rosés.
wiki.map.barolo.desc: King of Piedmontese wines. Nebbiolo from Langhe aged at least 38 months.
wiki.map.barossa.desc: Cradle of Australian Shiraz. Vines over 150 years old still producing.
wiki.map.beaujolais.desc: Light reds from Gamay grapes south of Burgundy. Famous for Beaujolais Nouveau on the third Thursday of November.
wiki.map.becherovka.desc: Czech herbal bitter from Karlovy Vary (1807). Considered Czechia's "13th natural spring".
wiki.map.bitter-kas.desc: Basque bitter soft drink inspired by Italian Bitter. A Spanish aperitif classic.
wiki.map.bordeaux.desc: World-reference French wine region. Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot dominate Médoc and Saint-Émilion.
wiki.map.brunello.desc: Sangiovese Grosso from Montalcino. At least five years of ageing before release.
wiki.map.burgundy.desc: Sacred land of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Unique climat system defined by terroir.
wiki.map.canada-dry.desc: Canadian ginger ale created by John McLaughlin in Toronto (1904). Dry and less sweet.
wiki.map.canadian-whisky.desc: Gimli (Manitoba) and other distilleries produce smooth whisky often high in rye. Base of Crown Royal.
wiki.map.cava.desc: Spanish traditional-method sparkling from Penedès. Macabeo, Xarel·lo, and Parellada.
wiki.map.cerveza-belgium.desc: Trappists, lambics, and gueuzes. The world's greatest beer diversity.
wiki.map.cerveza-dublin.desc: Stout capital of the world. Guinness has brewed at St. James's Gate since 1759.
wiki.map.cerveza-munich.desc: Helles, Dunkel, and Weissbier under the 1516 Purity Law. Birthplace of Oktoberfest.
wiki.map.cerveza-pilsner.desc: Pilsen, Czechia: birthplace of golden lager (1842). Global model for clear beer.
wiki.map.cerveza-portland.desc: Epicenter of the American craft revolution. Pacific Northwest hops.
wiki.map.chablis.desc: Mineral, cutting Chardonnay from northern Burgundy. Kimmeridgian soils with marine fossils.
wiki.map.champagne.desc: The only region allowed to use the name. Traditional method with second fermentation in bottle.
wiki.map.cherry-heering.desc: Danish cherry liqueur since 1818. Original ingredient of the Singapore Sling and Blood & Sand.
wiki.map.chianti.desc: Tuscan Sangiovese in the historic straw-covered bottle. Chianti Classico bears the Black Rooster.
wiki.map.chicha-morada.desc: Peruvian drink of purple corn, pineapple, and spices. Sweet, cold, and non-alcoholic, an Inca heritage.
wiki.map.club-mate.desc: German mate soft drink since 1924 (Münchsteinach). Iconic in Berlin's hacker and techno scenes.
wiki.map.coca-cola.desc: Recipe by pharmacist John Pemberton (Atlanta, 1886). The world's most iconic soda.
wiki.map.coffee-brazil.desc: World's largest producer. Minas Gerais concentrates the arabica output.
wiki.map.coffee-colombia.desc: Smooth, balanced Arabica from the Coffee Axis. UNESCO Heritage cultural landscape.
wiki.map.coffee-costa-rica.desc: Arabica-only by law since 1989. Tarrazú and Central Valley yield clean, bright, fruity coffees.
wiki.map.coffee-ethiopia.desc: Cradle of Coffea arabica. Yirgacheffe, Sidamo, and Harrar varieties offer distinct profiles.
wiki.map.coffee-honduras.desc: Copán and Marcala lead Honduras, one of Central America's largest producers. Sweet and balanced.
wiki.map.coffee-jamaica.desc: One of the world's finest and most expensive coffees, grown between 900 and 1700 m.
wiki.map.coffee-kenya.desc: Bright, fruity Arabicas from the highlands. Highly prized in specialty coffee.
wiki.map.coffee-panama.desc: The Geisha variety from Boquete revolutionized specialty coffee in 2004. Record auction prices for its floral-citrus profile.
wiki.map.coffee-sumatra.desc: Mandheling and Gayo grown by the typical Indonesian wet-hulling method. Dense body, earthy and cocoa notes.
wiki.map.coffee-vietnam.desc: Second-largest producer, mostly robusta from the central highlands. Symbol of the cà phê sữa đá with condensed milk.
wiki.map.coffee-yemen.desc: First coffee export port (Mocha, 15th century). Origin of the name mocha.
wiki.map.colchagua.desc: Chilean valley of Cabernet and Carménère, the lost grape of Bordeaux. Mediterranean climate.
wiki.map.cremant.desc: French sparkling wines outside Champagne made by the traditional method: Alsace, Loire, Burgundy, Jura.
wiki.map.creme-de-mure.desc: French liqueur of wild blackberries. Classic in Dick Bradsell's Bramble (1984).
wiki.map.creme-de-peche.desc: French peach liqueur from Savoy. Delicate and fruity.
wiki.map.creme-de-violette.desc: Liqueur made from violet petals. Key ingredient in the classic Aviation.
wiki.map.douro-wines.desc: The Douro yields more than just Port: it also produces powerful dry reds since the Barca Velha revolution (1952). UNESCO landscape.
wiki.map.dr-pepper.desc: The oldest soda in the USA (Waco, 1885). Secret blend of 23 flavors.
wiki.map.english-sparkling.desc: English sparkling wines from Sussex and Kent. Global warming has brought them close to Champagne level.
wiki.map.espresso-italy.desc: Italy invents espresso (Turin, 1884). The culture of caffè al banco.
wiki.map.etna.desc: Volcanic wines from the slopes of Mount Etna, with Nerello Mascalese. Unique minerality and freshness.
wiki.map.falernum.desc: Caribbean spiced syrup with clove, ginger, lime, and almond. Essential in tiki bartending.
wiki.map.fanta.desc: Created in WWII Germany (Essen, 1940) when Coca-Cola could no longer import syrup. Today a global brand with dozens of flavors.
wiki.map.fever-tree.desc: Premium London tonic (2005). Relaunched the culture of quality gin and tonic.
wiki.map.finnish-whisky.desc: Teerenpeli in Lahti has distilled since 2002 with local barley and subarctic lake water.
wiki.map.fireball.desc: Canadian whisky infused with cinnamon (1984). Viral phenomenon of the modern shot.
wiki.map.franciacorta.desc: The Italian Champagne from Lombardy. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir made by the traditional method.
wiki.map.genepi.desc: Alpine liqueur of artemisia (genepì). Tradition of Savoy and the Aosta Valley.
wiki.map.georgia-wines.desc: Cradle of wine (8,000 years). Kakheti keeps vinification in qvevri, buried amphorae — a UNESCO heritage.
wiki.map.gin-menorca.desc: Xoriguer has distilled in Mahón since the 18th century, a British legacy from the island's occupation. DO Gin de Mahón.
wiki.map.ginger-beer-jamaica.desc: Jamaican fermented ginger drink. Base of the Moscow Mule and Dark & Stormy.
wiki.map.guarana.desc: Brazilian soft drink from the Amazonian guaraná berry. Natural caffeine and sweetness.
wiki.map.hermitage.desc: Granite hill of Tain-l'Hermitage (Northern Rhône). Legendary Syrah, long-lived and deep wines.
wiki.map.horchata-valencia.desc: Valencian tiger-nut drink with PDO. Served ice-cold with fartons, a tradition of Alboraya since the 13th century.
wiki.map.inca-kola.desc: Peruvian yellow soda with lemon verbena. Outsells Coca-Cola in Peru.
wiki.map.indian-whisky.desc: Amrut (Bangalore) and Paul John (Goa) prove tropical climate accelerates maturation. Intense, spicy notes.
wiki.map.irn-bru.desc: Fluorescent orange Scottish soda. Scotland's other national drink since 1901.
wiki.map.jura.desc: Small French region of singular wines: oxidative Vin Jaune aged sous voile, like a fino sherry.
wiki.map.kefir.desc: Fermented milk with kefir grains, originally from the Caucasus. The oldest probiotic dairy tradition.
wiki.map.kofola.desc: Czech cola created in 1959 as a socialist alternative to Coca-Cola. Less sweet, flavored with herbs and licorice.
wiki.map.kombucha.desc: SCOBY-fermented tea, originally from Manchuria. Popularized in the West in the 1990s.
wiki.map.kvass.desc: Russian fermented drink made from rye bread. Very low alcohol (<1%), drunk as a summer soft drink.
wiki.map.licor-43.desc: Sweet Spanish liqueur with vanilla and 43 botanicals. Created in Cartagena in 1946.
wiki.map.limoncello.desc: Liqueur from Amalfi, Sorrento, or Capri lemons. Digestif served very cold in frozen glasses.
wiki.map.loire-valley.desc: Sancerre, Vouvray, Muscadet. Aromatic, mineral Chenin Blanc and Sauvignon Blanc.
wiki.map.malta-hatuey.desc: Cuban non-alcoholic malta, a tradition since 1942. Bitter and nutritious, served cold and sometimes with condensed milk.
wiki.map.marlborough.desc: New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc that revolutionized the variety in the 1980s.
wiki.map.mate.desc: South American infusion of Ilex paraguariensis. Shared in a gourd with bombilla.
wiki.map.mendoza.desc: Argentine capital of Malbec at the foot of the Andes. High-altitude wines.
wiki.map.midori.desc: Japanese melon liqueur from Suntory (1978). Neon green color and signature sweetness.
wiki.map.monkey-47.desc: Artisanal Black Forest gin with 47 botanicals, many of them wild. Created in 2010 by a retired Englishman.
wiki.map.moroccan-mint.desc: Gunpowder green tea with spearmint and plenty of sugar, poured from high into small glasses. A Maghreb social ritual.
wiki.map.mosel.desc: German slate-soil Rieslings along the Mosel river. Crystalline acidity.
wiki.map.mountain-dew.desc: Citrus soda from Knoxville (1940), loaded with caffeine. Icon of the American South and gamer culture.
wiki.map.napa.desc: Cradle of Californian wine. Benchmark Cabernet Sauvignon after the Judgment of Paris (1976).
wiki.map.nero-davola.desc: Flagship red grape of Sicily, grown near Avola. Powerful, fruity Mediterranean reds.
wiki.map.orange-bitters.desc: Citrus bitters made from bitter orange peel and spices. Nearly extinct during Prohibition, revived by the modern cocktail revival.
wiki.map.orangina.desc: Born in Algeria (Boufarik, 1936) and relaunched in Marseille. Real orange pulp in its bulbous bottle.
wiki.map.pastis.desc: Anise liqueur from Marseille with green anise and licorice. Drunk with iced water, turning white and cloudy.
wiki.map.pepsi.desc: Created in 1893 by Caleb Bradham in North Carolina. Historic rival of Coca-Cola.
wiki.map.pimms.desc: English gin-based aperitif (1823). Heart of the Pimm's Cup served at Wimbledon.
wiki.map.plymouth-gin.desc: Sweeter style than London Dry, distilled at Black Friars Distillery since 1793. The only gin with geographical protection in the UK.
wiki.map.portland-craft-gin.desc: Oregon led the American craft gin revolution with Aviation, New Deal, and other distilleries from the 2000s.
wiki.map.priorat.desc: Catalan DOCa of mineral reds grown on llicorella slate. Old Garnacha and Cariñena vines.
wiki.map.prosecco.desc: Venetian sparkling from Glera grape. Charmat method in large tanks — fresh and floral.
wiki.map.provence-rose.desc: Cradle of modern French rosé. Grenache, Cinsault, and Mourvèdre yield pale, elegant wines.
wiki.map.pulque.desc: Pre-Hispanic Mexican drink fermented from maguey aguamiel. Sacred to the Aztecs, still alive in the highlands.
wiki.map.ramune.desc: Japanese soda with a Codd marble bottle (1884). Original lemon-lime flavor.
wiki.map.rheingau.desc: Noble Rieslings of the Rhine. Birthplace of Kabinett and Spätlese.
wiki.map.rhone.desc: Powerful reds of Syrah and Grenache. Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Hermitage fly its flag.
wiki.map.rhum-haiti.desc: Barbancourt has distilled fresh-cane rhum agricole since 1862. Double distillation in a Charentais pot still.
wiki.map.rias-baixas.desc: Galician Albariño from the Atlantic rías. Marine salinity and minerality.
wiki.map.ribera-duero.desc: Robust, long-lived Tempranillo from the upper Duero. Home of Vega Sicilia.
wiki.map.rioja.desc: Spain's most prestigious DOCa. Aged Tempranillo: crianza, reserva, gran reserva.
wiki.map.ron-bermudas.desc: Gosling's Black Seal since 1806. Heart of the Dark & Stormy, the island's official cocktail.
wiki.map.ron-mexico.desc: Veracruz, Mexico's sugar-cane state, has produced smooth rums since the colonial era. Mocambo and Prohibido are benchmarks.
wiki.map.ron-nicaragua.desc: Flor de Caña has distilled in Chichigalpa since 1890, next to the San Cristóbal volcano. Rum with no added sugar.
wiki.map.ron-paraguay.desc: Paraguay makes light, white rums — less known abroad but with centuries of tradition.
wiki.map.rooibos.desc: South African infusion of Aspalathus linearis, exclusive to the Cederberg mountains. Caffeine-free, reddish, naturally sweet.
wiki.map.rye-indiana.desc: MGP in Lawrenceburg supplies most of the American rye bottled under independent labels. Backbone of the Manhattan.
wiki.map.sambuca.desc: Italian liqueur of star anise, elderflower, and licorice. Served with three coffee beans (le mosche, "the flies").
wiki.map.santorini.desc: Assyrtiko grown in koulouras (basket-shaped vines) on volcanic soils. One of the world's oldest winemaking traditions.
wiki.map.schweppes.desc: Jacob Schweppe invented commercial carbonated water in Geneva (1783). Father of tonic water.
wiki.map.sekt.desc: German sparkling wine from Riesling and other varieties. Tradition since the 19th century.
wiki.map.sidra-asturias.desc: Natural cider poured from height (escanciada). A millennia-old Celtic tradition.
wiki.map.sidra-normandie.desc: Cider made from bitter Norman apples. Base of Calvados.
wiki.map.slivovitz.desc: Traditional plum brandy from the Balkans. National symbol in Serbia, Bosnia, and Czechia.
wiki.map.sloe-gin.desc: Gin macerated with wild sloes (Prunus spinosa). A rural English tradition.
wiki.map.sonoma.desc: Elegant reds and coastal Chardonnays from California. More diverse and cooler than Napa.
wiki.map.sprite.desc: Clear lemon-lime created by Coca-Cola in 1961 as an answer to 7UP. Atlanta, Georgia.
wiki.map.stellenbosch.desc: South Africa's winemaking heart since 1679. Pinotage is its native grape.
wiki.map.taiwanese-whisky.desc: Kavalan (Yilan, 2005) has burst onto the world stage with rapid maturation from heat and humidity. Internationally awarded.
wiki.map.tea-assam.desc: Robust, malty black tea. Backbone of most English Breakfast blends.
wiki.map.tea-ceylon.desc: Bright, citrusy teas from Sri Lanka grown at different altitudes.
wiki.map.tea-darjeeling.desc: The Champagne of tea on Himalayan slopes. Iconic first flush and second flush.
wiki.map.tea-fujian.desc: Cradle of oolong and red teas (Wuyi Shan). Ancient cliffside cultivations.
wiki.map.tea-taiwan.desc: Floral oolongs from Alishan and Dong Ding. Gongfu cha culture.
wiki.map.tea-uji.desc: Cradle of Japanese matcha and gyokuro. A tradition since the 12th century.
wiki.map.tea-yunnan.desc: Home of fermented pu-erh. Ancient wild tea trees thousands of years old.
wiki.map.thums-up.desc: India's best-selling cola, created in 1977 after Coca-Cola's temporary departure. Bolder flavor than its rivals.
wiki.map.tia-maria.desc: Jamaican liqueur of Blue Mountain coffee and rum. Base of the modern Espresso Martini.
wiki.map.tokaj.desc: Hungarian Aszú from botrytized grapes. Called "the wine of kings, the king of wines" by Louis XIV.
wiki.map.triple-sec.desc: Orange liqueur created by Combier in Saumur (1834). Base of the Margarita, Sidecar, and Cosmopolitan.
wiki.map.turkish-rize.desc: Cultivated in Rize (Black Sea) since 1938. Brewed in a double çaydanlık teapot, served all day in tulip glasses.
wiki.map.txakoli.desc: Light, slightly sparkling Basque white wine. Poured from a height into a short glass.
wiki.map.vimto.desc: Red-fruit and spice concentrate created in Manchester (1908). Hugely popular in the UK and the Arab world during Ramadan.
wiki.map.vinho-verde.desc: Light, lightly sparkling whites from Portugal's Minho. Alvarinho and Loureiro grapes, very fresh and low in alcohol.
wiki.map.vodka-finland.desc: Koskenkorva and Finlandia distill with six-row barley and ultra-pure glacier water. A Nordic benchmark.
wiki.map.vodka-usa.desc: Tito's Handmade Vodka (Austin, 1997) triggered the American craft vodka boom. Corn base.
wiki.map.welsh-whisky.desc: Penderyn revives Welsh whisky (2000) after a century of silence. Distilled in a unique Faraday still.
wiki.map.willamette.desc: Oregon Pinot Noir comparable to Burgundy. Cool climate, ideal for the variety.
wiki.map.zubrowka.desc: Polish vodka flavored with bison grass from the Białowieża forest. A unique herbal flavor.
wiki.art.amaros.jagermeister.sub: The world's most famous German herbal liqueur
wiki.art.amaros.jagermeister.description: Jägermeister ("master hunter" in German) is a German herbal liqueur (35% ABV) made with 56 herbs, fruits, roots, and spices. Created in 1935 in Wolfenbüttel, it is the world's best-selling German digestif and one of the most recognizable liqueurs. While many associate it with party shots and Jägerbombs, it is a sophisticated amaro with a complex recipe that deserves to be taken seriously as both a cocktail ingredient and a digestif.
wiki.art.amaros.jagermeister.history: 1878: Wilhelm Mast founds a vinegar works in Wolfenbüttel. 1935: his son Curt Mast creates Jägermeister. 1960s-1970s: it establishes itself as the standard German digestif. 1980s: Sidney Frank Importing introduces it en masse to the American market as a party shot. 1997: the Jägerbomb (Jägermeister + Red Bull) is invented and becomes a global party phenomenon. 2000s: Jägermeister cold-shot machines appear in bars worldwide. 2010s: the cocktail revival begins to recognize Jägermeister as a legitimate, complex amaro.
wiki.art.amaros.jagermeister.origin: Wolfenbüttel, Lower Saxony, Germany. Curt Mast, son of vinegar-works founder Wilhelm Mast, created the recipe in 1935, inspired by the German tradition of hunter's liqueurs. The logo of a stag with a glowing cross between its antlers represents Saint Hubertus, patron saint of hunters. The original distillery remains in Wolfenbüttel and produces the entire global output.
wiki.art.amaros.jagermeister.production: 56 ingredients: saffron, Ceylon cinnamon, ginger root, star anise, cardamom, bitter orange peel, gentian root, lavender, poppy, red sandalwood, and dozens more herbs, roots, fruits, and barks from around the world. Individual macerates are prepared and rested in oak barrels for 1 year. They are blended, filtered, and bottled at 35% ABV. The entire process takes more than 12 months. Every bottle contains the same globally standardized blend.
wiki.art.amaros.jagermeister.tasting: Aroma: complex herbs, licorice, anise, cinnamon, gentian, dark citrus. Palate: sweet-herbal entry evolving quickly into gentian and root bitterness, warm spices (cinnamon, cardamom), licorice, balsamic notes. Finish: long, bitter-sweet, mentholated, and spiced. Served at -18°C (as the brand recommends), the cold mutes the sweetness and highlights the herbs. Manifest is softer, with oak and vanilla notes.
wiki.art.amaros.jagermeister.tips: Always serve at -18°C — from the freezer or the Tap Machine. At room temperature it loses balance and turns cloying. The Jäger Sour is the best way to showcase Jägermeister as a serious cocktail ingredient. Manifest (premium) is sipped neat at cellar temperature, like an Italian amaro. Don't dismiss the Jägerbomb — it is what it is, but it works. In Germany it is drunk as a digestif after a heavy meal, not as a party shot. Store in the freezer.
wiki.art.amaros.jagermeister.types: Jägermeister Original (35% ABV — the classic, 56 ingredients). Jägermeister Manifest (38% ABV — premium version with additional oak-barrel maturation, smoother and more complex). Jägermeister Cold Brew Coffee (33% ABV — with cold-brew coffee and cocoa, launched 2019). Jägermeister Scharf (33% ABV — with spicy ginger, German market). The Tap Machine chills to -18°C for perfect shots.
wiki.art.amaros.jagermeister.cocktails: Jägerbomb (Jägermeister, Red Bull — the world's most popular shot, simple but effective). Jäger Mule (Jägermeister, ginger beer, lime — the herbal Moscow Mule). Jäger Sour (Jägermeister, lemon, simple syrup, egg white — surprisingly elegant). Deer & Beer (Jägermeister + beer — German tradition). Jäger Old Fashioned (Jägermeister, bourbon, bitters — for cocktail nerds). Jäger Negroni (Jägermeister replaces Campari — a German herbal version).
wiki.art.amaros.orange-bitters.descripti: Orange Bitters are aromatic bitters made on a base of bitter orange (Citrus aurantium), essential in classic pre-Prohibition bartending. They were the Martini and Manhattan's original third ingredient before falling into oblivion during the 20th century. Their 2000s revival returned them to their rightful place: a bridge between bitter and citrus that balances and elevates any cocktail.
wiki.art.amaros.orange-bitters.history: 1862: Jerry Thomas documents orange bitters in his "Bartender's Guide". 1880-1920: ubiquitous in Victorian and Edwardian bartending — present in Martinis, Manhattans, and Gin Fizzes. 1920-1933: Prohibition destroys American cocktail culture. 1960s-1990s: orange bitters all but disappear from the market. 1991: Gary Regan creates Regans' Orange Bitters No. 6, starting the revival. 2007: Angostura launches its own version. Today they are considered the third essential bitters alongside Angostura and Peychaud's.
wiki.art.amaros.orange-bitters.origin: England and the United States, 19th century. Multiple producers created versions: Angostura (Trinidad, 2007), Regans' (Gary Regan, USA, 1991), Fee Brothers (Rochester, NY, 1864). The tradition of orange bitters is as old as cocktails themselves — they appear in recipes from Jerry Thomas's 1862 book.
wiki.art.amaros.orange-bitters.productio: Base of bitter orange peels (Citrus aurantium) macerated in high-proof neutral alcohol. Complementary spices are added: cardamom, coriander, juniper, gentian. Every brand has its own profile: Angostura Orange is more spiced, Regans' more citrus-forward, Fee Brothers sweeter. ABV ranges from 9% (Fee) to 45% (Angostura).
wiki.art.amaros.orange-bitters.tasting: Aroma: intense bitter orange, citrus peel, warm spices (cardamom, coriander). Palate: elegant orange bitterness, not sweet, with depth from gentian and spices. Finish: clean citrus with lingering bitterness. Orange bitters add complexity without dominating — the perfect balancer between sweetness and bitterness in cocktails.
wiki.art.amaros.orange-bitters.tips: 1-2 dashes are enough — they complement, not dominate. Perfect in any gin or vermouth cocktail. Regans' for a pure citrus profile, Angostura Orange for more spiced complexity. Transform a Gin & Tonic by adding 2 dashes. In a Dry Martini, orange bitters is the secret ingredient that sets a professional bartender apart. Store at room temperature; they keep for years.
wiki.art.amaros.orange-bitters.types: Angostura Orange Bitters (28% ABV, spiced and complex). Regans' Orange Bitters No. 6 (45% ABV, pure citrus, a bartender favorite). Fee Brothers West Indian Orange Bitters (9% ABV, sweeter, with glycerin). The Bitter Truth Orange Bitters (39% ABV, European style). Scrappy's Orange Bitters (artisanal, Seattle). Every brand has its own profile — a professional bar should have at least two.
wiki.art.amaros.orange-bitters.cocktails: Dry Martini (gin, dry vermouth, 1-2 dashes orange bitters — the original pre-Prohibition recipe). Bijou (gin, sweet vermouth, Chartreuse, orange bitters). Martinez (Old Tom gin, sweet vermouth, maraschino, orange bitters — the Martini's forerunner). Pegu Club (gin, curaçao, lime, Angostura + orange bitters). Adonis (sweet vermouth, sherry, orange bitters — a spirit-based low-proof cocktail). Old Fashioned variant (bourbon, orange bitters instead of Angostura for a more citrus profile).
wiki.art.amaros.peychauds-bitters.descri: Peychaud's Bitters are aromatic bitters created in New Orleans, fundamental to the Sazerac cocktail and to American cocktail culture. Unlike Angostura (more spiced), Peychaud's has a more floral, fruity profile with anise notes. They are the world's second most important bitters after Angostura and a must-have ingredient in any professional bar.
wiki.art.amaros.peychauds-bitters.histor: 1830s: Antoine Peychaud creates the bitters at his New Orleans pharmacy. 1838: they become popular in the city's coffee houses. 1850s: combined with absinthe and rye whiskey, they create the Sazerac, considered the first American cocktail. 1869: the brand is commercially registered. 2008: Sazerac Company acquires the brand. Peychaud's is declared the "official bitters of New Orleans" and protected as cultural heritage.
wiki.art.amaros.peychauds-bitters.origin: New Orleans, Louisiana, United States. Antoine Amédée Peychaud, a Creole pharmacist of Haitian descent, created the formula at his apothecary on Royal Street in the 1830s. He served them mixed with cognac in egg cups (coquetiers) — a word legend says gave rise to the term "cocktail".
wiki.art.amaros.peychauds-bitters.produc: Secret formula based on gentian, star anise, mint, flowers, cherry bark, and spices. Macerated in high-proof neutral alcohol (35% ABV). The distinctive red-pink color is natural, derived from the botanicals. Packaged in the iconic red-and-white label bottle.
wiki.art.amaros.peychauds-bitters.tastin: Aroma: intense floral, anise, cherry, fresh mint. Palate: sweet entry yielding to gentian bitterness, star anise, red fruit, soft spices. Color: distinctive red-pink that tints cocktails. Finish: lighter and more floral than Angostura, with lingering anise. Less bitter and fruitier than its Trinidadian rival.
wiki.art.amaros.peychauds-bitters.tips: Essential in any Creole/New Orleans cocktail. The pink tint they give is part of the Sazerac's visual identity. Not interchangeable with Angostura — the floral-anise profile is entirely different. A professional bar needs both. 3-5 dashes is the usual measure. Combining with absinthe amplifies the anise notes. Store at room temperature; they keep indefinitely.
wiki.art.amaros.peychauds-bitters.types: Peychaud's Original Aromatic Cocktail Bitters (the classic, 35% ABV, red label). There is no extended line like Angostura's — Peychaud's has stayed faithful to its unique formula since 1830. Artisanal imitations exist, but none replicate the original floral-anise profile exactly.
wiki.art.amaros.peychauds-bitters.cockta: Sazerac (rye whiskey, sugar, Peychaud's, absinthe rinse — the oldest American cocktail). Vieux Carré (rye, cognac, sweet vermouth, Bénédictine, Peychaud's + Angostura). De La Louisiane (rye, sweet vermouth, Bénédictine, Peychaud's, absinthe). Seelbach Cocktail (bourbon, triple sec, champagne, Peychaud's + Angostura). The Peychaud's + absinthe combination is the hallmark of New Orleans bartending.
wiki.art.amaros.suze.description: Suze is a French bitter gentian liqueur with a unique profile: bitter, earthy, and floral. Unlike Italian amari (which combine dozens of botanicals), Suze is minimalist — gentian is the absolute star. Its clean bitterness and versatility have made it the Parisian aperitif of choice and, more recently, a flagship ingredient in international modern bartending.
wiki.art.amaros.suze.history: 1889: Fernand Moureaux creates Suze in Paris. 1898: the brand is registered with its iconic yellow bottle. 1912: Pablo Picasso features a Suze bottle in his Cubist collage "Verre et bouteille de Suze", immortalizing it in art. 20th century: it becomes France's best-selling gentian aperitif. 1965: Pernod Ricard acquires the brand. 2010s: the cocktail revival discovers Suze as a Campari substitute to create more herbal, complex Negronis.
wiki.art.amaros.suze.origin: Maisons-Alfort, France. Fernand Moureaux created Suze in 1889, the same year the Eiffel Tower was inaugurated. The name reportedly comes from Suzanne, the sister of a friend of the creator. The gentian is hand-harvested in the mountains of the French Massif Central (Auvergne) and the Alps, at altitudes above 1,000 meters.
wiki.art.amaros.suze.production: Yellow gentian root (Gentiana lutea) is the base — wild plants of 15-20 years harvested by hand in French mountains. The roots are washed, cut, and macerated in neutral alcohol for months. Filtered, sugar is added (it's a liqueur, not a pure bitter) and bottled at 15% ABV. The golden yellow color is natural from the gentian. No artificial coloring.
wiki.art.amaros.suze.tasting: Aroma: earthy gentian, wildflowers, honey, subtle citrus. Palate: sweet-floral entry evolving into a deep, clean gentian bitterness — less aggressive than Campari, more herbal and earthy. Finish: long, bitter-sweet, with notes of root and damp earth. Bright golden yellow color. The profile is unique: neither Italian nor herbal like Chartreuse, but earthy and mountainous.
wiki.art.amaros.suze.tips: Serve very cold — straight from the freezer or on ice. Suze & Tonic is the perfect aperitif for anyone who finds Campari too bitter. In a White Negroni, the classic ratio is 1:1:1 (gin, Suze, Lillet Blanc). Suze works where Campari is too aggressive. Refrigerate after opening (15% ABV is low). The Picasso collage is a great talking point when serving guests.
wiki.art.amaros.suze.types: Suze Original (15% ABV, the classic and best-known version). Suze belongs to the French "gentiane" family that includes: Salers (drier, 16% ABV, from Cantal), Avèze (15% ABV, from Auvergne), Bonal Gentiane-Quina (16% ABV, with quinine). Suze is the sweetest and most approachable of the group — the ideal gateway to gentian bitters.
wiki.art.amaros.suze.cocktails: White Negroni (gin, Suze, Lillet Blanc — the modern reinvention of the Negroni). Suze & Tonic (Suze, tonic, lemon slice — the quintessential Parisian aperitif). Falling Leaves (bourbon, Suze, apple, lemon — autumnal cocktail). London Calling (gin, Suze, lemon, sherry — modern classic). Bitter Giuseppe (Suze or Cynar, sweet vermouth, lemon). The White Negroni is the cocktail that put Suze on the world map.
wiki.art.mixers.allspice-dram.sub: The Jamaican allspice liqueur for tiki
wiki.art.mixers.allspice-dram.descriptio: Allspice dram (also called pimento dram) is a Caribbean liqueur (22-30% ABV) made with Jamaican allspice (Pimenta dioica), the aromatic berry that blends cinnamon, clove, nutmeg, and pepper notes. A niche but essential ingredient in tiki and autumn/winter cocktails. Without allspice dram there is no authentic Lion's Tail, Ancient Mariner, or Three Dots and a Dash.
wiki.art.mixers.allspice-dram.origin: Jamaica, Caribbean. Allspice is native to Jamaica and Central America — the Spanish called it "pimienta" because of its shape. Jamaicans macerated it in overproof rum as medicine and digestive from the 18th century. St. Elizabeth Allspice Dram (Jamaica) is the best-known brand. The name "dram" comes from the Scottish whisky measure.
wiki.art.mixers.allspice-dram.production: Allspice berries (dried) are coarsely ground and macerated in high-proof Jamaican rum for several days. Filtered and sweetened with cane syrup. Bottled at 22-30% ABV. Homemade: 30 g crushed allspice + 350 ml overproof rum, macerate 5-7 days shaking daily, strain through fine mesh, add 150 ml rich simple syrup. Ready in a week.
wiki.art.mixers.allspice-dram.tips: Use 7-15 ml (½ oz max) — it is very concentrated. Natural partner for dark rum, bourbon, falernum, and citrus. The Lion's Tail is the perfect introduction to allspice dram — simple and spectacular. Making allspice dram at home is very easy and cheap. Store at room temperature. In autumn/winter, a barspoon in a bourbon Old Fashioned transforms the drink. The secret weapon of many tiki bartenders.
wiki.art.mixers.allspice-dram.types: St. Elizabeth Allspice Dram (22.5% ABV, Jamaica — the standard, balanced sweet-spice). Hamilton Pimento Dram (30% ABV — stronger and drier). The Bitter Truth Pimento Dram (22% ABV, Germany). Homemade allspice dram (crushed allspice + overproof rum + syrup, macerate 5-7 days — easy and superior to commercial). For cocktails, St. Elizabeth or homemade.
wiki.art.mixers.allspice-dram.cocktails: Lion's Tail (bourbon, allspice dram, lime, Angostura — the cocktail that showcases allspice dram best). Three Dots and a Dash (rhum, allspice dram, falernum, honey, lime, orange, Angostura — a complex Don the Beachcomber tiki). Ancient Mariner (rum, allspice dram, falernum, lime, grapefruit). Corn 'n' Oil variant (dark rum, falernum, allspice dram, lime, bitters). Saturn (gin, falernum, allspice dram, orgeat, lime, passion fruit).
wiki.art.mixers.champagne-prosecco.descr: Champagne and prosecco are the sparkling wines most used in cocktails — they bring elegant effervescence, acidity, and complexity no other mixer can replicate. Champagne (Champagne, France) for premium cocktails like the French 75; prosecco (Veneto, Italy) for the Aperol Spritz and Bellini. Together they appear in 15+ classic cocktails.
wiki.art.mixers.champagne-prosecco.origi: Champagne: Champagne region, northeastern France. Dom Pérignon did not invent champagne but perfected the méthode champenoise (second fermentation in bottle). Prosecco: Veneto and Friuli, northeastern Italy. Charmat method (second fermentation in tank), fruitier and less complex than champagne. Cava (Spain) and Crémant (France) are excellent alternatives for cocktails.
wiki.art.mixers.champagne-prosecco.produ: Champagne: traditional/méthode champenoise — second fermentation in bottle, ageing on lees, manual disgorgement. Minimum 15 months sur lie (3 years for vintage). Prosecco: Charmat method — second fermentation in a steel tank, faster, preserving fruity freshness. Cava: méthode champenoise like champagne but with Spanish grapes (Macabeo, Parellada, Xarel·lo).
wiki.art.mixers.champagne-prosecco.tips: NEVER shake a cocktail with sparkling wine — always pour at the end. French 75: shake gin/lemon/sugar, strain into a flute, top with chilled champagne. Spritz: build in a wine glass with ice, prosecco first, then Aperol, splash of soda. Use cava or crémant in place of champagne to cut costs without losing quality. Prosecco for sweet/fruity cocktails; champagne for dry/elegant ones. Always very cold (6-8°C).
wiki.art.mixers.champagne-prosecco.types: Champagne Brut (dry, the most versatile for cocktails — Moët, Veuve Clicquot). Champagne Extra Brut/Brut Nature (very dry, for purists). Prosecco DOC (the standard, light, fruity — La Marca, Mionetto). Prosecco DOCG (more complex, higher quality). Cava Brut (Spanish alternative, excellent value). Crémant (from Alsace, Loire, Burgundy — great quality, lower price than champagne). For Spritz: prosecco. For French 75: champagne or cava.
wiki.art.mixers.champagne-prosecco.cockt: French 75 (gin, lemon, sugar, champagne — the champagne cocktail par excellence). Aperol Spritz (Aperol, prosecco, soda — Europe's best-selling aperitif). Bellini (peach purée, prosecco — created at Harry's Bar, Venice). Mimosa (orange juice, champagne — brunch classic). Kir Royal (cassis, champagne). Champagne Cocktail (champagne, sugar, Angostura, cognac). Death in the Afternoon (absinthe, champagne — Hemingway's).
wiki.art.mixers.citrus-juices.descriptio: Citrus is the essential acid of bartending — it brings freshness, balance, and complexity no other ingredient can replicate. Lemon and lime are the two pillars, while grapefruit, orange, and yuzu extend the repertoire. The golden rule: always fresh juice, never bottled. Citrus juice loses its brightness in 4-8 hours due to oxidation — a professional bar squeezes to order or during shift mise en place.
wiki.art.mixers.citrus-juices.origin: Native to Southeast Asia, citrus reached the Mediterranean via Arab trade routes (10th-12th centuries). British sailors discovered that lime juice prevented scurvy (hence the nickname "limeys"). 19th-century bartending adopted citrus as a fundamental ingredient — the Sour (spirit + citrus + sweet) became the world's largest cocktail family.
wiki.art.mixers.citrus-juices.production: Squeeze with a hand juicer (Mexican elbow) or electric press. Strain to remove pulp and seeds. Super juice (modern technique) extracts more juice and flavor: peel the zest, blend with citric/malic acid, macerate 2h, add water, blend — yields 8x more than traditional juice and keeps 2 weeks. Oleo saccharum: peel citrus onto sugar and let macerate — it extracts the essential oils for use in punches and cordials.
wiki.art.mixers.citrus-juices.tips: ALWAYS fresh juice — never bottled. Squeeze 4-8 hours before service maximum. Lime juice oxidizes faster than lemon. A medium lemon yields ~30 ml (1 oz), a lime ~22 ml (¾ oz). Roll the citrus on the counter before cutting to extract more juice. Super juice is a revolution for high-volume bars — less waste, more consistency. For garnish, cut uniform 5 mm rounds. The oils from the peel (expressed onto the cocktail) add aromas the juice cannot.
wiki.art.mixers.citrus-juices.types: Lemon (Citrus limon): bright acid, universal, the base of Sours and Collins. Lime (Citrus aurantiifolia): more acidic and aromatic than lemon, essential in Daiquiris, Margaritas, Mojitos. Grapefruit (Citrus paradisi): bitter-sour, for Palomas and Hemingway Daiquiri. Orange (Citrus sinensis): sweet-sour, for Mimosas, screwdrivers, garnish. Yuzu: Japanese citrus, aromatic and complex, a modern-bar trend. Kaffir lime: aromatic leaves for infusions and tropical garnish.
wiki.art.mixers.citrus-juices.cocktails: Lemon: Whiskey Sour, Tom Collins, Sidecar, Lemon Drop, Corpse Reviver No. 2. Lime: Daiquiri, Margarita, Mojito, Gimlet, Caipirinha, Moscow Mule. Grapefruit: Paloma, Hemingway Daiquiri, Greyhound, Brown Derby. Orange: Mimosa, Tequila Sunrise, Blood & Sand, Garibaldi ("fluffy" orange juice). The citrus defines the cocktail family — lemon for European elegance, lime for tropical freshness.
wiki.art.mixers.coconut.description: Coconut in its various forms — cream of coconut, coconut milk, coconut water, and shredded coconut — is the ingredient that defines tropical and tiki bartending. No coconut, no Piña Colada, Painkiller, or Chi Chi. Cream of coconut (Coco López) brings sweetness, creamy texture, and intense tropical flavor that no other ingredient can replicate.
wiki.art.mixers.coconut.origin: Southeast Asia and the tropical Pacific. Coconut is grown in over 80 tropical countries. In cocktails, modern usage began in Puerto Rico: Ramón "Monchito" Marrero created the Piña Colada in 1954 at the Caribe Hilton using Coco López, the first commercial cream of coconut, invented by Don Ramón López Irizarry in 1948.
wiki.art.mixers.coconut.production: Coco López: shredded, pressed coconut pulp blended with sugar and emulsifiers. It is a processed, sweetened product, not natural coconut. Coconut milk: coconut pulp pressed in water, unsweetened. Coconut water: the natural liquid inside young coconuts. For bartending: Coco López is the industry standard, but real whipped coconut cream is superior.
wiki.art.mixers.coconut.tips: Coco López ALWAYS needs to be shaken vigorously before use — it separates in the can. For Piña Colada: blender with ice for frozen texture, or shaken with ice for the "on the rocks" version. Open Coco López lasts 1 week refrigerated. Coconut milk is better for cocktails where you don't want as much sweetness. Fat-wash with coconut oil: infuse a spirit with coconut oil, freeze, remove the fat — adds silky texture without sweetness.
wiki.art.mixers.coconut.types: Cream of coconut (Coco López — sweet, thick, sweetened, the Piña Colada standard). Coconut milk (less sweet, lighter, for less cloying cocktails). Coconut water (hydrating, light, for refreshing low-ABV drinks). Toasted shredded coconut (for garnish and rim). Coconut oil (for fat-washing spirits). Coco López vs. unsweetened coconut cream are VERY different products — check the recipe.
wiki.art.mixers.coconut.cocktails: Piña Colada (rum, cream of coconut, pineapple — Puerto Rico's official cocktail since 1978). Painkiller (rum, cream of coconut, pineapple, orange, nutmeg — Soggy Dollar Bar, BVI). Chi Chi (vodka, cream of coconut, pineapple — Piña Colada with vodka). Batida de Coco (cachaça, coconut milk, sugar — Brazilian). Swimming Pool (vodka, rum, Blue Curaçao, cream of coconut, pineapple). Coconut Daiquiri (rum, cream of coconut, lime).
wiki.art.mixers.coffee-espresso.sub: The star ingredient of modern bartending
wiki.art.mixers.coffee-espresso.descript: Coffee is the mixer that defines the modern era of bartending. The Espresso Martini (created in 1983) has become the world's most ordered cocktail of the 2020s. From the classic Irish Coffee to the Mexican Carajillo, coffee brings bitterness, aroma, caffeine, and complexity that connect with millions of consumers. A bartender who masters coffee cocktails masters the best-sellers.
wiki.art.mixers.coffee-espresso.origin: Ethiopia (origin of coffee, 9th century). In bartending: 1942 — Joe Sheridan creates the Irish Coffee at Foynes airport, Ireland. 1983 — Dick Bradsell creates the Espresso Martini (then called "Vodka Espresso") at Soho Brasserie in London, when a model asked for a cocktail to "wake me up and then knock me out". 2020s: the Espresso Martini becomes a global phenomenon.
wiki.art.mixers.coffee-espresso.producti: Espresso: water under pressure (9 bar) forced through finely ground coffee for 25-30 seconds. Produces crema (the golden foam) that is essential to the Espresso Martini's texture. Cold brew: coarsely ground coffee steeped in cold water for 12-24 hours, then filtered — concentrated, smooth, low in acid. For batched cocktails, concentrated cold brew is ideal because it does not get diluted by melting ice.
wiki.art.mixers.coffee-espresso.tips: Espresso MUST be fresh (under 1 minute) for the Espresso Martini — the hot crema creates the iconic foam when shaken. Shake vigorously 15-20 seconds for perfect foam. Without an espresso machine, concentrated cold brew + a dash of gomme syrup works. Mr Black > Kahlúa for premium Espresso Martinis (less sweet, more coffee). Irish Coffee: the cream is poured unwhipped (only lightly thickened) over the back of a spoon. 3 coffee beans as garnish on the Espresso Martini = tradition (health, wealth, happiness).
wiki.art.mixers.coffee-espresso.types: Espresso (double shot, 25-30 ml — the essential base, crema included). Cold brew (cold-steeped 12-24 h — smoother, less acidic, perfect for batched cocktails). Filter coffee (pour-over, lighter than espresso). Coffee liqueur (Kahlúa, Mr Black — already liqueurs, not pure mixers). Instant coffee (emergency only). For bartending: fresh espresso always > cold brew > instant.
wiki.art.mixers.coffee-espresso.cocktail: Espresso Martini (vodka, Kahlúa, fresh espresso, syrup — the world's most famous coffee cocktail). Irish Coffee (Irish whiskey, hot coffee, sugar, unwhipped cream — the comforting original). Carajillo (Licor 43, espresso over ice — the Latin coffee cocktail). White Russian (vodka, Kahlúa, cream — The Dude abides). Black Russian (vodka, Kahlúa — without cream). Revolver (bourbon, Kahlúa, orange bitters — the caffeinated Old Fashioned).
wiki.art.mixers.cola.description: Cola (Coca-Cola, Pepsi, and their variants) is the world's most-consumed soft drink and a fundamental cocktail mixer. The Cuba Libre (rum + cola + lime) is one of the 5 best-selling cocktails globally. Although not an "author" ingredient, every professional bartender must master cola cocktails — they are the top sellers in any bar in the world.
wiki.art.mixers.cola.origin: Atlanta, Georgia, USA. 1886: John Pemberton, a pharmacist, creates Coca-Cola as a medicinal tonic with coca leaf extract and kola nut. 1893: Caleb Bradham creates Pepsi-Cola in North Carolina. 1900: rum is combined with Coca-Cola in Cuba after the Spanish-American War — the Cuba Libre is born. Cola became the 20th-century universal mixer.
wiki.art.mixers.cola.production: Carbonated water + sugar (or HFCS) + kola nut extract + caramel + phosphoric acid + vanilla + cinnamon + citrus + secret spices. Coca-Cola's recipe is famously kept in a vault in Atlanta. Craft colas use natural ingredients and cane sugar. The brown color comes from caramel. Premium colas have less sugar and more pronounced spices.
wiki.art.mixers.cola.tips: Always use freshly opened cola — it loses fizz quickly. Mexican Coke (cane sugar) makes a noticeably better Cuba Libre. Standard ratio: 1:2-1:3 (spirit:cola). Always add lime in the Cuba Libre — without lime it's not a Cuba Libre, just a Rum & Coke. Craft cola (Fever-Tree) elevates any whisky and cola. The Kalimotxo is the perfect guilty pleasure for parties. Never use diet cola in cocktails — the artificial taste shows up immediately.
wiki.art.mixers.cola.types: Coca-Cola Original (the world reference). Pepsi (slightly sweeter). Mexican Coke (made with cane sugar — preferred by bartenders for its cleaner taste). Craft cola (Fentimans, Fever-Tree, Maine Root — less sweet, more spiced). Cola Zero/Diet (sugar-free — changes the balance of the cocktail). For bartending, Mexican Coke or craft cola always beat regular HFCS cola.
wiki.art.mixers.cola.cocktails: Cuba Libre (rum, cola, lime — the most famous Latin highball). Jack & Coke (Jack Daniel's bourbon + cola — the quintessential American combo). Long Island Iced Tea (vodka, gin, rum, tequila, Cointreau, lemon, cola — looks like tea, hits like a truck). Fernandito/Fernet con Cola (Fernet-Branca, cola — Argentina's national drink). Kalimotxo (red wine, cola — Basque/Spanish tradition). Rum & Coke (rum, cola — simple and universal).
wiki.art.mixers.creme-de-violette.sub: The floral liqueur that makes the Aviation
wiki.art.mixers.creme-de-violette.descri: Crème de violette is a floral liqueur (16-20% ABV) made from violet flowers, bringing a spectacular purple hue and a delicate floral flavor. It is the ingredient that gives the Aviation its iconic lavender-blue tint. It disappeared from the market for decades until the cocktail revival brought it back. Today it is a niche modifier, but essential for any bar serving the full classics.
wiki.art.mixers.creme-de-violette.origin: France and Austria, 19th century. Floral liqueurs were popular in Victorian Europe. Crème de violette was produced mainly in France (Dijon, Paris) and Austria. It nearly vanished in the second half of the 20th century. 2007: Rothman & Winter (Austria) relaunches its Crème de Violette, followed by The Bitter Truth (Germany) — the cocktail revival brings it back for the Aviation.
wiki.art.mixers.creme-de-violette.produc: Violet flowers (Viola odorata) are macerated in neutral alcohol. Filtered and sugar is added. Some brands use violet extract rather than fresh flowers. The purple color varies from pale to intense depending on brand and concentration. Rothman & Winter macerates fresh violets from the Austrian Alps. The low ABV (16-22%) makes it a modifier rather than a sipping liqueur.
wiki.art.mixers.creme-de-violette.tips: Use with extreme restraint — 7-10 ml (one or two bar spoons) is enough. Too much crème de violette makes the cocktail taste like soap. In the Aviation, the classic ratio is 60 ml gin, 15 ml maraschino, 7 ml crème de violette, 22 ml lemon. The subtle lavender hue is the visual signature — if it's deep purple, it's too much. Store at room temperature. It is a one-cocktail ingredient in most bars, but that cocktail (Aviation) is worth it.
wiki.art.mixers.creme-de-violette.types: Rothman & Winter Crème de Violette (20% ABV, Austria — the modern standard, balanced floral). The Bitter Truth Violet Liqueur (22% ABV, Germany — more intense). Giffard Crème de Violette (16% ABV, France — sweeter). Tempus Fugit Crème de Violette (22% ABV, Switzerland — premium, complex). Monin Violet Syrup (non-alcoholic — alternative for bars that don't want another liqueur). For the Aviation: Rothman & Winter is the benchmark.
wiki.art.mixers.creme-de-violette.cockta: Aviation (gin, maraschino, crème de violette, lemon — the cocktail that justifies crème de violette's existence, with its iconic lavender color). Blue Moon (gin, crème de violette, lemon — simpler, more violet). Violet Fizz (gin, crème de violette, lemon, soda, egg white). Spring Forward (gin, crème de violette, St-Germain, lemon). Water Lily (gin, crème de violette, Cointreau, lemon — perfect balance).
wiki.art.mixers.eggs-dairy.sub: Texture, foam, and creaminess in cocktails
wiki.art.mixers.eggs-dairy.description: Eggs and dairy bring texture, foam, and creaminess that no other ingredient can replicate. Egg white creates the silky foam of Sours; the whole egg gives the velvety body of Flips; cream adds luxury to Alexander and White Russian. They are technical ingredients that separate a competent bartender from an excellent one.
wiki.art.mixers.eggs-dairy.origin: Egg white in cocktails is documented from the 1860s in recipe books such as Jerry Thomas's. Flips (whole egg) date back to 17th-century English taverns. Cream appears in the Irish Coffee (1942), Alexander (1915), and Ramos Gin Fizz (1888). Aquafaba (chickpea liquid) emerged as a vegan alternative in the 2010s.
wiki.art.mixers.eggs-dairy.production: Egg white: separate yolk and white. Use ~30 ml (1 white) per cocktail. Dry shake technique: shake first WITHOUT ice for 10-15 seconds to emulsify, then add ice and shake again. This creates maximum foam. Aquafaba: use straight from the chickpea can, same amount as egg white (30 ml). Cream for Irish Coffee: lightly whip by hand (not fully whipped) until it thickens but still flows.
wiki.art.mixers.eggs-dairy.tips: The dry shake technique (no ice first) is MANDATORY for perfect foam. Reverse dry shake (ice first, strain, then no ice) produces even denser foam. Aquafaba works identically to egg white — impossible to tell apart in a blind tasting. For guests worried about raw egg: use pasteurized eggs or aquafaba. Irish Coffee cream: hand-whip with a fork until it just thickens — never fully stiff. A dash of Angostura on the foam is visual art and flavor.
wiki.art.mixers.eggs-dairy.types: Egg white (for silky foam in Sours and Fizzes). Whole egg (for Flips — richer and creamier). Cream/heavy cream (for Alexander, White Russian, Irish Coffee). Milk (for clarified Milk Punch — a clarification technique). Aquafaba (canned chickpea liquid — perfect vegan substitute for egg white). Whipped cream (for Irish Coffee, Hot Chocolate). Butter (for butter-washing spirits).
wiki.art.mixers.eggs-dairy.cocktails: EGG WHITE: Whiskey Sour (bourbon, lemon, syrup, egg white — the iconic silky foam). Pisco Sour (pisco, lemon, syrup, egg white, Angostura). Ramos Gin Fizz (gin, lemon, lime, cream, egg white, orange flower water, soda — shake 12 minutes or use a blender). Clover Club (gin, raspberry, lemon, egg white). WHOLE EGG: Eggnog (brandy, egg, milk, sugar, nutmeg). Porto Flip (port, cognac, egg). CREAM: Alexander (gin/brandy, crème de cacao, cream). White Russian (vodka, Kahlúa, cream). Irish Coffee.
wiki.art.mixers.ginger-beer.description: Ginger beer is a carbonated drink made with fresh ginger that brings spice, sweetness, and effervescence to cocktails. Unlike ginger ale (mild and subtle), ginger beer has a real ginger punch that makes it indispensable for Moscow Mules, Dark 'n' Stormys, and dozens of modern highballs. The original was alcoholic (fermented); the modern version is a soft drink.
wiki.art.mixers.ginger-beer.origin: England, 18th century. Original ginger beer was naturally fermented with ginger, sugar, water, and a "ginger beer plant" (a yeast-bacteria symbiosis). It was massively exported to the British colonies. The modern non-alcoholic version became popular in the 20th century. Key brands: Fever-Tree (UK), Bundaberg (Australia), Gosling's (Bermuda), Reed's (USA).
wiki.art.mixers.ginger-beer.production: Traditional method: fermentation of fresh grated ginger with sugar, water, and yeast for 2-5 days — produces natural alcohol (0.5-2% ABV). Modern (commercial) method: carbonated water + ginger extract/juice + sugar + citric acid — no fermentation, 0% alcohol. Premium versions (Fever-Tree, Q Mixers) use fresh ginger from Nigeria, Cochin (India), or Fiji. The heat varies enormously between brands.
wiki.art.mixers.ginger-beer.tips: Always use ginger beer (not ginger ale) for cocktails — the ginger punch is essential. Fever-Tree for balance, Bundaberg for more heat. The Moscow Mule is served in a copper mug by tradition, not for flavor. Standard ratio: 1:2 (spirit:ginger beer). Open just before using — it loses fizz quickly. Pairs extraordinarily well with dark rum, bourbon, tequila, and mezcal. Store refrigerated.
wiki.art.mixers.ginger-beer.types: Standard ginger beer (Fever-Tree, Q Mixers — balanced, versatile). Extra-spicy ginger beer (Bundaberg, Reed's Extra — intense ginger). Light ginger beer (less sugar, for lighter highballs). Ginger ale (NOT the same — milder, less ginger, more carbonation; Canada Dry, Schweppes). Artisanal/fermented ginger beer (slightly alcoholic, hazy, more complex). For cocktails, always prefer ginger beer over ginger ale.
wiki.art.mixers.ginger-beer.cocktails: Moscow Mule (vodka, ginger beer, lime — served in a copper mug). Dark 'n' Stormy (Gosling's dark rum, ginger beer — a Bermudian trademark). Kentucky Mule (bourbon, ginger beer, lime). Mexican Mule (tequila, ginger beer, lime). Gin-Gin Mule (gin, ginger beer, mint, lime — Audrey Saunders classic). Penicillin (scotch, honey-ginger, lemon — uses ginger beer as inspiration for the syrup).
wiki.art.mixers.herbs-spices.description: Fresh herbs and spices are the aromatics that turn a good cocktail into a memorable one. The mint of the Mojito, the basil of the Gin Basil Smash, the rosemary of the Rosemary Gimlet, the cinnamon of the Hot Toddy — every herb and spice brings a unique aromatic profile. Mastering their use (muddling, garnish, infusion, flaming) is a fundamental skill of modern bartending.
wiki.art.mixers.herbs-spices.origin: Aromatic herbs have been used in drinks since antiquity — the Romans infused wine with herbs. In bartending: mint has been iconic since the Mint Julep (1803) and Mojito (1920s). Basil arrived with the Gin Basil Smash (Jörg Meyer, 2008). Rosemary and thyme trended in the 2010s. Spices (cinnamon, nutmeg, pepper) have featured in punches since the 17th century.
wiki.art.mixers.herbs-spices.production: Muddling: press the leaves gently against the glass to release essential oils — NEVER crush aggressively (it releases bitter chlorophyll). Infused syrup: add herbs to hot simple syrup, let cool, strain. Flamed garnish: light a rosemary sprig with a lighter — the smoke perfumes the cocktail spectacularly. Expressed oils: rub herbs between your palms over the cocktail to release essential oils.
wiki.art.mixers.herbs-spices.tips: MINT: clap the mint between your hands before using as garnish — it releases oils without bruising. MUDDLING: press and twist, never smash — chlorophyll from torn leaves makes the cocktail bitter. ROSEMARY: flaming it as a garnish is spectacular and perfumes the cocktail. Nutmeg ALWAYS freshly grated — pre-ground has no aroma. Herbs wilt quickly: store in water like flowers or wrapped in damp paper in the fridge. The Gin Basil Smash is the most important herb cocktail of the last 20 years.
wiki.art.mixers.herbs-spices.types: HERBS: Mint (Mojito, Julep, Southside — muddled gently). Basil (Gin Basil Smash, Strawberry Basil Smash — muddled). Rosemary (Rosemary Gimlet — infused in syrup or as flamed garnish). Thyme (as aromatic garnish). Sage (in syrup for autumn cocktails). Cilantro (in Mexican tropical cocktails). SPICES: Cinnamon (as a stick for garnish or syrup). Nutmeg (grated over Flips and Eggnog). Black pepper (Penicillin garnish). Star anise (garnish in absinthe cocktails). Fresh ginger (muddled or in syrup).
wiki.art.mixers.herbs-spices.cocktails: MINT: Mojito, Mint Julep, Southside, Grasshopper. BASIL: Gin Basil Smash (gin, basil, lemon, syrup — a modern classic). ROSEMARY: Rosemary Gimlet, rosemary syrup in Whiskey Sour. CINNAMON: Hot Toddy, Mulled Wine, cinnamon syrup in an autumn Old Fashioned. NUTMEG: grated over Eggnog, Flip, Brandy Alexander. GINGER: muddled in a Moscow Mule variation, ginger syrup in Penicillin.
wiki.art.mixers.juices.description: Beyond citrus (lemon, lime, grapefruit, orange — covered in their own article), there are essential juices in bartending: pineapple, cranberry, tomato, passion fruit, apple, and pomegranate. Each defines iconic cocktails and brings flavors impossible to replicate with other ingredients.
wiki.art.mixers.juices.origin: Fruit juices have been used in drinks since antiquity. In modern bartending: pineapple juice became popular with tiki (1930s-1960s), tomato juice with the Bloody Mary (1920s), cranberry with the Cosmopolitan (1990s), and passion fruit with the Pornstar Martini (2000s). Each juice has its golden era in cocktail history.
wiki.art.mixers.juices.production: Pineapple: juice fresh pineapple (best) or use canned unsweetened juice (Dole). Cranberry: always packaged (Ocean Spray or equivalent — fresh cranberry is too acidic to juice). Tomato: quality packaged (Clamato for Michelada). Passion fruit: frozen purée (Funkin, Boiron) or fresh maracuyá pulp. Pomegranate: for real grenadine, reduce pomegranate juice with sugar 1:1. Peach: fresh purée for an authentic Bellini.
wiki.art.mixers.juices.tips: Fresh pineapple always beats canned, but Dole is acceptable. Pure cranberry juice is too acidic — use cranberry cocktail (with some sugar). For Bloody Mary: tomato juice is only the base — the magic is in the spices (Worcestershire, Tabasco, horseradish, celery, salt, pepper). Frozen passion fruit purée is consistent and practical. Homemade grenadine (pomegranate + sugar) vs. the artificial (Rose's) are completely different products. Keep open juices 3-5 days maximum refrigerated.
wiki.art.mixers.juices.types: Pineapple (fresh or canned — Piña Colada, Mai Tai, Jungle Bird, Singapore Sling). Cranberry (Cosmopolitan, Sea Breeze, Cape Codder). Tomato (Bloody Mary, Michelada — always quality packaged). Passion fruit (Pornstar Martini, Hurricane — pulp or purée). Apple (Apple Martini, Calvados cocktails). Pomegranate (real grenadine, Tequila Sunrise). Peach (Bellini — ideally fresh purée).
wiki.art.mixers.juices.cocktails: PINEAPPLE: Piña Colada, Jungle Bird, Singapore Sling, Painkiller. CRANBERRY: Cosmopolitan, Sea Breeze, Bay Breeze, Madras. TOMATO: Bloody Mary, Bloody Caesar, Michelada, Red Snapper. PASSION FRUIT: Pornstar Martini, Hurricane, Passion Fruit Martini. APPLE: Apple Martini, Calvados Sour. POMEGRANATE: homemade grenadine for Tequila Sunrise, Jack Rose, Singapore Sling.
wiki.art.mixers.soda-water.sub: The most essential and underrated mixer
wiki.art.mixers.soda-water.description: Soda water (club soda, seltzer) is the most fundamental mixer in bartending — it brings effervescence, dilution, and freshness without adding flavor. It is the ingredient that turns a stirred cocktail into a refreshing long drink. Without soda there is no Collins, Fizz, Spritz, Highball, or Mojito. Carbonation quality matters enormously — flat soda ruins any cocktail.
wiki.art.mixers.soda-water.origin: 1767: Joseph Priestley (England) discovers how to artificially carbonate water. 1783: Johann Jacob Schweppe commercializes the first carbonated water in Geneva, Switzerland — founding Schweppes. 1800s: American soda fountains become social hubs. Soda is adopted in bartending to create Collins, Fizzes, and Rickeys. Today: SodaStream and professional soda machines allow at-home and in-bar carbonation.
wiki.art.mixers.soda-water.production: Purified water is carbonated by injecting CO₂ at high pressure (3-4 volumes of CO₂). Club soda: minerals (sodium bicarbonate, potassium chloride, sodium sulfate) are added for a neutral-mineral taste. Seltzer: only water + CO₂, nothing else. Professional siphon: a CO₂ cartridge pressurizes the water on the spot. Soda machines (SodaStream): carbonate tap water with compressed CO₂.
wiki.art.mixers.soda-water.tips: ALWAYS add the soda at the end and DO NOT shake — it destroys the carbonation. Pour gently down the side of the glass. Use freshly opened soda (it loses fizz in minutes). A professional siphon is the best investment for a bar — always fresh carbonation. Topo Chico has the best carbonation of any mineral water. Standard ratio: 1:2-1:3 (spirit:soda). Soda has no flavor, but the absence of soda ruins a Collins.
wiki.art.mixers.soda-water.types: Soda water/club soda (carbonated water with added minerals — bicarbonate, sodium chloride — the most used in bars). Seltzer (pure carbonated water without added minerals — cleaner). Sparkling mineral water (Perrier, San Pellegrino — natural carbonation, spring minerals). Siphon soda (the classic bar siphon, strong pressure). Topo Chico (Mexican mineral water, intense carbonation, bartender favorite). For bartending, club soda or a professional siphon.
wiki.art.mixers.soda-water.cocktails: Tom Collins (gin, lemon, sugar, soda). Whiskey Highball (whisky, soda — the Japanese ritual). Mojito (rum, mint, lime, sugar, soda). Gin Fizz (gin, lemon, sugar, soda — shaken, no ice, soda at the end). Aperol Spritz (Aperol, prosecco, splash of soda). Paloma (tequila, grapefruit, lime, soda). Americano (Campari, sweet vermouth, soda). Vodka Soda (the simplest long drink in the world).
wiki.art.mixers.syrups.description: Syrups are the backbone of balance in bartending — they bring sweetness, texture, and flavor without diluting the cocktail. From simple syrup (sugar + water) to complex spice, flower, and fruit syrups, mastering syrups means mastering flavor balance. A professional bartender prepares their own; the difference from the industrial ones is immediate and noticeable.
wiki.art.mixers.syrups.origin: The use of syrups in drinks traces back to ancient Persia (sharbat, from the Arabic "sharab" = drink), which gave rise to the words "sorbet" and "syrup". Medieval apothecaries used medicinal syrups. In the 19th century, American bartenders adopted simple syrup as the standard sweetener for cocktails — replacing sugar cubes that didn't always dissolve well.
wiki.art.mixers.syrups.production: Simple syrup: 1:1 ratio (sugar:hot water), dissolve without boiling, cool, bottle. Rich simple syrup: 2:1 (denser, sweeter, longer shelf life). Demerara syrup: demerara sugar + water (molasses notes, perfect for Old Fashioneds). Honey syrup: honey + hot water 1:1 (pure honey is too viscous). Flavored syrups: infuse simple syrup with spices, herbs, or fruits during preparation. All last 2-4 weeks refrigerated (adding 1 oz of vodka extends to 1 month).
wiki.art.mixers.syrups.tips: Prepare fresh syrups weekly — the difference from industrial ones is huge. Simple syrup 1:1 dissolves better than 2:1 in cold cocktails. Honey syrup always diluted (1:1 with water); pure honey doesn't mix well cold. Label with the preparation date. Add 1 oz of vodka per bottle as preservative. Real grenadine (pomegranate + sugar) vs. artificial (red coloring) are completely different products. Invest in squeeze bottles to dispense syrups accurately.
wiki.art.mixers.syrups.types: Simple syrup 1:1 (universal standard, base for everything). Rich syrup 2:1 (more body, less dilution). Demerara syrup (for Old Fashioned, Jungle Bird). Honey syrup (for Bee's Knees, Penicillin, Gold Rush). Agave syrup (for Margaritas, Palomas — complements tequila). Orgeat (almond, for Mai Tai, Japanese Cocktail). Real grenadine (reduced pomegranate, for Jack Rose, Tequila Sunrise). Falernum (Caribbean spices, lime, almond — for tiki). Cinnamon, lavender, rosemary, ginger syrups — the possibilities are endless.
wiki.art.mixers.syrups.cocktails: Old Fashioned (rich demerara syrup). Whiskey Sour (simple syrup). Daiquiri (simple syrup). Bee's Knees (honey syrup). Penicillin (honey-ginger syrup). Mai Tai (orgeat). Margarita (agave syrup). Jack Rose (grenadine). Tom Collins (simple syrup). Zombie (falernum + grenadine). The syrup defines the cocktail's character — simple syrup is neutral, demerara adds depth, honey adds texture.
wiki.art.mixers.tonic-water.description: Tonic water is a carbonated drink with quinine that transforms simple spirits into sophisticated cocktails. Originating as an antimalarial medicine in British colonial India, today it is the most important mixer in global bartending. The premium tonic revolution (Fever-Tree, 1724, East Imperial) proved the mixer matters as much as the spirit — a great gin with bad tonic is a bad Gin & Tonic.
wiki.art.mixers.tonic-water.origin: British India, 19th century. British soldiers and colonists drank quinine dissolved in carbonated water to prevent malaria. The bitter taste was unpleasant, so they began to add gin, sugar, and lime — and the Gin & Tonic was born. The first commercial tonic was produced by Schweppes in London in 1870.
wiki.art.mixers.tonic-water.production: Purified water is carbonated with high-pressure CO₂. Quinine (cinchona bark extract, Cinchona officinalis) is added as the bittering agent — the amount is regulated by law (max 83 mg/liter in the EU). Sweetened with sugar, agave syrup, or artificial sweeteners. Premium tonics use natural quinine from Africa or South America and cane sugar; industrial ones use synthetic quinine and corn syrup.
wiki.art.mixers.tonic-water.tips: The spirit-to-tonic ratio is crucial — 1:2 for intense flavor, 1:3 for refreshing. Always pour the tonic down the side of the glass (never directly on the ice) to preserve carbonation. Use freshly opened tonic — it loses fizz within hours. Fever-Tree Indian with London Dry gin; Mediterranean tonic with botanical gins. Tonic glows under UV light thanks to the quinine — a great trick to impress guests. Serve in a balloon glass with lots of ice.
